Esophagitis

Pathophysiology

Various causes damage the mucosa, leading to inflammation of the esophagus.

  1. Injury to the mucosaPills, caustics, allergens, infection, or reflux
  2. InflammationOf the esophagus
  3. Mucosal damageCan deepen or scar

What the injury does

  • AMucosal inflammationDamaged mucosa → odynophagia, heartburn, and chest pain
  • BUlcersDeeper injury → bleeding, with hematemesis and melena
  • CStricturesHealing narrows the lumen → dysphagia and obstruction
  • DPerforationFull-thickness injury → pneumomediastinum and mediastinitis
  • EBarrett esophagusChronic injury → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → esophageal adenocarcinoma

Etiology

  • Swallowed
  • 1Pill-inducedNSAIDs, KCl, doxycycline, and bisphosphonates; pills lodge in the mid-esophagus, where the aortic arch or an enlarged left atrium narrows it, especially when taken lying down with little water
  • 2CausticStrong alkali causes liquefactive necrosis that penetrates deeply; strong acid causes coagulative necrosis, more superficial, with skip lesions
  • 3EosinophilicAn allergic reaction to food and air antigens, with asthma, allergic rhinitis, or atopic dermatitis
  • Infection
  • 4InfectiousImpaired cell-mediated immunity, as with HIV, chemotherapy, or corticosteroids: Candida in 88%, HSV in 10%, and CMV in 2%
  • From the stomach
  • 5Reflux-associatedGERD; conditions that are nonresponsive to PPIs

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms

  • Dysphagia
  • Odynophagia
  • Heartburn
  • Chest pain
  • Food impaction

Complications

  • Strictures and ulcers
  • Obstruction
  • Bleedinghematemesis and melena
  • Perforationpneumomediastinum and mediastinitis
  • Aspirationpneumonia

Barrett esophagus

  1. Intestinal metaplasia
  2. Dysplasia
  3. Esophageal adenocarcinoma

Diagnosis

  1. EGD with biopsyProximal, mid, and distal esophagus
  2. Endoscopic patternPoints to the cause
  3. HistologyConfirms it
  • 1Pill-inducedAn ulcer in the middle third, at the aortic arch or left atrium; symptoms within hours to 10 days of the pill
  • 2CausticEGD within 24 hours grades the injury and predicts strictures; after 96 hours, friable tissue risks perforation
  • 3EosinophilicRings, longitudinal furrows, white exudates, and strictures; 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field; biopsy after an 8-week PPI trial to separate it from GERD
  • 4InfectiousCandida: white plaques that do not wash off; HSV: small, deep ulcers, with multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry type A inclusions; CMV: large, shallow ulcers, with intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions
  • 5Reflux-associatedWorked up as GERD

If there is a complication

  • BleedingEGD with biopsy
  • PerforationContrast esophagram and CXR, followed by surgery

Note: Endoscopy is normal in up to 10% of eosinophilic esophagitis, so biopsies are taken even when the mucosa looks normal.

Treatment

Always give PPIs for esophagitis to prevent further mucosal damage, then treat the cause.

  • 1Pill-inducedStop the offending drug; take pills with at least 6 oz of water and stay upright for 30 minutes
  • 2CausticSecure the airway, NPO, EGD within 24 hours to grade the injury, do not induce vomiting, and surgery for perforation; strictures are the main late complication
  • 3EosinophilicA PPI first; then elimination of trigger foods (cow's milk, wheat, peanuts and tree nuts, egg, soy, and seafood) or swallowed topical steroids, fluticasone or budesonide, for 8 weeks; dilation of strictures once treated
  • 4InfectiousCandida: oral fluconazole for 14–21 days, always systemic rather than topical; antivirals for HSV and CMV
  • 5Reflux-associatedTreat

Review article

Esophagitis: routes of mucosal injury and relationships to other foregut disease

Esophagitis is inflammation of the esophagus that follows mucosal damage from pills, caustics, allergens, infection, or reflux. The route of injury largely determines management, and endoscopy with biopsy identifies the cause by its pattern and histology. Presentation is dominated by dysphagia, odynophagia, heartburn, chest pain, and, in eosinophilic disease, food impaction, and the principal threats are bleeding, perforation, strictures, and progression through Barrett esophagus to adenocarcinoma. Here, we review the etiology, diagnosis, complications, and management of esophagitis, and consider how it relates to GERD, esophageal motility disorders, gastritis, and PUD.

Key points

  • Esophagitis is a common endpoint of mucosal injury, and identifying the cause determines treatment.
  • Pills lodge in the mid-esophagus, alkali penetrates deeper than acid, and infection follows impaired cell-mediated immunity.
  • EGD with biopsy separates the causes: white plaques in Candida, small deep ulcers in HSV, large shallow ulcers in CMV, and 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field in eosinophilic esophagitis.
  • PPIs are given in all cases, while caustic ingestion requires EGD within 24 hours and no induced vomiting.
  • Odynophagia favors esophagitis over GERD and motility disorders.

Pathophysiology

Pills, caustics, allergens, infection, and reflux all injure the esophageal mucosa, and the resulting inflammation causes odynophagia, heartburn, and chest pain. Deeper injury forms ulcers that bleed, with hematemesis and melena, and healing can narrow the lumen, causing strictures with dysphagia and obstruction. Full-thickness injury perforates, causing pneumomediastinum and mediastinitis, and chronic injury can progress through intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Etiology and mechanisms

Causes are best grouped by how injury reaches the mucosa. Pills, including NSAIDs, KCl, doxycycline, and bisphosphonates, lodge in the mid-esophagus, where the aortic arch or an enlarged left atrium narrows it, especially when taken lying down with little water. Strong alkali causes liquefactive necrosis that penetrates deeply, whereas strong acid causes coagulative necrosis that is more superficial, with skip lesions. Eosinophilic esophagitis is an allergic reaction to food and air antigens, in patients with asthma, allergic rhinitis, or atopic dermatitis. Infection follows impaired cell-mediated immunity, as with HIV, chemotherapy, or corticosteroids, and is due to Candida in 88%, HSV in 10%, and CMV in 2%. Reflux-associated disease arises from GERD, including conditions nonresponsive to PPIs.

Clinical presentation and complications

Patients present with dysphagia, odynophagia, heartburn, and chest pain, and eosinophilic esophagitis often presents with food impaction. Complications include bleeding (hematemesis, melena), perforation (pneumomediastinum, mediastinitis), strictures and ulcers, obstruction, and aspiration pneumonia. Barrett esophagus may also develop, in which intestinal metaplasia progresses through dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Diagnosis

EGD with biopsies of the proximal, mid, and distal esophagus identifies the cause by its endoscopic pattern, and histology confirms it. Pill injury produces an ulcer in the middle third, at the aortic arch or left atrium, with symptoms within hours to 10 days of the pill. In caustic ingestion, EGD within 24 hours grades the injury and predicts strictures, whereas after 96 hours friable tissue risks perforation. Eosinophilic esophagitis shows rings, longitudinal furrows, white exudates, and strictures, with 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, and biopsy after an 8-week PPI trial separates it from GERD; endoscopy is normal in up to 10%, so biopsies are taken even when the mucosa looks normal.

Candida produces white plaques that do not wash off, HSV small, deep ulcers with multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry type A inclusions, and CMV large, shallow ulcers with intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions. Reflux-associated disease is worked up as GERD. Bleeding is evaluated by EGD with biopsy, and perforation by contrast esophagram and CXR, followed by surgery.

Management

PPIs are given in all cases to prevent further mucosal damage, followed by treatment of the cause. Offending pills are stopped, and pills are taken with at least 6 oz of water, staying upright for 30 minutes. Caustic ingestion requires securing the airway, NPO, EGD within 24 hours to grade the injury, avoidance of induced vomiting, and surgery for perforation, and strictures are the main late complication. Eosinophilic esophagitis is treated first with a PPI, then with elimination of trigger foods (cow's milk, wheat, peanuts and tree nuts, egg, soy, and seafood) or swallowed topical fluticasone or budesonide for 8 weeks, and strictures are dilated once it is treated. Candida esophagitis is treated with oral fluconazole for 14–21 days, always systemic rather than topical, and HSV and CMV with antivirals. Reflux-associated disease is treated as GERD.

Relationships to other conditions

. Reflux is one cause of esophagitis, and the two share dysphagia, heartburn, chest pain, bleeding, perforation, aspiration, and Barrett esophagus. Odynophagia favors esophagitis and dyspepsia favors GERD, whereas rings, furrows, atopy, food impaction, and persistent eosinophils after a PPI trial favor eosinophilic esophagitis.

. These share dysphagia and aspiration but are neuromuscular rather than mucosal. Dysphagia to solids and liquids from onset favors a motility disorder, for which manometry is the gold standard. Scleroderma links the two, as a weak LES promotes reflux.

and PUD. NSAIDs cause all three by different mechanisms: a lodged pill injures the esophagus directly, whereas COX inhibition injures the stomach. Pain on swallowing favors esophagitis, and epigastric pain that changes with meals favors PUD. Perforation produces pneumomediastinum in esophagitis, assessed by contrast esophagram and CXR, and pneumoperitoneum in PUD, assessed by upright CXR. Intestinal metaplasia is common to both, but Barrett esophagus leads to esophageal adenocarcinoma, whereas chronic H. pylori infection leads to gastric cancer.

Cardiac disease. As chest pain overlaps with cardiac causes, an ECG should be obtained first.

Viral hepatitis. CMV and HSV also cause hepatitis in immunocompromised patients.

Esophageal Motility Disorders

Pathophysiology

Neuromuscular dysfunctions of the esophagus cause dysphagia.

  1. Neuromuscular dysfunctionOf nerves or smooth muscle
  2. Abnormal motilityIn the LES or mid-distal esophagus
  3. DysphagiaFood does not pass normally

What the dysfunction does

  • AFailed LES relaxationDecreased NO and VIP → increased LES tone, as in achalasia
  • BDisorganized contractionsUncoordinated mid-distal motility → dysphagia, as in diffuse esophageal spasm
  • CAtrophy and fibrosisWeakened smooth muscle → decreased LES tone and motility, as in scleroderma
  • DRetained foodStasis in the esophagus → aspiration pneumonia and cancer

Etiology

  • 1AchalasiaIdiopathic or Trypanosoma cruzi → decreased myenteric plexus activity → decreased NO and VIP neurotransmitter activity → increased LES tone and decreased mid-distal esophageal motility
  • 2Diffuse esophageal spasmTrigger, possibly increased ACh release → simultaneous, premature contractions → disorganized mid-distal esophageal motility
  • 3Esophageal sclerodermaSystemic sclerosis, often limited (CREST): atrophy and fibrosis of the distal smooth muscle → decreased LES tone and decreased mid-distal esophageal motility; proximal motility is preserved

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms

  • Dysphagia to solids and liquids
  • Regurgitation
  • Chest pain
  • Weight loss
  • Heartburn

By disorder

  • 1AchalasiaProgressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation, and weight loss; heartburn in 27–42%, often mistreated as GERD
  • 2Diffuse esophageal spasmEpisodic chest pain and intermittent dysphagia, set off by eating quickly or by hot or cold drinks; the pain can mimic angina
  • 3Esophageal sclerodermaSevere reflux; CREST: calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia

Complications

  • Aspirationpneumonia
  • Cancersquamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma in achalasia

Note: Reflux symptoms that persist despite PPIs should raise suspicion of achalasia.

Diagnosis

  1. Barium swallowFirst test
  2. EGDExcludes pseudoachalasia from cancer
  3. Manometry Gold standardHigh-resolution, Chicago classification
  • 1AchalasiaBarium: a bird's beak with a dilated esophagus; manometry: IRP over 15 mm Hg with absent peristalsis; type I without pressurization, type II with panesophageal pressurization, and type III with premature, spastic contractions
  • 2Diffuse esophageal spasmBarium: a corkscrew or rosary-bead esophagus; manometry: premature contractions in 20% or more of swallows
  • 3Esophageal sclerodermaManometry: weak distal peristalsis and low LES pressure, with proximal motility preserved

Other causes of dysphagia

ForFavored byObtain
PseudoachalasiaA tumor at the gastroesophageal junction or fundusEGD
Zenker diverticulumOlder men; regurgitation of food, halitosis, aspiration, and food sticking in the throatBarium swallow; manometry is unhelpful
Schatzki ringIntermittent dysphagia to solids, or food impactionBarium swallow and EGD
Plummer-Vinson syndromeMiddle-aged women with iron-deficiency anemia and postcricoid dysphagiaIron studies and EGD for an upper esophageal web
Eosinophilic esophagitisAtopy and food impactionEGD with biopsy

Note: Zenker diverticulum is a false diverticulum, herniating through the Killian triangle between the cricopharyngeus and the inferior pharyngeal constrictor.

Treatment

  • 1AchalasiaPneumatic dilation, first line for most types, or myotomy: Heller with a partial fundoplication, or POEM, preferred for type III; CCB, nitrates, or botulinum injection if unfit for these; type II responds best and type III least
  • 2Diffuse esophageal spasmCCB or nitrates; pneumatic dilation or botulinum injection are other options
  • 3Esophageal sclerodermaPPIs; avoid Nissen fundoplication

Other causes of dysphagia

  • Zenker diverticulumCricopharyngeal myotomy with diverticulectomy, open or endoscopic
  • Schatzki ringDilation, then a PPI to prevent recurrence
  • Plummer-Vinson syndromeIron replacement, and dilation of the web if needed; watch for squamous cell carcinoma

Review article

Esophageal motility disorders: neuromuscular failure of the LES and esophageal body

Esophageal motility disorders are neuromuscular dysfunctions of the esophagus that cause dysphagia. Achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm, and esophageal scleroderma are separated by the state of the LES and the pattern of mid-distal motility, seen on barium swallow and defined by high-resolution manometry, the gold standard. Endoscopy excludes pseudoachalasia, and structural causes of dysphagia, including Zenker diverticulum, Schatzki ring, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, and eosinophilic esophagitis, must be distinguished. Complications include aspiration pneumonia and cancer. Here, we review their mechanisms, diagnosis, and treatment, and consider how they relate to esophagitis and GERD.

Key points

  • LES tone separates the disorders: increased in achalasia and decreased in esophageal scleroderma.
  • Achalasia causes progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, a bird's beak on barium swallow, and an IRP over 15 mm Hg with absent peristalsis on manometry.
  • Diffuse esophageal spasm causes episodic chest pain and a corkscrew esophagus.
  • EGD excludes pseudoachalasia from a tumor at the gastroesophageal junction.
  • Achalasia is treated by disrupting the LES, whereas scleroderma is treated with PPIs and Nissen fundoplication is avoided.

Pathophysiology

Neuromuscular dysfunction in the LES or mid-distal esophagus stops food passing normally, causing dysphagia. In achalasia, decreased NO and VIP raise LES tone; in diffuse esophageal spasm, mid-distal contractions become uncoordinated; and in scleroderma, atrophy and fibrosis weaken smooth muscle, decreasing LES tone and motility. Food that stays in the esophagus predisposes to aspiration pneumonia and cancer.

Etiology and mechanisms

Achalasia is idiopathic or due to Trypanosoma cruzi. Decreased myenteric plexus activity lowers NO and VIP neurotransmitter activity, which increases LES tone and decreases mid-distal esophageal motility. In diffuse esophageal spasm, a trigger, possibly increased ACh release, produces simultaneous, premature contractions and disorganized mid-distal motility. In esophageal scleroderma, systemic sclerosis, often the limited form (CREST), causes atrophy and fibrosis of the distal smooth muscle, decreasing LES tone and mid-distal motility while proximal motility is preserved.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation, chest pain, weight loss, and heartburn. Achalasia causes progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation, and weight loss, with heartburn in 27–42% that is often mistreated as GERD, so reflux symptoms that persist despite PPIs should raise suspicion of achalasia. Diffuse esophageal spasm causes episodic chest pain and intermittent dysphagia, set off by eating quickly or by hot or cold drinks, and the pain can mimic angina. Esophageal scleroderma causes severe reflux, within CREST: calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasia. Complications are aspiration pneumonia and cancer, squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma in achalasia.

Diagnosis

Barium swallow is the first test, EGD excludes pseudoachalasia from cancer, and high-resolution manometry, interpreted by the Chicago classification, is the gold standard. Achalasia shows a bird's beak with a dilated esophagus on barium, and an IRP over 15 mm Hg with absent peristalsis on manometry: type I without pressurization, type II with panesophageal pressurization, and type III with premature, spastic contractions. Diffuse esophageal spasm shows a corkscrew or rosary-bead esophagus, with premature contractions in 20% or more of swallows, and esophageal scleroderma weak distal peristalsis and low LES pressure, with proximal motility preserved.

Other causes of dysphagia must be distinguished. Pseudoachalasia reflects a tumor at the gastroesophageal junction or fundus, found by EGD. Zenker diverticulum affects older men, with regurgitation of food, halitosis, aspiration, and food sticking in the throat, and is shown by barium swallow, as manometry is unhelpful; it is a false diverticulum herniating through the Killian triangle between the cricopharyngeus and the inferior pharyngeal constrictor. Schatzki ring causes intermittent dysphagia to solids or food impaction, shown by barium swallow and EGD. Plummer-Vinson syndrome affects middle-aged women with iron-deficiency anemia and postcricoid dysphagia, investigated with iron studies and EGD for an upper esophageal web, and eosinophilic esophagitis presents with atopy and food impaction, diagnosed by EGD with biopsy.

Management

Achalasia is treated with pneumatic dilation, first line for most types, or myotomy, Heller with a partial fundoplication or POEM, which is preferred for type III; CCB, nitrates, or botulinum injection are used if patients are unfit for these, and type II responds best and type III least. Diffuse esophageal spasm is treated with CCB or nitrates, with pneumatic dilation or botulinum injection as other options. Esophageal scleroderma is treated with PPIs, and Nissen fundoplication is avoided. Zenker diverticulum is treated with cricopharyngeal myotomy and diverticulectomy, open or endoscopic, Schatzki ring with dilation followed by a PPI to prevent recurrence, and Plummer-Vinson syndrome with iron replacement and dilation of the web if needed, with surveillance for squamous cell carcinoma.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both cause dysphagia and aspiration, but motility disorders are neuromuscular rather than mucosal. Dysphagia to solids and liquids from onset favors a motility disorder, whereas odynophagia favors esophagitis, and food impaction with atopy favors eosinophilic esophagitis.

. Achalasia and scleroderma are opposites at the LES, and scleroderma behaves like severe GERD because low LES tone permits reflux. Treatments are therefore opposed: Heller myotomy lowers LES pressure and Nissen fundoplication tightens it, so each would worsen the other condition, and achalasia should be suspected when reflux symptoms persist despite PPIs.

Autoimmune liver disease. Scleroderma (CREST) is associated with PBC.

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)

Pathophysiology

HCl enters the esophagus, causing mucosal damage.

  1. Weak barrier or high pressureDecreased LES tone, hiatal hernia, or increased intragastric pressure
  2. HCl enters the esophagusMore so with increased HCl production
  3. Mucosal damageCan progress to Barrett esophagus

What the reflux does

  • AFailed barrierDecreased LES tone or a hiatal hernia lets HCl pass
  • BRaised pressureIncreased intragastric pressure pushes HCl upward
  • CMucosal injuryHCl damages the esophagus → heartburn, dyspepsia, and chest pain
  • DBarrett esophagusChronic injury → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → esophageal adenocarcinoma
  • EAspirationRefluxed HCl reaches the airway → aspiration pneumonia

Etiology

  • 1Decreased LES toneTransient LES relaxations or a low resting pressure; smoking, alcohol, and caffeine; drugs such as nitrates, CCB, anticholinergics, theophylline, and morphine
  • 2Hiatal herniasSliding hernias (type I), over 95%; paraesophageal hernias (types II–IV) can also cause volvulus and strangulation
  • 3Increased HCl productionSmoking, alcohol, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
  • 4Increased intragastric pressureObesity, gastroparesis, and pregnancy

Note: Aspirin and other NSAIDs are also risk factors for GERD.

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms

  • Heartburn
  • Regurgitation
  • Dysphagia
  • Dyspepsia
  • Chest pain

Extraesophageal

  • Chronic cough
  • Asthma
  • Laryngitis and hoarseness
  • Sore throat
  • Dental erosions

Complications

  • Bleedinghematemesis and melena
  • Perforationpneumomediastinum and mediastinitis
  • Strictureprogressive dysphagia
  • Obstruction
  • Aspirationpneumonia

Barrett esophagus

  1. Intestinal metaplasia
  2. Dysplasia
  3. Esophageal adenocarcinoma
  • Defined bySalmon-colored mucosa 1 cm or more above the gastroesophageal junction, with goblet cells
  • Risk factorsMen, White, over 50, central obesity, smoking, and a family history; screen if chronic reflux comes with 3 or more
  • Cancer riskFewer than 5% develop adenocarcinoma

Diagnosis

  1. ECGIf there is chest pain
  2. Alarm features?EGD first if present
  3. PPI trial8 weeks, before the first meal
  4. EGD and pH monitoringIf there is no improvement

Alarm features

  • Dysphagia
  • Odynophagia
  • Anemia
  • Weight loss
  • Hematemesis or melena

Tests

  • Ambulatory pH monitoringThe only test of abnormal acid exposure: a wireless capsule for 48–96 hours, or 24-hour pH-impedance
  • ManometryBefore antireflux surgery, to exclude achalasia or a scleroderma-like esophagus
  • Barium swallowStrictures, hiatal hernia, and tumors; little role in uncomplicated reflux

If there is a complication

  • BleedingEGD with biopsy
  • PerforationContrast esophagram and CXR, followed by surgery

Treatment

Always prescribe PPIs or H2R antagonists.

Lifestyle

  • Weight loss
  • Raise the head of the bed
  • No meals 2–3 hours before bed
  • Avoid chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, and spicy food
  • Stop smoking

Medicines and surgery

  • PPIStandard dose before the first meal, for 8 weeks
  • Nighttime symptomsAdd a bedtime H2RA
  • On NSAIDsStop the offending drug
  • Refractory to treatmentNissen fundoplication, after manometry; avoided in scleroderma
  • Paraesophageal herniaSurgical repair; emergency surgery for volvulus or incarceration

Barrett surveillance

  • No dysplasiaEGD every 5 years if under 3 cm, every 3 years if 3 cm or more
  • Indefinite dysplasiaRepeat EGD in 6 months on twice-daily PPI
  • Low- or high-grade dysplasiaEndoscopic eradication, such as radiofrequency ablation

Review article

Gastroesophageal reflux disease: failure of the antireflux barrier and its consequences

GERD occurs when HCl enters the esophagus and causes mucosal damage. Reflux is favored by decreased LES tone, including transient LES relaxations, hiatal hernia, increased HCl production, and increased intragastric pressure. Symptoms are heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia, dyspepsia, and chest pain, with extraesophageal symptoms such as cough, asthma, and laryngitis, and the main long-term concern is Barrett esophagus. Here, we review its causes, stepwise diagnosis, and treatment, and consider how it relates to esophagitis, motility disorders, and PUD.

Key points

  • Four mechanisms drive reflux: decreased LES tone, hiatal hernia, increased HCl production, and increased intragastric pressure.
  • Chest pain requires an ECG, and alarm features require EGD before a PPI trial.
  • Failure of an 8-week PPI trial leads to EGD and ambulatory pH monitoring, the only test of abnormal acid exposure.
  • Barrett esophagus is salmon-colored mucosa 1 cm or more above the gastroesophageal junction with goblet cells, surveyed every 3–5 years without dysplasia.

Pathophysiology

Decreased LES tone or a hiatal hernia lets HCl pass into the esophagus, and increased intragastric pressure pushes it upward, more so when HCl production is increased. The HCl damages the esophagus, causing heartburn, dyspepsia, and chest pain. Chronic injury can progress through intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma, and refluxed HCl that reaches the airway causes aspiration pneumonia.

Etiology and mechanisms

LES tone is decreased by transient LES relaxations or a low resting pressure, by smoking, alcohol, and caffeine, and by drugs such as nitrates, CCB, anticholinergics, theophylline, and morphine. Hiatal hernias promote reflux; sliding hernias (type I) make up over 95%, and paraesophageal hernias (types II–IV) can also cause volvulus and strangulation. HCl production is increased by smoking, alcohol, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and aspirin and other NSAIDs are also risk factors. Intragastric pressure is increased by obesity, gastroparesis, and pregnancy.

Clinical presentation and complications

Patients present with heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia, dyspepsia, and chest pain, and extraesophageal symptoms include chronic cough, asthma, laryngitis and hoarseness, sore throat, and dental erosions. Complications are bleeding (hematemesis, melena), perforation (pneumomediastinum, mediastinitis), strictures with progressive dysphagia, obstruction, aspiration pneumonia, and Barrett esophagus, in which intestinal metaplasia progresses through dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Barrett esophagus is salmon-colored mucosa 1 cm or more above the gastroesophageal junction with goblet cells; its risk factors are male sex, White race, age over 50, central obesity, smoking, and a family history, screening is advised when chronic reflux comes with 3 or more, and fewer than 5% develop adenocarcinoma.

Diagnosis

Chest pain is first evaluated with an ECG. Alarm features, namely dysphagia, odynophagia, anemia, weight loss, and hematemesis or melena, call for EGD first; otherwise a PPI trial of 8 weeks, taken before the first meal, is initiated, and EGD with pH monitoring follows if there is no improvement. Ambulatory pH monitoring is the only test of abnormal acid exposure, by a wireless capsule for 48–96 hours or 24-hour pH-impedance. Manometry is performed before antireflux surgery to exclude achalasia or a scleroderma-like esophagus, and barium swallow shows strictures, hiatal hernia, and tumors but has little role in uncomplicated reflux. Bleeding is evaluated by EGD with biopsy, and perforation by contrast esophagram and CXR, followed by surgery.

Management

PPIs or H2R antagonists are always prescribed. Lifestyle measures are weight loss, raising the head of the bed, no meals 2–3 hours before bed, avoiding chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, and spicy food, and stopping smoking. A PPI is given at standard dose before the first meal for 8 weeks, and a bedtime H2RA is added for nighttime symptoms. Patients on NSAIDs stop the offending drug, refractory disease is treated with Nissen fundoplication after manometry, avoided in scleroderma, and a paraesophageal hernia is repaired surgically, as an emergency for volvulus or incarceration. In Barrett esophagus, EGD is repeated every 5 years without dysplasia if the segment is under 3 cm and every 3 years if 3 cm or more, in 6 months on twice-daily PPI for indefinite dysplasia, and low- or high-grade dysplasia is treated by endoscopic eradication, such as radiofrequency ablation.

Relationships to other conditions

. GERD is one cause of esophagitis, and the two share most symptoms and complications. Odynophagia favors esophagitis, and dyspepsia favors GERD.

. Scleroderma produces reflux through low LES tone, whereas achalasia has high LES tone and is often mistreated as GERD. Manometry confirms normal peristalsis before Nissen fundoplication, which is avoided in scleroderma.

. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome links the two through increased HCl production, NSAIDs are risk factors for both, and PPIs treat both.

Cardiac disease. Chest pain is presumed cardiac until proven otherwise, particularly with cardiovascular risk factors.

Gastritis

Pathophysiology

Damage to the stomach leads to inflammation of the stomach's mucosal lining.

Associated with:

  • Antrum
  • Shallow erosions
  • Shallow mucosal layers
  1. Damage to the stomachDrugs, infection, stress, or autoimmunity
  2. Mucosal inflammationOr atrophy in autoimmune gastritis
  3. Shallow erosionsDo not pass the muscularis mucosae

What the damage does

  • AWeakened mucus layerCOX inhibition → decreased PG → decreased mucus production
  • BIncreased HClNSAIDs, alcohol, H. pylori, and increased CN X activity → erosions
  • CMucosal ischemiaHypovolemia from severe burns → Curling ulcers
  • DParietal cell lossAutoantibodies → decreased HCl and IF → fundal atrophy

Etiology

  • Erosive
  • 1NSAIDs and alcoholCOX inhibition → decreased PG → increased HCl production and decreased mucus production
  • 2H. pyloriUrease makes ammonia, which shields it from acid; infection → increased gastrin production → increased HCl production
  • Stress
  • 3Curling ulcersSevere burns → hypovolemia → mucosal ischemia
  • 4Cushing ulcersIncreased ICP → increased CN X activity → increased submucosal activity → increased HCl production
  • Autoimmune
  • 5Autoimmune gastritisAutoantibodies attack parietal cells → decreased HCl and IF production → atrophy of the body and fundus, sparing the antrum, rather than inflammation or erosions; often with autoimmune thyroid disease

Note: Curling and Cushing ulcers are not true ulcers because they do not erode past the muscularis mucosae.

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms

  • Often none
  • Epigastric pain
  • Bloating, nausea, and vomiting
  • Bleeding from erosions: hematemesis or melena
  • Autoimmune: found through anemia

Autoimmune gastritis

  1. Parietal cell lossDecreased IF and HCl
  2. B12 malabsorptionOver 2–5 years
  3. Pernicious anemiaMacrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils
  4. Neurological damagePeripheral neuropathy, then subacute combined degeneration

Low acid also raises gastrin, which makes ECL cells grow and can cause a type 1 gastric carcinoid.

Complications

  • H. pylori and NSAIDs
  • Gastric adenocarcinomaH. pylori → atrophy → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia
  • Gastric MALT lymphomachronic H. pylori infection
  • Type 1 gastric carcinoidautoimmune gastritis, from high gastrin
  • Iron and B12 deficiencyatrophic gastritis
  • Hemorrhagestress gastritis without prophylaxis

Gastric adenocarcinoma

  • Intestinal type Most commonForms glands; H. pylori, atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, smoking, and salt-preserved, smoked, or N-nitroso foods
  • Diffuse typeNo cell adhesion (CDH1 mutations), signet ring cells; infiltrates the wall → linitis plastica (leather bottle stomach); blood group A
  • Metastatic signsVirchow node (left supraclavicular), Sister Mary Joseph nodule (umbilicus), Irish node (left axilla), Krukenberg tumor (ovary), Blumer shelf (pelvic cul-de-sac)
  • Paraneoplastic signsAcanthosis nigricans, diffuse seborrheic keratoses, and Trousseau syndrome

Ménétrier disease

  • MechanismExcess TGF-α activates EGFR → giant folds in the body and fundus, sparing the antrum
  • EffectsDecreased acid; protein loss → hypoalbuminemia and edema
  • WhoMostly men, median age 55; a self-limited form in children follows CMV
  • CourseProgressive and premalignant in adults

Diagnosis

  • DyspepsiaH. pylori testing: urea breath test, the most accurate noninvasive test, or stool antigen
  • Alarm features or age 60 or olderEGD with biopsies from 5 sites; alarm features are weight loss, bleeding, dysphagia, a mass, persistent vomiting, and family history of gastric cancer
  • Autoimmune gastritisAnti-parietal cell (sensitive) and anti-IF (specific) antibodies; body and fundus atrophy with intestinal metaplasia on biopsy; B12 and iron
  • Pernicious anemiaFBC: macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils; one-third have no macrocytosis
  • Ménétrier diseaseEGD: giant folds; deep biopsy if mucosal biopsy is normal; low albumin
  • After eradicationNoninvasive test 4–6 weeks after finishing ABX or PPI

Treatment

  • H. pylori gastritisEradicate (regimens on ), then confirm cure
  • NSAIDs or alcoholStop the cause; PPI
  • Critically ill (stress prophylaxis)PPI first line, H2R antagonist second line
  • H. pylori-negative dyspepsia, under 60Empiric PPI; then a prokinetic or tricyclic antidepressant
  • Autoimmune gastritisIM B12 1000 µg daily or alternate days for 1–2 weeks, then IM or high-dose oral B12 for life; replace iron; EGD every 3 years if atrophy is advanced
  • Gastric MALT lymphomaH. pylori eradication if t(11;18) negative (80% complete response); otherwise radiotherapy or systemic therapy
  • Ménétrier diseaseHigh-protein diet, PPI, and albumin; treat CMV or H. pylori; total gastrectomy if refractory

Review article

Gastritis: superficial mucosal injury and the boundary with peptic ulcer disease

Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach's mucosal lining following damage to the stomach, and is associated with the antrum, shallow erosions, and shallow mucosal layers. Causes include NSAIDs and alcohol, H. pylori, Curling and Cushing ulcers, and autoimmune gastritis. Here, we review these mechanisms and consider how gastritis relates to PUD.

Key points

  • NSAIDs and alcohol act through COX inhibition, and H. pylori through increased gastrin.
  • Curling ulcers follow severe burns, and Cushing ulcers follow increased ICP.
  • Autoimmune gastritis decreases HCl and IF, producing fundal atrophy rather than inflammation or erosions.
  • Autoimmune gastritis causes pernicious anemia through IF loss, and its high gastrin can cause a type 1 gastric carcinoid.
  • Chronic H. pylori gastritis leads to intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma, so it is always eradicated.

Pathophysiology

Damage to the stomach inflames the mucosa and forms shallow erosions that do not pass the muscularis mucosae. COX inhibition decreases PG and so decreases mucus production, while NSAIDs, alcohol, H. pylori, and increased CN X activity increase HCl. Hypovolemia from severe burns causes mucosal ischemia in Curling ulcers. In autoimmune gastritis, autoantibodies against parietal cells decrease HCl and IF, causing fundal atrophy rather than erosions.

Etiology and mechanisms

NSAIDs and alcohol cause COX inhibition, which decreases PG, increasing HCl production and decreasing mucus production. H. pylori infection increases gastrin production and therefore HCl production. In Curling ulcers, severe burns cause hypovolemia and mucosal ischemia. In Cushing ulcers, increased ICP increases CN X activity and submucosal activity, which increases HCl production. In autoimmune gastritis, autoantibodies attack parietal cells, decreasing HCl and IF production and causing fundal atrophy rather than inflammation or erosions. H. pylori survives gastric acid because its urease makes ammonia. Autoimmune gastritis affects the body and fundus and spares the antrum, and often accompanies autoimmune thyroid disease.

Clinical presentation and complications

Gastritis is often asymptomatic; otherwise it causes epigastric pain, bloating, nausea, and vomiting, and erosions can bleed with hematemesis or melena. Autoimmune gastritis is usually found through anemia: parietal cell loss decreases IF and HCl, B12 malabsorption develops over 2–5 years, and pernicious anemia follows, with macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils, then peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration. Low acid raises gastrin, which makes ECL cells grow and can cause a type 1 gastric carcinoid. Other complications are peptic ulcer from H. pylori and NSAIDs; gastric adenocarcinoma, as H. pylori leads to atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and dysplasia; gastric MALT lymphoma from chronic H. pylori infection; iron and B12 deficiency from atrophic gastritis; and hemorrhage in stress gastritis without prophylaxis. Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma, the most common, forms glands and is linked to H. pylori, atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, smoking, and salt-preserved, smoked, or N-nitroso foods. Diffuse-type adenocarcinoma lacks cell adhesion, often with CDH1 mutations, has signet ring cells, infiltrates the wall as linitis plastica, or leather bottle stomach, and is linked to blood group A. Metastatic signs are the Virchow node (left supraclavicular), Sister Mary Joseph nodule (umbilicus), Irish node (left axilla), Krukenberg tumor (ovary), and Blumer shelf (pelvic cul-de-sac); paraneoplastic signs are acanthosis nigricans, diffuse seborrheic keratoses, and Trousseau syndrome. In Ménétrier disease, excess TGF-α activates EGFR and causes giant folds in the body and fundus, sparing the antrum, with decreased acid and protein loss that leads to hypoalbuminemia and edema. It affects mostly men, at a median age of 55, is progressive and premalignant in adults, and has a self-limited form in children after CMV.

Diagnosis

Dyspepsia is evaluated with H. pylori testing, by urea breath test, the most accurate noninvasive test, or stool antigen. Alarm features (weight loss, bleeding, dysphagia, a mass, persistent vomiting, and family history of gastric cancer) or age 60 or older call for EGD with biopsies from 5 sites. Autoimmune gastritis shows anti-parietal cell antibodies, which are sensitive, and anti-IF antibodies, which are specific, with body and fundus atrophy and intestinal metaplasia on biopsy, and B12 and iron are checked. In pernicious anemia, the FBC shows macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils, though one-third have no macrocytosis. Ménétrier disease shows giant folds on EGD, confirmed by biopsy, which may need to be deep, with low albumin. Eradication is confirmed by a noninvasive test 4–6 weeks after finishing ABX or PPI.

Management

H. pylori gastritis is eradicated, using the regimens for PUD, and cure is confirmed. Gastritis from NSAIDs or alcohol is treated by stopping the cause and giving a PPI. Critically ill patients receive stress prophylaxis with a PPI first line or an H2R antagonist second line. H. pylori-negative dyspepsia under 60 is treated with an empiric PPI, then a prokinetic or tricyclic antidepressant. Autoimmune gastritis is treated with IM B12 1000 µg daily or on alternate days for 1–2 weeks, then IM or high-dose oral B12 for life, iron replacement, and EGD every 3 years if atrophy is advanced. Gastric MALT lymphoma is treated by H. pylori eradication if t(11;18) negative, with an 80% complete response, and otherwise by radiotherapy or systemic therapy. Ménétrier disease is treated with a high-protein diet, PPI, and albumin, treatment of CMV or H. pylori, and total gastrectomy if refractory.

A note on terminology

Curling and Cushing ulcers are not true ulcers because they do not erode past the muscularis mucosae.

Relationships to other conditions

. Depth is the boundary: gastritis stays superficial, whereas PUD extends beyond the muscularis mucosae. NSAIDs, alcohol, and H. pylori cause both.

Autoimmune vs H. pylori gastritis. Autoimmune gastritis targets the body and fundus, where parietal cells live, and causes low acid with high gastrin. H. pylori gastritis typically starts in the antrum. Autoimmune disease also leads to B12 deficiency and raises the risk of gastric carcinoid tumors.

. Autoimmune gastritis can accompany conditions such as Hashimoto thyroiditis and vitiligo.

Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)

Pathophysiology

Damage to the stomach leads to ulceration of the mucosal lining, which extends beyond the muscularis mucosae.

  1. Damage to the stomachH. pylori, NSAIDs, alcohol, or gastrinomas
  2. Mucosal breachAcid reaches deeper layers
  3. UlcerBeyond the muscularis mucosae

What the ulcer does

  • AWeakened barrierH. pylori, NSAIDs, and alcohol damage the mucosa and decrease mucus
  • BIncreased HClIncreased gastrin or decreased PG → more acid at the mucosa
  • CUlcer craterInjury passes the muscularis mucosae → epigastric pain
  • DVessel erosionThe ulcer reaches a vessel → bleeding, with hematemesis and melena

  • 1H. pylori Most commonGram-negative, urease-positive, and multiple flagella; lives in the gastric mucosa; causes 90% of duodenal and 70–90% of gastric ulcers; urease makes ammonia, which neutralizes acid around it

  • 2NSAIDs and alcohol 2nd most commonCOX inhibition → decreased PG → increased HCl production and decreased mucus production
  • 3GastrinomasConditions such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome → gastrin production → increased HCl production; 20–30% with MEN1; refractory or multiple ulcers, including jejunal ulcers, with diarrhea

Chronic H. pylori infection leads to

  2. Atrophy and intestinal metaplasia
  3. Dysplasia and gastric cancer

Review article

Peptic ulcer disease: H. pylori, NSAIDs, and the balance of acid and mucosal defense

PUD is ulceration of the mucosal lining that extends beyond the muscularis mucosae. H. pylori is the most common cause, followed by NSAIDs and alcohol, and gastrinomas are a less common cause. Gastric and duodenal ulcers have opposite pain patterns. Bleeding, perforation, and gastric outlet obstruction are the major complications. Here, we review its etiology, diagnosis, and management, and consider its relationship to gastritis, GERD, and cancer.

Key points

  • H. pylori is the most common cause, and first-line eradication is triple therapy.
  • Gastric ulcer pain worsens with eating; duodenal ulcer pain improves with eating and worsens with fasting.
  • Stop PPIs 2 weeks before H. pylori testing, and ABX and bismuth 4 weeks before.
  • If H. pylori is absent, check gastrin and then a secretin stimulation test.

Pathophysiology

H. pylori, NSAIDs, and alcohol damage the mucosa and decrease mucus, and increased gastrin or decreased PG brings more acid to it. Once injury passes the muscularis mucosae, an ulcer forms, causing epigastric pain. An ulcer that reaches a vessel bleeds, with hematemesis and melena, and full-thickness injury perforates, causing pneumoperitoneum and peritonitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

H. pylori is gram-negative and urease-positive, has multiple flagella, and lives in the gastric mucosa. Its virulence factors are ureases, cytotoxins (VacA, CagA), mucinases, phospholipases, and PAF. Chronic infection leads to gastritis, then atrophy and intestinal metaplasia, then dysplasia and gastric cancer, and to gastric MALT lymphoma. NSAIDs and alcohol, the second most common cause, act through COX inhibition, decreasing PG, increasing HCl production, and decreasing mucus production. Gastrinomas, as in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, increase gastrin production and therefore HCl production. H. pylori causes 90% of duodenal and 70–90% of gastric ulcers, and its urease makes ammonia, which neutralizes acid around it. Gastrinomas occur with MEN1 in 20–30%, and cause refractory or multiple ulcers, including jejunal ulcers, with diarrhea.

Clinical presentation and complications

Pain is epigastric, dull, and burning in both types; gastric ulcer pain is worse with eating and better with fasting, and duodenal ulcer pain is the reverse. Other symptoms are nausea, vomiting, heartburn, bloating, fullness, belching, and fatigue. Complications are bleeding (hematemesis, melena), perforation (pneumoperitoneum, peritonitis), gastric outlet obstruction (vomiting, pain, malnutrition, succussion splash), intestinal metaplasia, gastric cancer, and gastric MALT lymphoma. Gastric ulcers are usually on the lesser curvature, with pain 15–30 minutes after meals, and duodenal ulcers in the duodenal bulb, with pain 2–3 hours after meals and at night. A bleeding posterior duodenal ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery, and a lesser curvature ulcer the left gastric artery.

Diagnosis

Perforation is evaluated with an upright CXR, and bleeding with EGD with biopsy. H. pylori is detected by urea breath test, stool antigen test, rapid urease test, or histology. PPIs are stopped 2 weeks before testing, and ABX and bismuth 4 weeks before testing. If no H. pylori is detected, gastrin levels are checked, followed by a secretin stimulation test for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. EGD is the gold standard, used for age over 50 with new dyspepsia or for alarm features at any age. A fasting gastrin over 1000 pg/mL, 10 times normal, is diagnostic of gastrinoma, after stopping PPIs for 1 week; if it is equivocal, a paradoxical rise over 120 pg/mL after secretin confirms it, and MEN1 is screened with calcium, PTH, and prolactin.

Management

Perforation is treated with IV fluids, IV PPI, IV ABX, and surgery, and bleeding with IV fluids, IV PPI, EGD, and surgery. Acid is suppressed with antacids, H2R antagonists, and PPIs, and the mucosa is protected with misoprostol, sucralfate, and bismuth. First-line H. pylori eradication is triple therapy, bd for 7–14 days: PPI, amoxicillin (metronidazole if allergic), and clarithromycin. Alternative regimens are PPI, amoxicillin, and levofloxacin; PPI, metronidazole, tetracycline, and bismuth; and PPI, amoxicillin, and rifabutin. NSAID ulcers are treated by stopping the NSAID or lowering the dose, with misoprostol to prevent ulcers in those who must continue, and gastrinoma with a high-dose PPI and resection if localized. A refractory ulcer, over 5 mm and not healed after 8–12 weeks of PPI, prompts a search for persistent H. pylori, NSAIDs, gastrinoma, or cancer, then vagotomy or partial gastrectomy. Cure is confirmed by urea breath test 4–6 weeks after treatment.

Relationships to other conditions

. The two share causes, but PUD extends beyond the muscularis mucosae, whereas gastritis and Curling and Cushing ulcers do not.

and . All are treated with PPIs and can bleed. Perforation produces pneumoperitoneum here, assessed by upright CXR, and pneumomediastinum in the esophagus, assessed by contrast esophagram and CXR.

. Gastrinomas also cause chronic secretory diarrhea, so ulcers with diarrhea suggest Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Malignancy. Gastric ulcers can be malignant and are biopsied, whereas duodenal ulcers are rarely malignant. MEN1 links gastrinomas to .

Gastric Tumors

Pathophysiology

A chronic stimulus or mutation, such as H. pylori, high gastrin, or a KIT mutation, drives uncontrolled growth in one layer of the stomach wall, forming a mass that bleeds, obstructs, spreads, or secretes hormones.

  1. Chronic stimulus or mutationH. pylori, gastrin, or KIT
  2. Uncontrolled growthIn one layer of the wall
  3. MassMucosal or beneath the mucosa
  4. Bleeding, obstruction, or spreadOr hormone release

What the tumor does

  • ABleedingUlcerated tumor → melena, hematemesis, or occult loss → iron deficiency anemia
  • BObstructionTumor at the antrum or pylorus → early satiety and vomiting; at the cardia → dysphagia
  • CSpreadLymphatics → Virchow node; peritoneum → ascites and Krukenberg tumor; portal blood → liver
  • DHormonesNET → gastrin or serotonin; type 2 NET comes with ZES and peptic ulcers

Etiology

  • Benign
  • 1Polyps Most commonFundic gland polyps (most common; PPI use and FAP), hyperplastic polyps (H. pylori and atrophic gastritis), adenomas (precancerous), and hamartomas (Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and juvenile polyposis); over 90% are found incidentally
  • 2LeiomyomaBenign smooth muscle tumor of the muscularis propria; desmin and SMA positive, KIT and CD34 negative
  • 3LipomaSubmucosal fat; yellow and soft; no biopsy needed when EUS is typical
  • Malignant
  • 4AdenocarcinomaThe main gastric cancer: intestinal type from H. pylori through atrophy and metaplasia, or diffuse type with CDH1 loss; see below
  • 5LymphomaMALT lymphoma, driven by H. pylori in over 90%, or DLBCL; together nearly 90% of gastric lymphomas; most often in the antrum
  • 6SarcomaLeiomyosarcoma is exceptionally rare, about 1% of malignant gastric tumors; SMA positive, KIT and DOG1 negative
  • Malignant potential varies
  • 7GISTFrom the interstitial cells of Cajal in the muscularis propria; stomach in 60%; KIT (CD117) mutation in 75–80%, PDGFRA in 5–10%; DOG1 most specific; NF1 and Carney triad
  • 8NET (carcinoid)From ECL cells: type 1 with autoimmune gastritis and high gastrin (70–80%), type 2 with ZES and MEN1, type 3 sporadic and aggressive

4 Adenocarcinoma: how it develops

  1. H. pylori gastritisChronic inflammation
  2. Atrophic gastritisLoss of glands
  3. Intestinal metaplasiaUp to 10 times the risk
  4. DysplasiaPrecancerous
  5. Intestinal-type adenocarcinomaGland-forming mass or ulcer
  • Intestinal typeGlands; mass or nonhealing ulcer; precursor lesions (atrophic gastritis, metaplasia, pernicious anemia); H. pylori; more common in men; the most common type, now declining
  • Diffuse typeNo cell adhesion (CDH1, E-cadherin); signet ring cells; infiltrates the wall without a mass → linitis plastica (leather bottle stomach); no precursor lesion; equal in men and women; blood type A

4 Adenocarcinoma: risk factors

  • InfectionH. pylori; EBV (proximal stomach)
  • Diet and habitsHigh salt, smoked and cured foods, N-nitroso compounds, low vitamins A and C, no refrigeration, and smoking
  • Proximal and GEJ tumorsObesity and GERD; bile reflux after gastric surgery
  • Stomach diseaseAtrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, and gastric ulcers
  • InheritedCDH1 (hereditary diffuse gastric cancer), FAP (10% risk), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (29% risk), and blood type A

Note: Distal, intestinal-type cancer has fallen with better diet and H. pylori treatment, while proximal and GEJ cancers are rising.

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms

  • Often none (polyps, leiomyoma, lipoma, small NETs)
  • Dyspepsia and early satiety
  • Weight loss
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Dysphagia (proximal tumors)
  • Melena or hematemesis
  • Iron deficiency anemia
  • Epigastric mass
  • B symptoms (lymphoma)

4 Adenocarcinoma: signs of spread

  • Virchow nodeLeft supraclavicular node, reached through the thoracic duct
  • Sister Mary Joseph nodePeriumbilical nodule
  • Irish nodeLeft axillary node
  • Krukenberg tumorSignet ring cell metastases to the ovaries, often bilateral
  • Blumer shelfMass in the rectouterine or rectovesical pouch
  • Ascites and hepatomegalyPeritoneal carcinomatosis and liver metastases
  • Skin signsLeser-Trélat sign (sudden, multiple seborrheic keratoses) and acanthosis nigricans

Complications

  • Bleedingadenocarcinoma, GIST, lymphoma, and hyperplastic polyps
  • Gastric outlet obstructionantral tumors; large polyps or lipomas
  • Perforation and fistulaadvanced adenocarcinoma; rare in lymphoma
  • Transformationadenoma → adenocarcinoma; MALT lymphoma → DLBCL in 2–8%
  • Tumor ruptureGIST, raising recurrence
  • Carcinoid syndromerare; NET with liver metastases

Diagnosis

  • +Any suspected gastric tumorEGD with biopsies; biopsy the surrounding mucosa for atrophy, metaplasia, and H. pylori
  • 1PolypsBiopsy or remove: fundic gland polyps over 1 cm, hyperplastic polyps over 0.5 cm, and all adenomas
  • 2, 3, 7Lesion beneath the mucosaEUS: GIST and leiomyoma are hypoechoic from the muscularis propria; a lipoma is homogeneously hyperechoic; EUS-guided FNA for tissue
  • 7GISTContrast CT, the first-line imaging, for size and spread to the liver and peritoneum; KIT (CD117) and DOG1 staining
  • 5LymphomaBiopsy with immunohistochemistry: MALT lymphoma cells are CD19, CD20, and CD79a positive and CD5, CD10, and cyclin D1 negative, with lymphoepithelial lesions; test for H. pylori and t(11;18); staging
  • 8NETSerum gastrin and gastric pH: high gastrin with low acid in type 1, high gastrin with high acid in type 2, normal gastrin in type 3; chromogranin A and synaptophysin on biopsy; Ki-67 grade; MEN1 screen (PTH, calcium, prolactin) in type 2; urinary 5-HIAA if carcinoid syndrome

4 Adenocarcinoma: diagnosis and staging

  1. EGD with multiple biopsiesBiopsy every suspicious ulcer; 7 biopsies raise sensitivity to 98%
  2. EUSDepth (T stage) and nodes; T1 may suit endoscopic resection
  3. CT chest, abdomen, and pelvisDistant metastases
  4. PET-CTIf CT shows no metastases
  5. Staging laparoscopyPeritoneal washings; finds peritoneal disease in up to 40%
  • HER2Amplified in 12–27%, which guides targeted treatment
  • Tumor markersCEA and CA 19-9 add little to diagnosis

Note: Any gastric ulcer that looks suspicious is biopsied, because cancer can present as a nonhealing ulcer.

Treatment

  • 1PolypsFundic gland: remove if over 1 cm; hyperplastic: eradicate H. pylori, after which most regress within a year, and remove if over 0.5 cm; adenoma: endoscopic resection, then EGD at 1 year and every 3–5 years
  • 2, 3Leiomyoma, lipomaNone if small and silent; excision or enucleation if symptomatic
  • 5MALT lymphomaH. pylori eradication, even if testing is negative (over 75% respond); confirm cure at 6 weeks and repeat EGD in 3–6 months; radiotherapy or rituximab if H. pylori negative or t(11;18) positive
  • 5DLBCLChemotherapy; it grows independently of H. pylori
  • 6SarcomaSurgical resection
  • 7GISTComplete (R0) resection without rupturing the tumor; adjuvant imatinib for high risk; imatinib first line if unresectable or metastatic
  • 8NETUnder 1 cm: surveillance; 1–2 cm: EMR or ESD; type 1: somatostatin analogs if multiple or recurrent; type 2: high-dose PPI and MEN1 care; type 3: gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy

4 Adenocarcinoma: treatment by stage

  • Confined to the mucosa or superficial submucosaEndoscopic resection (EMR or ESD) if there are no high-risk features
  • Deeper tumors or nodesPerioperative chemotherapy, then gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy (node stations 1–11)
  • Distal tumorsSubtotal (distal) gastrectomy
  • Proximal, extensive, or diffuse tumorsTotal gastrectomy, needed for signet ring cell histology
  • CDH1 germline mutationProphylactic total gastrectomy
  • Unresectable or metastaticPalliative chemotherapy; HER2-directed treatment if amplified; radiotherapy for palliation
  • PrognosisOver 50% of localized distal cancers are cured, but only 10–20% are found early in the United States; disseminated disease is almost never cured
  • ScreeningRoutine endoscopy in Japan and South Korea finds cancers early

Review article

Gastric tumors: from incidental polyps to adenocarcinoma, lymphoma, and tumors beneath the mucosa

Gastric tumors arise from every layer of the stomach wall: polyps, adenocarcinoma, neuroendocrine tumors, and lymphoma from the mucosa, lipomas from the submucosa, and leiomyomas, GISTs, and sarcomas from the muscularis propria. Most polyps and benign tumors beneath the mucosa are found incidentally, whereas adenocarcinoma, the main gastric cancer, usually presents late with weight loss, bleeding, or signs of spread. Chronic stimuli such as H. pylori and high gastrin, and mutations such as those of KIT and CDH1, link many of these tumors to their causes and treatments. Here, we review the pathophysiology, etiology, presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of gastric tumors, with particular attention to adenocarcinoma, and consider how they relate to gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Key points

  • Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma follows H. pylori gastritis through atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and dysplasia, whereas diffuse-type adenocarcinoma lacks cell adhesion from CDH1 loss, contains signet ring cells, and causes linitis plastica.
  • Adenocarcinoma spreads to the Virchow, Sister Mary Joseph, and Irish nodes, the ovaries as Krukenberg tumors, the rectal pouch as a Blumer shelf, the peritoneum, and the liver.
  • Adenocarcinoma is diagnosed by EGD with multiple biopsies and staged by EUS, CT, PET-CT, and staging laparoscopy; early tumors suit endoscopic resection, and deeper tumors need perioperative chemotherapy and gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy.
  • MALT lymphoma is driven by H. pylori in over 90% and responds to its eradication in over 75%, except when t(11;18) is present.
  • GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal with KIT or PDGFRA mutations, stain for KIT and DOG1, and are resected, with imatinib for high-risk or metastatic disease.
  • Type 1 gastric NETs arise from ECL cells driven by the high gastrin of autoimmune gastritis, type 2 from ZES with MEN1, and type 3 sporadically with aggressive behavior.

Pathophysiology

A chronic stimulus or mutation, such as H. pylori, high gastrin, or a KIT mutation, drives uncontrolled growth in one layer of the stomach wall and forms a mass, whether in the mucosa or beneath it. The mass can then cause harm in four ways. An ulcerated tumor bleeds, causing melena, hematemesis, or occult loss with iron deficiency anemia. A tumor at the antrum or pylorus obstructs the outlet, causing early satiety and vomiting, whereas one at the cardia causes dysphagia. Malignant tumors spread through lymphatics to the Virchow node, across the peritoneum to cause ascites and Krukenberg tumors, and through portal blood to the liver. Finally, NETs release hormones such as gastrin or serotonin, and type 2 NETs arise with ZES and its peptic ulcers.

Etiology

Polyps are the most common gastric tumors, and over 90% are found incidentally. Fundic gland polyps are the most common type and are linked to PPI use and FAP; hyperplastic polyps arise from the chronic inflammation of H. pylori and atrophic gastritis; adenomas are precancerous; and hamartomas occur in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and juvenile polyposis. Leiomyomas are benign smooth muscle tumors of the muscularis propria that stain for desmin and SMA but not for KIT or CD34, and lipomas are yellow, soft collections of submucosal fat that need no biopsy when their EUS appearance is typical.

Among malignant tumors, adenocarcinoma is the main gastric cancer. Gastric lymphomas are mostly MALT lymphoma, driven by H. pylori in over 90%, or DLBCL, which together make up nearly 90% and most often affect the antrum. Leiomyosarcoma is exceptionally rare, about 1% of malignant gastric tumors, and stains for SMA but not for KIT or DOG1. Two tumors have variable malignant potential. GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal in the muscularis propria, occur in the stomach in 60%, carry KIT (CD117) mutations in 75–80% and PDGFRA mutations in 5–10%, stain most specifically for DOG1, and occur in NF1 and the Carney triad. NETs, or carcinoids, arise from ECL cells: type 1 with autoimmune gastritis and high gastrin, making up 70–80%; type 2 with ZES and MEN1; and type 3 sporadically, with aggressive behavior.

Intestinal-type adenocarcinoma develops in steps: H. pylori causes chronic gastritis, which progresses to atrophic gastritis with loss of glands, then to intestinal metaplasia, which raises the risk up to 10 times, then to dysplasia, and finally to a gland-forming mass or ulcer. It is the most common type, follows precursor lesions such as atrophic gastritis, metaplasia, and pernicious anemia, is more common in men, and is declining. Diffuse-type adenocarcinoma has no cell adhesion because of CDH1 (E-cadherin) loss, contains signet ring cells, and infiltrates the wall without a mass, producing linitis plastica, the leather bottle stomach; it has no precursor lesion, affects men and women equally, and is linked to blood type A.

Risk factors for adenocarcinoma include infection with H. pylori or, for the proximal stomach, EBV; diets high in salt, smoked and cured foods, and N-nitroso compounds and low in vitamins A and C, with no refrigeration; and smoking. Obesity, GERD, and bile reflux after gastric surgery raise the risk of proximal and GEJ tumors. Atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, and gastric ulcers predispose, as do inherited factors: CDH1 mutations in hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, FAP with a 10% risk, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome with a 29% risk, and blood type A. Distal, intestinal-type cancer has fallen with better diet and treatment of H. pylori, while proximal and GEJ cancers are rising.

Symptoms and complications

Polyps, leiomyomas, lipomas, and small NETs often cause no symptoms. Otherwise, gastric tumors cause dyspepsia, early satiety, weight loss, nausea and vomiting, dysphagia with proximal tumors, melena or hematemesis, iron deficiency anemia, and an epigastric mass, and lymphoma can cause B symptoms. Adenocarcinoma often reveals itself by its spread: a left supraclavicular Virchow node, reached through the thoracic duct; a periumbilical Sister Mary Joseph node; a left axillary Irish node; Krukenberg tumors, signet ring cell metastases to the ovaries that are often bilateral; a Blumer shelf, a mass in the rectouterine or rectovesical pouch; ascites and hepatomegaly from peritoneal carcinomatosis and liver metastases; and skin signs, the Leser-Trélat sign of sudden, multiple seborrheic keratoses and acanthosis nigricans.

Complications include bleeding from adenocarcinoma, GISTs, lymphoma, and hyperplastic polyps; gastric outlet obstruction from antral tumors and large polyps or lipomas; perforation and fistula in advanced adenocarcinoma, which are rare in lymphoma; transformation of adenomas to adenocarcinoma and of MALT lymphoma to DLBCL in 2–8%; rupture of a GIST, which raises recurrence; and, rarely, carcinoid syndrome from a NET with liver metastases.

Diagnosis

Any suspected gastric tumor is examined by EGD with biopsies, including biopsies of the surrounding mucosa for atrophy, metaplasia, and H. pylori. Polyps are biopsied or removed, including fundic gland polyps over 1 cm, hyperplastic polyps over 0.5 cm, and all adenomas. Lesions beneath the mucosa are characterized by EUS, on which GISTs and leiomyomas are hypoechoic and arise from the muscularis propria, whereas a lipoma is homogeneously hyperechoic, and EUS-guided FNA obtains tissue. GISTs are imaged first with contrast CT, which shows their size and spread to the liver and peritoneum, and are confirmed by KIT (CD117) and DOG1 staining. Lymphoma is confirmed by biopsy with immunohistochemistry: MALT lymphoma cells are CD19, CD20, and CD79a positive and CD5, CD10, and cyclin D1 negative, with lymphoepithelial lesions, and testing for H. pylori and t(11;18) and staging follow. NETs are typed by serum gastrin and gastric pH, with high gastrin and low acid in type 1, high gastrin and high acid in type 2, and normal gastrin in type 3; biopsies stain for chromogranin A and synaptophysin and are graded by Ki-67, patients with type 2 tumors are screened for MEN1 with PTH, calcium, and prolactin, and urinary 5-HIAA is measured if carcinoid syndrome is suspected.

Adenocarcinoma is diagnosed by EGD with multiple biopsies, and every suspicious ulcer is biopsied, because cancer can present as a nonhealing ulcer; seven biopsies raise sensitivity to 98%. EUS then defines the depth, or T stage, and the nodes, since T1 tumors may suit endoscopic resection. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis looks for distant metastases, PET-CT follows if CT shows none, and staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings finds peritoneal disease in up to 40%. HER2 is amplified in 12–27% and guides targeted treatment, whereas tumor markers such as CEA and CA 19-9 add little to diagnosis.

Treatment

Fundic gland polyps are removed if over 1 cm. Hyperplastic polyps are treated by eradicating H. pylori, after which most regress within a year, and are removed if over 0.5 cm. Adenomas are resected endoscopically, with EGD at 1 year and every 3–5 years after. Leiomyomas and lipomas need no treatment when small and silent, but are excised or enucleated when symptomatic. MALT lymphoma is treated by eradicating H. pylori, even when testing is negative, with a response in over 75%; cure is confirmed at 6 weeks and EGD repeated in 3–6 months, and radiotherapy or rituximab is used when H. pylori is absent or t(11;18) is present. DLBCL grows independently of H. pylori and is treated with chemotherapy. Sarcomas are resected. GISTs are removed completely, without rupture, with adjuvant imatinib for high-risk tumors and imatinib as first-line treatment when unresectable or metastatic. NETs under 1 cm are watched, those of 1–2 cm are removed by EMR or ESD, type 1 tumors that are multiple or recurrent can be treated with somatostatin analogs, type 2 tumors need high-dose PPI and care of MEN1, and type 3 tumors need gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy.

Adenocarcinoma confined to the mucosa or superficial submucosa without high-risk features can be removed endoscopically by EMR or ESD. Deeper tumors and those with involved nodes are treated with perioperative chemotherapy and gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy, which removes node stations 1–11. Distal tumors are treated by subtotal gastrectomy, whereas proximal, extensive, or diffuse tumors need total gastrectomy, which signet ring cell histology requires, and carriers of a germline CDH1 mutation may have a prophylactic total gastrectomy. Unresectable or metastatic disease is treated with palliative chemotherapy, HER2-directed treatment when HER2 is amplified, and radiotherapy for palliation. Over 50% of localized distal cancers are cured, but only 10–20% of cancers in the United States are found early and disseminated disease is almost never cured, whereas routine endoscopy in Japan and South Korea finds cancers early.

Relationships to other conditions

. Chronic gastritis is the soil for three gastric tumors. H. pylori gastritis leads to intestinal-type adenocarcinoma through atrophy and metaplasia and to MALT lymphoma through chronic lymphoid stimulation, whereas autoimmune gastritis leads to type 1 NETs through the high gastrin of achlorhydria. Eradicating H. pylori treats MALT lymphoma and hyperplastic polyps and lowers the risk of adenocarcinoma.

and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. A gastric adenocarcinoma can look like a benign ulcer, so suspicious gastric ulcers are biopsied and their healing confirmed. Both type 1 and type 2 NETs have high gastrin, but in type 1 acid is low from atrophic gastritis, whereas in type 2 a gastrinoma with ZES makes acid high and causes peptic ulcers; gastric pH separates them.

GIST and leiomyoma. Both arise from the muscularis propria and look alike on EUS as hypoechoic masses, so staining separates them: GISTs stain for KIT and DOG1, whereas leiomyomas stain for desmin and SMA and leiomyosarcomas for SMA, and neither stains for KIT. Many tumors once called leiomyosarcomas were GISTs, which is why gastric leiomyosarcoma is now so rare.

Review article

Malabsorption: separating mucosal injury from failed digestion

Malabsorption syndromes divide into true malabsorption, with mucosal injury and normal enzyme function, and maldigestion, with altered enzyme function and no mucosal injury. Celiac disease, Whipple disease, and tropical sprue injure the mucosa, whereas pancreatic insufficiency, bile salt deficiency, and lactose intolerance impair digestion. Here, we review their mechanisms, nutrient-specific consequences, and treatment, and consider how they relate to diarrhea and IBD.

Key points

  • The D-xylose test differentiates malabsorption from maldigestion.
  • Celiac disease is confirmed by EGD with biopsy after serology.
  • Consequences follow the lost nutrient: carbohydrate, protein, fat, or micronutrient.
  • Micronutrient deficiency is treated by replacement and IV fluids.

Pathophysiology

Mucosal injury blunts the villi and decreases absorption in true malabsorption, whereas decreased enzymes or bile salts leave food undigested in maldigestion. Either way, nutrients stay in the lumen. Undigested carbohydrate causes osmotic diarrhea and gas from bacterial digestion, with abdominal pain and flatulence; undigested fat causes steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies; and iron, B12, and folate deficiency cause anemia.

Etiology and mechanisms

Celiac disease is associated with HLA DQ2/8 and triggered by gliadin from gluten in wheat, rye, and barley. Gliadin binds antigen-presenting cells, which activate T helper cells and then B cells, producing IgA antibodies: tTG, DGP, and EMA. Whipple disease is Tropheryma whipplei infection with mucosal damage. Tropical sprue is E. coli and Klebsiella overgrowth in tropical areas with mucosal injury. Pancreatic insufficiency follows acute or chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, and pancreatic cancer or surgery. Bile salt deficiency, a partial maldigestion, follows cirrhosis, hepatocellular injury, biliary tree obstruction, and impaired enterohepatic circulation. Lactose intolerance, also a partial maldigestion, follows genetic mutations and gastroenteritis. Celiac disease is associated with type 1 diabetes and other autoimmune disease, IgA deficiency, and dermatitis herpetiformis. Tropheryma whipplei is a gram-positive bacillus that infects macrophages and also involves the joints, heart, and CNS, and tropical sprue follows coliform overgrowth (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter) after over 1 month in tropical areas. In SIBO, colonic bacteria grow in the small bowel because of stasis, from motility disorders or blind loops, or low acid, and they deconjugate bile salts and damage the mucosa. Abetalipoproteinemia is an autosomal recessive MTTP mutation that prevents apo B lipoproteins from forming, so enterocytes cannot export chylomicrons and fat stays in the mucosa.

Clinical presentation and complications

Carbohydrate malabsorption causes osmotic diarrhea, bowel distention, and increased gas production from bacterial digestion, with abdominal pain and flatulence. Protein malabsorption causes muscle atrophy and weight loss. Fat malabsorption causes steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies: vitamin A (night blindness), vitamin D (hypocalcemia, osteomalacia, osteoporosis), vitamin E (neuropathy, hemolytic anemia), and vitamin K (coagulopathy). Micronutrient malabsorption causes iron, B12, and folate deficiency, leading to anemia. Celiac disease causes iron deficiency anemia, osteoporosis, fatigue, and arthralgia, and dermatitis herpetiformis, intensely itchy vesicles on extensor surfaces, is pathognomonic. Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma is a rare complication, more likely in refractory disease, and a gluten-free diet lowers the risk. Whipple disease causes weight loss, diarrhea, fever, and migratory large-joint arthralgia, often first, with endocarditis and CNS signs. Tropical sprue causes chronic diarrhea after a traveler's diarrhea-like illness, with B12 and folate deficiency and anemia. SIBO causes bloating, flatulence, and watery diarrhea or steatorrhea, with low B12 and normal or high folate. Abetalipoproteinemia presents in infancy with failure to thrive and steatorrhea, and vitamin E deficiency causes acanthocytes, retinitis pigmentosa, and ataxia.

Diagnosis

The D-xylose test first differentiates malabsorption from maldigestion. Celiac disease is evaluated by serology (tTG, DGP, EMA, HLA), infectious causes by history taking, and confirmation is by EGD with biopsy. Pancreatic function is assessed by fecal elastase, lactose intolerance by hydrogen breath test, and bile salt deficiency by LFTs or biopsy. Celiac serology is done on a gluten diet for 6–8 weeks, measuring tTG-IgA with total IgA, since IgA deficiency gives a false negative and IgG tests are used instead. Duodenal biopsies, 1–2 from the bulb and 4 from the distal duodenum, show villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytes. Whipple disease shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages on small bowel biopsy, and tropical sprue is diagnosed from the travel history after excluding other causes. Fecal elastase is unaffected by enzyme replacement. SIBO is shown by a glucose or lactulose breath test, abetalipoproteinemia by acanthocytes with very low cholesterol, LDL, and VLDL, and dermatitis herpetiformis by direct immunofluorescence of skin beside a lesion.

Management

Micronutrient deficiency is treated by replacing the micronutrients and giving IV fluids. Celiac disease is treated with a gluten-free diet; Whipple disease and tropical sprue with ABX; pancreatic insufficiency with enzyme replacement; bile salt deficiency by treating the liver disease or cholestasis; and lactose intolerance with lactase replacement or a lactose-free diet. The gluten-free diet is strict and lifelong, with dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis. Whipple disease is treated with ceftriaxone or penicillin G for 2 weeks, then TMP-SMX for at least 12 months, and tropical sprue with tetracycline, TMP-SMX, or a quinolone, plus folic acid and iron, for 3–6 months, with parenteral B12. SIBO is treated with rifaximin for 2 weeks, treatment of the cause, and B12 replacement, and abetalipoproteinemia with a low-fat diet and very large doses of oral vitamin E and other fat-soluble vitamins.

Relationships to other conditions

. Every cause here produces chronic osmotic diarrhea, which has a high osmotic gap and stops with fasting, unlike secretory diarrhea.

. Ileal Crohn disease reproduces malabsorption: fat, B12, and bile salts are lost, with oxalate stones and gallstones as consequences.

. PBC and PSC cause fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies through the same bile salt mechanism.

. Repeated attacks link pancreatitis to pancreatic insufficiency, which fecal elastase identifies.

Diverticular Diseases

Pathophysiology

Increased sigmoid colon intraluminal pressure pushes the mucosa and submucosa out through the muscularis externa, forming diverticula.

  1. Low fiber and constipationPlus obesity and older age
  2. Increased intraluminal pressureIn the sigmoid colon
  3. DiverticulaMucosa and submucosa push out

What the pressure does

  • ARaised pressureLow fiber and constipation → increased sigmoid intraluminal pressure
  • BFalse diverticulumMucosa and submucosa herniate through the muscularis externa where the vasa recta enter
  • CBleedingA vessel beside the diverticulum bleeds → LGIB with hematochezia
  • DDiverticulitisFecalith → obstruction → back pressure and bacterial colonization → LLQ pain
  • EPerforationInflamed diverticulum ruptures → abscess, pneumoperitoneum, and peritonitis

Etiology

  • 1DiverticulosisLow-fiber diet, constipation, obesity, and older age → increased sigmoid colon intraluminal pressure → formation of diverticula; over half of people over 60; left-sided in up to 90% in Western countries
  • 2DiverticulitisFecalith → obstruction of diverticula → increased back pressure and bacterial colonization → LLQ pain and inflammation; only ~4% of people with diverticulosis

Meckel diverticulum

  • CauseThe vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct fails to close; the most common congenital GI anomaly
  • Rule of 2s2% of people, 2% symptomatic, under age 2, males twice as often, 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, up to 2 inches long, 2 types of ectopic tissue
  • BleedingAcid from ectopic gastric mucosa → painless rectal bleeding, currant jelly or brick-colored in children; ~50% of LGIB under age 2
  • AdultsSmall bowel obstruction is the most common complication; also intussusception

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms

  • Diverticulosis: usually none
  • Diverticulitis: LLQ pain
  • Fever
  • Leukocytosis

Complications

  • LGIBpainless hematochezia; from the right colon in 50–90%
  • Abscesspersistent pain and fever refractory to treatment
  • Enterovesical fistulapneumaturia, fecaluria, and UTI
  • Perforationpneumoperitoneum and peritonitis
  • Pylephlebitisseptic portal or mesenteric vein clot; mortality up to 25%
  • Recurrenceup to 30% after a first episode

Diagnosis

  • PerforationAbdominal x-ray and CT AP
  • BleedingColonoscopy
  • Suspected diverticulitisCT AP with contrast; FBC and CRP: leukocytosis and raised CRP
  • Meckel diverticulumMeckel scan: technetium-99m taken up by ectopic gastric mucosa

Avoid colonoscopy during acute diverticulitis; perform it 6–8 weeks after recovery.

Treatment

  • PerforationLaparotomy, with Hartmann procedure or primary anastomosis
  • BleedingColonoscopy
  • AbscessABX, percutaneous drainage, and surgery
  • FistulaSurgery
  • Uncomplicated diverticulitisOutpatient: liquid diet and paracetamol, not NSAIDs; ABX (amoxicillin-clavulanate, or a fluoroquinolone with metronidazole, 7–10 days) if immunocompromised, comorbid, or CRP over 140
  • AdmitFever, unable to keep hydrated, immunocompromised, or comorbid: IV ABX
  • OtherwiseIncrease fiber intake; nuts and seeds are safe
  • Meckel diverticulumSurgical excision if symptomatic

Monitor severity for potential colectomy.
