Review article

Diverticular diseases: from pressure-driven outpouching to inflammation

Increased sigmoid colon intraluminal pressure pushes the mucosa and submucosa out through the muscularis externa, forming diverticula. Diverticulitis follows when a fecalith obstructs a diverticulum. LLQ pain is the main symptom, and complications include LGIB, abscess, enterovesical fistula, and perforation. Here, we review their mechanisms and management, and consider how they relate to ischemic colitis, IBD, and IBS.

Key points

  • Low-fiber diet, constipation, obesity, and older age raise sigmoid pressure.
  • Suspected diverticulitis is evaluated with CT AP with contrast.
  • Avoid colonoscopy during acute diverticulitis; perform it 6–8 weeks after recovery.
  • Treatment follows the complication, and severity is monitored for potential colectomy.

Pathophysiology

Low fiber and constipation increase sigmoid intraluminal pressure, which pushes mucosa and submucosa through the muscularis externa where the vasa recta enter, forming false diverticula. A vessel beside a diverticulum can bleed, causing LGIB with hematochezia. A fecalith can obstruct a diverticulum, and the back pressure and bacterial colonization that follow cause diverticulitis with LLQ pain. An inflamed diverticulum can rupture, causing abscess, pneumoperitoneum, and peritonitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

Diverticulosis follows a low-fiber diet, constipation, obesity, and older age, which increase sigmoid colon intraluminal pressure and form diverticula. In diverticulitis, a fecalith obstructs a diverticulum, causing increased back pressure and bacterial colonization, with LLQ pain and inflammation. Diverticulosis affects over half of people over 60 and is left-sided in up to 90% in Western countries, but only ~4% develop diverticulitis. Meckel diverticulum forms when the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct fails to close and is the most common congenital GI anomaly. Its rule of 2s is 2% of people, 2% symptomatic, under age 2, males twice as often, 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, up to 2 inches long, and 2 types of ectopic tissue. Acid from ectopic gastric mucosa causes painless rectal bleeding, currant jelly or brick-colored in children, and accounts for ~50% of LGIB under age 2; in adults, small bowel obstruction is the most common complication, and intussusception also occurs.

Clinical presentation and complications

The main symptom is LLQ pain. Complications are LGIB (hematochezia), abscess (persistent pain and fever refractory to treatment), enterovesical fistula (pneumaturia, fecaluria, UTI), and perforation (pneumoperitoneum, peritonitis). Diverticulosis is usually asymptomatic, while diverticulitis causes LLQ pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Diverticular bleeding is painless and comes from the right colon in 50–90%. Pylephlebitis, a septic portal or mesenteric vein clot, carries a mortality of up to 25%, and up to 30% have a recurrence after a first episode.

Diagnosis

Perforation is evaluated by abdominal x-ray and CT AP, bleeding by colonoscopy, and suspected diverticulitis by CT AP with contrast. Colonoscopy is avoided during acute diverticulitis and performed 6–8 weeks after recovery. Diverticulitis shows leukocytosis and raised CRP. Meckel diverticulum is shown by a Meckel scan, in which technetium-99m is taken up by ectopic gastric mucosa.

Management

Perforation is treated by laparotomy, bleeding by colonoscopy, abscess by ABX, percutaneous drainage, and surgery, fistula by surgery, and infection by ABX. Otherwise, fiber intake is increased. Severity is monitored for potential colectomy. Uncomplicated diverticulitis is treated as an outpatient with a liquid diet and paracetamol rather than NSAIDs, with ABX (amoxicillin-clavulanate, or a fluoroquinolone with metronidazole, for 7–10 days) if the patient is immunocompromised, comorbid, or has a CRP over 140. Fever, inability to keep hydrated, immunocompromise, or comorbidity calls for admission and IV ABX. Perforation is treated by laparotomy with a Hartmann procedure or primary anastomosis. Nuts and seeds are safe, and a symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is excised.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both cause LLQ pain and hematochezia, but diverticular bleeding is typically painless, whereas ischemic colitis causes pain with bleeding after hypoperfusion.

. Enterovesical fistula with pneumaturia, fecaluria, and UTI occurs in both.

. The mechanisms mirror each other: a fecalith obstructs a blind pouch, and pressure and infection follow. Diverticulitis causes LLQ pain, and appendicitis RLQ pain.

. Both can cause pain and altered bowel habit, but IBS has no structural damage.

Review article

Inflammatory bowel disease: contrasting Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis

IBD comprises Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, which differ in location, depth, and lesion pattern. Crohn disease occurs anywhere in the GIT with transmural skip lesions, whereas ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum and confined to the colon. Their complications therefore differ, while extraintestinal features overlap. Here, we review their pathology, etiology, complications, and stepwise treatment, and consider how they relate to IBS, malabsorption, and PSC.

Key points

  • Crohn disease is transmural with skip lesions; ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum.
  • Smoking is a risk factor for Crohn disease and decreases the risk of ulcerative colitis.
  • Fecal calprotectin and ESR/CRP rule out IBS.
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis occurs only in UC among the extraintestinal features listed.

Pathophysiology

Genes and environment cause immune dysregulation, with Th1 predominating in Crohn disease and Th2 in ulcerative colitis, and the result is chronic inflammation. Crohn disease involves every layer of the wall, in skip lesions, so tracts through the wall form enterovesical, enteroenteral, and enterocutaneous fistulas, and scarring causes small bowel obstruction. Ulcerative colitis spreads continuously from the rectum, causing bloody diarrhea. Chronic inflammation raises the risk of colorectal cancer.

Pathology

Crohn disease occurs anywhere in the GIT, most commonly in the ileum, is rectum-sparing, and causes RLQ pain. Lesions skip, diarrhea is watery and bloody in flare-ups, ulcers are transmural, granulomas may be present, and there is Th1 dysregulation. Ulcerative colitis involves the colon only, starts at the rectum, and causes LLQ pain. Lesions are continuous, diarrhea is bloody (hematochezia), ulcers are submucosal, there are no granulomas, and there is Th2 dysregulation.

Etiology

Crohn disease is associated with family history, NOD-2 mutations, Western diet, and smoking. Ulcerative colitis is associated with family history, HLA DRB1, and Western diet, and smoking decreases risk.

Clinical presentation and complications

In Crohn disease, malabsorption is especially marked when the ileum is involved. Decreased fat absorption causes steatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies, and increased free oxalate levels with nephrolithiasis from oxalate. Decreased B12 absorption causes anemia. Decreased enterohepatic circulation decreases bile salt recycling and increases cholesterol, causing cholelithiasis. Fistulas and abscesses include enterovesical fistula (pneumaturia, fecaluria, UTI), enteroenteral fistula (diarrhea), enterocutaneous fistula (increased drainage), and perianal abscesses. Strictures cause small bowel obstruction with cramping, abdominal pain and distention, vomiting, and obstipation. In ulcerative colitis, colitis causes pain, fever, and bloody stools, and decreased myenteric plexus activity leads to megacolon, tenesmus, and perforation; chronic inflammation leads to colorectal cancer. Extraintestinal features are arthralgia, uveitis, pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum, hypercoagulability (VTE, DVT, PE), and primary sclerosing cholangitis. Crohn disease also causes oral aphthous ulcers, and at least 5% of patients with ulcerative colitis develop colorectal cancer over time. Toxic megacolon follows severe colitis, usually ulcerative colitis or C. difficile, and can be precipitated by opioids, anticholinergics, and antimotility drugs. It requires a colon over 6 cm on x-ray, at least 3 of fever over 38 °C, heart rate over 120, neutrophilia, or anemia, and 1 of dehydration, confusion, electrolyte disturbance, or hypotension; it is the leading cause of death in ulcerative colitis.

Diagnosis

Perforation and small bowel obstruction are evaluated by abdominal x-ray, and nephrolithiasis or cholelithiasis by ultrasound. IBS is ruled out with fecal calprotectin and ESR/CRP, and infectious diarrhea with stool culture, O&P, and C. diff. Otherwise, ileocolonoscopy or colonoscopy with biopsy is obtained. In Crohn disease, colonoscopy shows skip lesions and cobblestone mucosa, noncaseating granulomas are found in up to 33%, small bowel follow-through shows a string sign from stricture or spasm, and ASCA is more common. In ulcerative colitis, colonoscopy shows continuous inflammation from the rectum, friable mucosa, and pseudopolyps, biopsy shows cryptitis, crypt distortion, and crypt abscesses, a barium enema in longstanding disease shows a stove-pipe, or lead-pipe, colon, and p-ANCA is positive in 60–70%. Colonoscopy surveillance for colorectal cancer is done every 1–2 years in ulcerative colitis.

Management

Treatment moves up a pyramid with severity. 5-ASA and sulfasalazine are maintenance for UC; corticosteroids (prednisone, budesonide) are for induction and flare-ups; immunomodulators (AZA, 6-MP, MTX) are maintenance for Crohn disease; biological therapy comprises certolizumab, infliximab, adalimumab, ustekinumab, and vedolizumab; and surgery is the top tier. Colectomy cures ulcerative colitis and is used for failed medical therapy, fulminant colitis, toxic megacolon, perforation, uncontrolled bleeding, or dysplasia. Toxic megacolon is treated with an IV corticosteroid for 3 days, then infliximab or cyclosporine for 3 days, and subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy if this fails. Crohn disease is treated surgically by resection or stricturoplasty for complications, and recurs at the anastomosis in ~90%.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both cause pain and altered bowel habit, but IBS has no structural damage and normal inflammatory markers.

. Ileal Crohn disease produces the same fat, B12, and bile salt losses.

. Most PSC patients have IBD, usually ulcerative colitis, and the combination raises colorectal cancer risk.

. Bloody diarrhea overlaps, so infection is excluded before IBD is diagnosed.

. Ileal disease leads to cholesterol gallstones through lost bile salts.

Pathophysiology

IBS is a type of DGBI that stems from visceral hypersensitivity, altered microbiome, and hypermotility.

Note: There is a lack of structural damage.

  1. TriggerCarbohydrates and gas in the bowel
  2. Stretch receptor stimulationSignals rise to the CNS
  3. Abdominal painWith altered bowel habit

  • BStretch receptorsGas and osmotic effects stimulate them → reflex contraction
  • CCNS amplificationVisceral hypersensitivity → abdominal pain
  • DHypermotilityIncreased gut motility → diarrhea

  • 1Visceral hypersensitivityPsychiatric disorders, fibromyalgia, depression, and anxiety → increased CNS amplification of stretch receptor stimulation from osmotic effects of carbohydrates → abdominal pain
  • 2Altered microbiomeGut microbiome metabolizes carbohydrates into gas → stimulates stretch receptors → reflex contraction → abdominal pain
  • 3HypermotilityIncreased gut motility → diarrhea

Symptoms and complications

Predominant bowel pattern

  • Abdominal pain
  • Diarrhea
  • Constipation
  • Mixed

Alarm features: look for another cause

  • Onset at 50 or older
  • Blood in the stool
  • Fever or night sweats
  • Nocturnal diarrhea
  • Weight loss
  • Iron deficiency anemia, raised CRP, or raised fecal calprotectin
  • Family history of colorectal cancer, IBD, or celiac disease

Diagnosis

Rome V criteria

  1. Abdominal pain or discomfortRecurrent but not continuous, for at least 3 days per month
  2. And 2 of the followingRelated to defecation, changes in stool frequency, and changes in stool appearance

If there is

  • DiarrheaCeliac serology with total IgA, Fecal calprotectin, ESR/CRP, O&P, C. diff, and colonoscopy with biopsy
  • Alarm featuresColonoscopy with random biopsies of the left and right colon

Treatment

  • Reduce triggersLow FODMAP diet

  • Relieve diarrheaLoperamide; then rifaximin or eluxadoline (not after cholecystectomy); alosetron for women with severe disease (risk of ischemic colitis)
  • Global symptomsSoluble fiber such as psyllium, not insoluble fiber
  • RefractoryPsychological therapy

Review article

Irritable bowel syndrome: a disorder of gut-brain interaction without structural damage

IBS is a type of DGBI that stems from visceral hypersensitivity, altered microbiome, and hypermotility, with a lack of structural damage. Patients have recurrent abdominal pain with a predominant bowel pattern of diarrhea, constipation, or both. Diagnosis uses the Rome V criteria. Here, we review its mechanisms, diagnosis, and symptom-directed treatment, and consider how it is distinguished from IBD.

Key points

  • IBS has no structural damage.
  • Rome V requires recurrent pain for at least 3 days per month with 2 of 3 criteria.
  • Treatment is directed at the dominant symptom.

Pathophysiology

There is no structural damage. An altered microbiome turns carbohydrates into gas, and gas and osmotic effects stimulate stretch receptors, causing reflex contraction. Visceral hypersensitivity means the CNS amplifies these signals, causing abdominal pain, and hypermotility causes diarrhea.

Etiology and mechanisms

In visceral hypersensitivity, psychiatric disorders, fibromyalgia, depression, and anxiety increase CNS amplification of stretch receptor stimulation from osmotic effects of carbohydrates, causing abdominal pain. In altered microbiome, the gut microbiome metabolizes carbohydrates into gas, which stimulates stretch receptors and reflex contraction, causing abdominal pain. In hypermotility, increased gut motility causes diarrhea.

Clinical presentation

The predominant bowel pattern is abdominal pain with diarrhea, constipation, or mixed. Alarm features that point to another cause are onset at 50 or older, blood in the stool, fever or night sweats, nocturnal diarrhea, weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, raised CRP or fecal calprotectin, a family history of colorectal cancer, IBD, or celiac disease, and recent ABX.

Diagnosis

The Rome V criteria require recurrent but not continuous abdominal pain or discomfort for at least 3 days per month, and 2 of the following: related to defecation, changes in stool frequency, and changes in stool appearance. Perforation is evaluated by abdominal x-ray and CT AP. Diarrhea is evaluated by fecal calprotectin, ESR/CRP, O&P, C. diff, and colonoscopy with biopsy. Diarrhea also calls for celiac serology with total IgA, and alarm features call for colonoscopy with random biopsies of the left and right colon.

Management

Triggers are reduced with a low FODMAP diet. Abdominal pain is relieved with TCAs and peppermint oil, constipation with laxatives, and diarrhea with loperamide. Abdominal pain is treated with antispasmodics such as dicyclomine first, then peppermint oil, then TCAs, with rifaximin if these fail. Constipation is treated with PEG first, then lubiprostone, linaclotide, or plecanitide. Diarrhea is treated with loperamide, then rifaximin or eluxadoline, which is avoided after cholecystectomy, and alosetron for women with severe disease, which carries a risk of ischemic colitis. Soluble fiber such as psyllium, not insoluble fiber, improves global symptoms, and psychological therapy helps refractory disease.

Relationships to other conditions

. Inflammatory markers separate them: fecal calprotectin and ESR/CRP are normal in IBS.

. Carbohydrates drive symptoms in both, through osmotic effects and gas. Celiac disease must be excluded when symptoms suggest IBS.

. Alarm features such as iron-deficiency anemia, rectal bleeding, weight loss, and nocturnal symptoms call for further investigation.

Pathophysiology

  • Dysentery

  1. Injury or added solutesInfection, hormones, drugs, or malabsorption
  2. Water enters the lumenOr is not absorbed
  3. DiarrheaWatery or bloody

How fluid reaches the stool

  • ASecretoryChannel stimulation → increased secretory activity → watery stools
  • BOsmoticUnabsorbed solutes pull water into the lumen → watery stools
  • CInflammatoryDirect mucosal damage → neutrophilic infiltration → bloody, mucoid stools
  • DDecreased absorptionLess water returns from the lumen → high-volume stools

Etiology

  • Acute
  • 1Non-inflammatoryEnterotoxic bacteria: S. aureus (picnic), B. cereus (rice), ETEC (travel), and V. cholerae (travel; rice-water stools)
    Viruses: norovirus (cruise) and rotavirus (childcare)
    Parasites: Giardia (river water) and Cryptosporidium (immunocompromised patients)
    Decreased absorption and channel stimulation → increased secretory activity → watery, high-volume stools
  • 2InflammatoryInvasive bacteria: Salmonella (poultry), Shigella (travel, food), Campylobacter (food), EHEC/STEC (food), and C. difficile (ABX, especially clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, and penicillins)
    Parasites: Entamoeba histolytica (travel)
    Neutrophilic infiltration → increased goblet cell activity → increased mucus production, bleeding, increased fecal WBC, and increased calprotectin → bloody, mucoid stools (dysentery)
  • Chronic
  • 3SecretoryHormonal changes: increased VIP from vipomas (WDHA: watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria), increased gastrin from gastrinomas, and increased serotonin from carcinoid syndrome (liver metastases; flushing, wheezing, and tricuspid valve disease) → channel stimulation → increased secretory activity → watery stools
    Stimulant laxatives: senna and bisacodyl
  • 4OsmoticMalabsorption: celiac disease, Whipple disease, and tropical sprue
    Maldigestion: EPI, bile salt deficiency, and lactose intolerance
    Osmotic laxatives: lactulose, polyethylene glycol, and magnesium citrate
  • 5InflammatoryIBD, microscopic colitis, and chronic infections

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms

  • Abdominal pain
  • Watery diarrhea
  • Bloody diarrhea

Complications of acute diarrhea

  • Fluid statusHypovolemia, hypokalemia, and NAGMA
  • ColitisMegacolon, tenesmus, and perforation
  • HUSSTEC, Shigella (translocation-induced coagulopathy) → AKI, thrombocytopenia, and hemolytic anemia

Complications of chronic diarrhea

  • Fluid status disturbances
  • Malabsorption

Specific causes

  • C. difficileMild diarrhea to pseudomembranous colitis, toxic megacolon, and septic shock; 3–5% of healthy adults carry it
  • Microscopic colitisChronic watery, nonbloody diarrhea, 4–9 stools a day, often nocturnal; mostly older women; NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, statins, and smoking
  • Carcinoid syndromeTryptophan diverted to serotonin → niacin deficiency (pellagra)

Diagnosis

Acute diarrhea

  • HUS or AKIFBC and BMP
  • Initial workupFecal WBC, fecal calprotectin, stool culture, O&P, and norovirus and rotavirus testing
  • C. difficileOnly if there is diarrhea: 2-step testing, with GDH or NAAT, then toxin A and B

Chronic diarrhea

  • Initial workupFecal WBC, fecal calprotectin, and FOBT
  • InflammatoryCheck for infection and colonoscopy; microscopic colitis needs biopsies: a collagen band over 10 µm (collagenous) or 20 or more intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 cells (lymphocytic)
  • Non-inflammatoryStool osmotic gap (under 50 mOsm/kg secretory, over 75 osmotic), laxative use, and hormone levels: VIP, gastrin, and urine 5-HIAA for carcinoid

Treatment

  • HypovolemiaORS (salt, water, and glucose, absorbed together by the sodium-glucose cotransporter) or IV fluids
  • Severe colitis or immunocompromisedABX
  • HUSAvoid ABX and loperamide; use fluids, blood, or dialysis if needed
  • C. difficileStop unnecessary ABX; oral fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin for 10 days, metronidazole only if neither is available; recurrence: fidaxomicin, bezlotoxumab, or fecal microbiota transplant; wash hands with soap, since alcohol gel does not kill spores
  • STECNo ABX, which raise the risk of HUS
  • CholeraORS; doxycycline
  • Microscopic colitisStop culprit drugs; budesonide for 6–8 weeks
  • Carcinoid syndromeOctreotide or lanreotide

Loperamide can be used in most diarrhea, but avoid it in HUS, C. diff, toxic megacolon, and with fever or bloody stools.

Review article

Diarrhea: a mechanistic framework of secretory, osmotic, and inflammatory disease

Diarrhea is classified by duration and mechanism. Acute disease is non-inflammatory or inflammatory, and chronic disease is secretory, osmotic, or inflammatory. Inflammatory disease has increased fecal WBC and calprotectin and produces bloody, mucoid stools, whereas secretory and osmotic disease are watery. Here, we review the causes, complications, workup, and treatment of diarrhea, and consider how it relates to malabsorption, IBD, and PUD.

Key points

  • Fecal WBC and calprotectin separate non-inflammatory from inflammatory disease.
  • Exposure history points to the organism in acute diarrhea.
  • HUS follows STEC or Shigella and is managed by avoiding ABX and loperamide.
  • Loperamide is avoided in HUS, C. diff, toxic megacolon, and with fever or bloody stools.

Pathophysiology

Fluid reaches the stool in several ways. In secretory diarrhea, channel stimulation increases secretory activity, causing watery stools. In osmotic diarrhea, unabsorbed solutes pull water into the lumen, also causing watery stools. In inflammatory diarrhea, direct mucosal damage and neutrophilic infiltration cause bloody, mucoid stools. When absorption falls, less water returns from the lumen, causing high-volume stools.

Etiology and mechanisms

Acute non-inflammatory diarrhea has no fecal WBC or calprotectin and produces watery, high-volume stools. Causes are enterotoxic bacteria (S. aureus from picnics, B. cereus from rice, ETEC and V. cholerae from travel), viruses (norovirus on cruises, rotavirus in childcare), and parasites (Giardia from river water, Cryptosporidium in immunocompromised patients). They decrease absorption and stimulate channels, increasing secretory activity. Acute inflammatory diarrhea has increased fecal WBC and calprotectin and presents as dysentery. Causes are invasive bacteria (Salmonella from poultry, Shigella from travel and food, Campylobacter and EHEC/STEC from food, C. difficile from ABX) and parasites (Entamoeba histolytica from travel). Neutrophilic infiltration increases goblet cell activity and mucus production, with bleeding. Chronic secretory diarrhea has no direct mucosal damage and arises from hormonal changes (increased VIP from vipomas, gastrin from gastrinomas, and serotonin from carcinoid syndrome) and stimulant laxatives (senna, bisacodyl), through channel stimulation. Chronic osmotic diarrhea has no direct mucosal damage and arises through osmotic effects of malabsorption (celiac disease, Whipple disease, tropical sprue), maldigestion (EPI, bile salt deficiency, lactose intolerance), and osmotic laxatives (lactulose, polyethylene glycol, magnesium citrate). Chronic inflammatory diarrhea has direct mucosal damage, with bloody, mucoid stools, from IBD and chronic infections. V. cholerae causes rice-water stools, and C. difficile follows ABX, especially clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, and penicillins. Vipomas cause WDHA: watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria. Carcinoid syndrome follows liver metastases and causes flushing, wheezing, and tricuspid valve disease. Microscopic colitis is a chronic inflammatory cause alongside IBD.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are abdominal pain and watery or bloody diarrhea. Acute complications are fluid status disturbances (hypovolemia, hypokalemia, NAGMA), colitis (megacolon, tenesmus, perforation), and HUS from STEC or Shigella (translocation-induced coagulopathy), with AKI, thrombocytopenia, and hemolytic anemia. Chronic complications are fluid status disturbances and malabsorption. C. difficile ranges from mild diarrhea to pseudomembranous colitis, toxic megacolon, and septic shock, and 3–5% of healthy adults carry it. Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery, nonbloody diarrhea, 4–9 stools a day and often nocturnal, mostly in older women, and is linked to NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, statins, and smoking. In carcinoid syndrome, tryptophan is diverted to serotonin, causing niacin deficiency (pellagra).

Diagnosis

In acute diarrhea, HUS or AKI is evaluated with FBC and BMP, and the initial workup is fecal WBC, fecal calprotectin, stool culture, O&P, and norovirus and rotavirus testing. In chronic diarrhea, the initial workup is fecal WBC, fecal calprotectin, and FOBT. Inflammatory disease is evaluated by checking for infection and colonoscopy, and non-inflammatory disease by stool osmotic gap, laxative use, and hormone levels. C. difficile is tested only if there is diarrhea, by 2-step testing with GDH or NAAT, then toxin A and B. A stool osmotic gap under 50 mOsm/kg indicates secretory diarrhea and over 75 osmotic diarrhea, and hormone levels include VIP, gastrin, and urine 5-HIAA for carcinoid. Microscopic colitis needs biopsies, showing a collagen band over 10 µm in collagenous colitis or 20 or more intraepithelial lymphocytes per 100 cells in lymphocytic colitis.

Management

Hypovolemia is treated with IV or PO fluids, and severe colitis or immunocompromise with ABX. HUS is managed by avoiding ABX and loperamide, and by using fluids, blood, or dialysis if needed. Loperamide can be used in most diarrhea, but is avoided in HUS, C. diff, toxic megacolon, and with fever or bloody stools. Hypovolemia is treated with ORS, whose salt, water, and glucose are absorbed together by the sodium-glucose cotransporter, or IV fluids. C. difficile is treated by stopping unnecessary ABX and giving oral fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin for 10 days, with metronidazole only if neither is available; recurrence is treated with fidaxomicin, bezlotoxumab, or fecal microbiota transplant, and hands are washed with soap, since alcohol gel does not kill spores. STEC is not treated with ABX, which raise the risk of HUS. Cholera is treated with ORS and doxycycline, microscopic colitis by stopping culprit drugs and giving budesonide for 6–8 weeks, and carcinoid syndrome with octreotide or lanreotide.

Relationships to other conditions

. Chronic osmotic diarrhea is the shared endpoint; a high stool osmotic gap and resolution with fasting favor it over secretory disease.

and . Fecal calprotectin and ESR/CRP separate inflammatory disease from IBS. Infectious diarrhea must be excluded before IBD is diagnosed, using stool culture, O&P, and C. diff.

. Gastrinomas cause both ulcers and secretory diarrhea.

. Bloody diarrhea with pain in an older patient after hypotension suggests ischemic colitis rather than infection.

Intestinal Ischemia

Pathophysiology

Arterial occlusion, venous occlusion, or hypoperfusion causes loss of blood supply to the intestines.

  1. Occlusion or hypoperfusionArterial, venous, or low flow
  2. Decreased oxygen supplyWorse with increased demand after eating
  3. Infarction and necrosisIf flow is not restored

What ischemia does

  • ADecreased oxygen supplyBlocked or low flow reaches the bowel → abdominal pain
  • BAnaerobic respirationOxygen-starved cells → AGMA
  • CLeaky vesselsIncreased vascular permeability → hematochezia
  • DInfarctionProlonged ischemia → necrosis, with out-of-proportion abdominal pain
  • EPerforationFull-thickness necrosis → pneumoperitoneum and peritonitis

Etiology

  • Acute mesenteric ischemia
  • 1ArterialThrombosis (atherosclerosis), embolism (history of A-fib or AAA), or hypoperfusion (shock) → decreased perfusion or blocking of the SMA Most common or IMA → infarction and necrosis → out-of-proportion abdominal pain; embolism, usually cardiac, 40–50%; thrombosis 25–30%; nonocclusive (NOMI) ~20%, from vasospasm in critically ill patients on vasopressors
  • 2VenousMesenteric thrombosis (hypercoagulation: malignancy, oral contraceptives, pregnancy, factor V Leiden, or protein C or S deficiency) or portal thrombosis (cirrhosis) → venous occlusion of the portal vein, SMV, or IMV → venous congestion → decreased oxygen supply
  • Chronic mesenteric ischemia
  • 3AtherosclerosisAtherosclerosis of 2 of the following: celiac trunk, SMA, and IMA → decreased oxygen supply with increased oxygen demand when eating → postprandial abdominal pain, 15–30 minutes after meals and lasting up to 4 hours → fear of eating and weight loss
  • Ischemic colitis
  • 4Hypoperfusion of the IMAShock or history of vasopressor usage → decreased oxygen supply to the splenic flexure (Griffiths point), descending colon, and rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck point); these watershed areas account for ~70% → LLQ pain and hematochezia

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms

  • Acute: pain out of proportion to examination
  • Chronic: postprandial pain and weight loss
  • Hematochezia

Complications

  • AGMAincreased vascular permeability and anaerobic respiration
  • Perforationpneumoperitoneum and peritonitis
  • Death60–80% in acute mesenteric ischemia; under 5% in nongangrenous ischemic colitis

Diagnosis

  • 1–3Acute or chronic mesenteric ischemiaCT angiogram: preferred, even with renal impairment; lactate and LDH rise only late
  • 4Ischemic colitisCT AP and colonoscopy with biopsy, within 48 hours

Treatment

  • Bowel decompressionNPO, IV fluids, and NGT
  • Prevent sepsisABX
  • Prevent clottingHeparin
  • RevascularizationEndovascular procedures and surgery
  • AvoidVasopressors and alpha-agonists, which cause vasospasm
  • NOMITreat the low-flow state; catheter-directed papaverine
  • Venous thrombosisAnticoagulation
  • Ischemic colitisMild: supportive; moderate: broad-spectrum ABX and surgical review; severe: surgery

Review article

Intestinal ischemia: arterial, venous, and low-flow injury to the bowel

Arterial occlusion, venous occlusion, or hypoperfusion causes loss of blood supply to the intestines. Acute mesenteric ischemia presents with out-of-proportion abdominal pain, chronic mesenteric ischemia with postprandial pain, and ischemic colitis with LLQ pain and hematochezia. Here, we review these three patterns, their workup, and their treatment, and consider how they relate to other causes of abdominal pain and bloody stools.

Key points

  • The SMA is the most commonly affected vessel in acute mesenteric ischemia.
  • Chronic mesenteric ischemia requires atherosclerosis of 2 of the celiac trunk, SMA, and IMA.
  • CT angiogram evaluates mesenteric ischemia; CT AP and colonoscopy evaluate ischemic colitis.
  • Treatment combines bowel decompression, ABX, heparin, and revascularization.

Pathophysiology

Arterial occlusion, venous occlusion, or hypoperfusion decreases oxygen supply to the bowel, causing abdominal pain, and increased demand after eating makes this worse in chronic disease. Anaerobic respiration causes AGMA, and increased vascular permeability causes hematochezia. Prolonged ischemia causes infarction and necrosis, with out-of-proportion abdominal pain, and full-thickness necrosis perforates, causing pneumoperitoneum and peritonitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

Acute arterial ischemia follows thrombosis (atherosclerosis), embolism (history of A-fib or AAA), or hypoperfusion (shock), which decrease perfusion or block the SMA, most commonly, or IMA, causing infarction and necrosis with out-of-proportion abdominal pain. Acute venous ischemia follows mesenteric thrombosis (hypercoagulation) or portal thrombosis (cirrhosis), with venous occlusion of the portal vein, SMV, or IMV, venous congestion, and decreased oxygen supply. Chronic mesenteric ischemia follows atherosclerosis of 2 of the celiac trunk, SMA, and IMA; decreased oxygen supply cannot meet increased oxygen demand when eating, causing postprandial abdominal pain. Ischemic colitis follows shock or a history of vasopressor usage, with hypoperfusion of the IMA and decreased oxygen supply to the splenic flexure, descending colon, and rectosigmoid junction, causing LLQ pain and hematochezia. Of acute mesenteric ischemia, embolism, usually cardiac, accounts for 40–50%, thrombosis for 25–30%, and nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia (NOMI) for ~20%, from vasospasm in critically ill patients on vasopressors. Venous thrombosis follows malignancy, oral contraceptives, pregnancy, factor V Leiden, or protein C or S deficiency. In chronic mesenteric ischemia, pain begins 15–30 minutes after meals and lasts up to 4 hours, causing fear of eating and weight loss. Ischemic colitis mostly affects the watershed areas, the splenic flexure (Griffiths point) and rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck point), which account for ~70%.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are abdominal pain and hematochezia. Complications are AGMA, from increased vascular permeability and anaerobic respiration, and perforation (pneumoperitoneum, peritonitis). Acute ischemia causes pain out of proportion to examination, and chronic ischemia postprandial pain and weight loss. Mortality is 60–80% in acute mesenteric ischemia, and under 5% in nongangrenous ischemic colitis.

Diagnosis

Acute or chronic mesenteric ischemia is evaluated by CT angiogram, and ischemic colitis by CT AP and colonoscopy. CT angiography is preferred even with renal impairment, and lactate and LDH rise only late. Ischemic colitis is confirmed by colonoscopy with biopsy within 48 hours.

Management

Bowel decompression uses NPO, IV fluids, and NGT. ABX prevent sepsis, heparin prevents clotting, and revascularization uses endovascular procedures and surgery. Vasopressors and alpha-agonists are avoided, since they cause vasospasm. NOMI is treated by correcting the low-flow state, with catheter-directed papaverine, and venous thrombosis with anticoagulation. Mild ischemic colitis is managed supportively, moderate disease with broad-spectrum ABX and surgical review, and severe disease with surgery.

Relationships to other conditions

. The same low-flow logic applies: shock injures the watershed splenic flexure in the colon and zone 3 in the liver.

. Both cause LLQ pain and hematochezia. Painless, large-volume bleeding favors diverticulosis, whereas ischemic colitis causes pain with bleeding.

and infectious colitis. Bloody diarrhea is shared, but a recent episode of hypotension or vasopressor use points to ischemia.

Embolic disease. A-fib embolizes to both the SMA and the brain, so the same source explains both.

Hepatocellular Injury: Vascular Causes

Causes of hepatocellular injury VITAMIN + other

  1. VVascular

Pathophysiology

Decreased blood flow into (arterial) or out of (venous) the liver leads to hypoxia of zone 3 (centrilobular) hepatocytes, causing hepatocellular injury.

  1. Decreased inflow or outflowArterial or venous
  2. Zone 3 hypoxiaCentrilobular hepatocytes
  3. Hepatocellular injuryNecrosis or atrophy

What hypoxia does

  • ADecreased inflowShock or cardiac arrest → decreased hepatic perfusion
  • BBlocked outflowRHF or clot → increased sinusoidal pressure → sinusoidal congestion
  • CZone 3 necrosisHepatocytes that receive the least oxygen die first
  • DEnzyme releaseDying hepatocytes → increased AST and ALT, often over 1000 U/L
  • EChronic congestionZone 3 atrophy → nutmeg liver and cardiac cirrhosis

Etiology

  • Arterial
  • 1Ischemic hepatitis ("shock liver")Shock (cardiogenic, hypovolemic, septic) or cardiac arrest → decreased hepatic perfusion → zone 3 hypoxia → centrilobular necrosis → increased AST/ALT, often over 1000 U/L
  • Venous
  • 2Hepatic vein congestion (congestive hepatopathy)RHF, also tricuspid regurgitation and constrictive pericarditis → increased CVP and hepatic venous pressure → sinusoidal congestion, zone 3 atrophy, and necrosis → nutmeg liver and cardiac cirrhosis if chronic
  • 3Hepatic vein clot (Budd-Chiari syndrome)Myeloproliferative neoplasms (polycythemia vera, JAK2) Most common, pregnancy, OCPs, PNH, and malignancy (e.g. HCC) → thrombosis of hepatic veins or IVC → blocked hepatic outflow and increased sinusoidal pressure → hepatomegaly, ascites, and RUQ pain
  • Portal and sinusoidal
  • 4Portal vein thrombosisCirrhosis Most common, myeloproliferative and other prothrombotic states, and abdominal inflammation such as pancreatitis → blocked portal inflow → portal hypertension, with varices and splenomegaly but near-normal liver function unless cirrhotic
  • 5Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (veno-occlusive disease)Conditioning for hematopoietic cell transplant, especially busulfan, or drugs such as cyclophosphamide and oxaliplatin → damaged zone 3 sinusoidal endothelium → sinusoidal obstruction → jaundice, painful hepatomegaly, and ascites or weight gain

Symptoms and complications

Each cause has a distinct pattern:

Feature Ischemic hepatitis Congestive hepatopathy Budd-Chiari syndrome
Onset Acute, 1–3 days after hypotension Usually chronic Acute or chronic
Key features Often no symptoms; nausea, RUQ pain RUQ discomfort, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema Triad of RUQ pain, hepatomegaly, and ascites
JVD Depends on the cause of shock Present, with hepatojugular reflux Absent
AST/ALT Massive rise, often over 1000 U/L; falls within 7–10 days Mild rise, often with increased bilirubin Variable; very high in acute disease

Symptoms

  • RUQ pain
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Ascites
  • Jaundice
  • Nausea

Complications

  • Acute liver failure coagulopathy (increased INR), hepatic encephalopathy, hypoglycemia
  • Cardiac cirrhosis long-standing congestion
  • Portal hypertension ascites, varices, splenomegaly

Diagnosis

  • +Any vascular causeLFTs and INR to assess liver function
  • 1Ischemic hepatitisHistory of hypotension; serial LFTs: rapid rise, then rapid fall; LDH: markedly increased
  • 2Congestive hepatopathyEchocardiogram and BNP
  • 3Budd-Chiari syndromeDoppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins First line; CT or MR venography to confirm; hypercoagulability workup (JAK2 V617F)
  • 4Portal vein thrombosisDoppler ultrasound; LFTs normal or near normal unless cirrhotic; chronic clot forms a portal cavernoma
  • 5Sinusoidal obstruction syndromeClinical: bilirubin 2 mg/dL or more with 2 of painful hepatomegaly, weight gain over 5%, or ascites, usually within 21 days of transplant; Doppler: reduced or reversed portal flow

Check for JVD: present in heart failure, absent in Budd-Chiari syndrome.

Treatment

  • 1Ischemic hepatitisRestore perfusion and treat the cause of shock (fluids, vasopressors, cardiac support)
  • 2Congestive hepatopathyTreat heart failure (e.g. diuretics)
  • 3Budd-Chiari syndromeAnticoagulation and treat the underlying cause, then step up as below
  • 4Portal vein thrombosisEarly anticoagulation; treat portal hypertension and the cause
  • 5Sinusoidal obstruction syndromeDefibrotide, the only approved drug, started early

Review article

Vascular liver injury: inflow failure, outflow congestion, and zone 3 hypoxia

Decreased blood flow into or out of the liver leads to hypoxia of zone 3 (centrilobular) hepatocytes, causing hepatocellular injury. Ischemic hepatitis reflects failed arterial inflow, whereas congestive hepatopathy and Budd-Chiari syndrome reflect impaired venous outflow. Each has a distinct tempo and enzyme pattern. Here, we review their mechanisms, differentiation, and treatment, and consider how they relate to other causes of very high aminotransferases.

Key points

  • Ischemic hepatitis causes a massive AST/ALT rise that falls within 7–10 days.
  • JVD is present in heart failure and absent in Budd-Chiari syndrome.
  • Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins is first line for Budd-Chiari syndrome.
  • Budd-Chiari treatment steps up from anticoagulation to transplant.

Pathophysiology

Shock or cardiac arrest decreases hepatic perfusion, whereas right heart failure or a clot blocks outflow, raising sinusoidal pressure and causing sinusoidal congestion. Either way, zone 3 hepatocytes receive the least oxygen and die first, releasing AST and ALT, which often exceed 1000 U/L. Chronic congestion causes zone 3 atrophy, leading to nutmeg liver and cardiac cirrhosis.

Etiology and mechanisms

Ischemic hepatitis ("shock liver") follows shock (cardiogenic, hypovolemic, septic) or cardiac arrest: decreased hepatic perfusion causes zone 3 hypoxia and centrilobular necrosis, with increased AST/ALT, often over 1000 U/L. Congestive hepatopathy follows RHF, as well as tricuspid regurgitation and constrictive pericarditis: increased CVP and hepatic venous pressure cause sinusoidal congestion, zone 3 atrophy, and necrosis, producing nutmeg liver and, if chronic, cardiac cirrhosis. Budd-Chiari syndrome is thrombosis of the hepatic veins or IVC, most commonly from myeloproliferative neoplasms (polycythemia vera, JAK2), and also from pregnancy, OCPs, PNH, and malignancy (e.g. HCC). Blocked hepatic outflow and increased sinusoidal pressure cause hepatomegaly, ascites, and RUQ pain. Portal vein thrombosis is most often due to cirrhosis, and otherwise to myeloproliferative and other prothrombotic states or abdominal inflammation such as pancreatitis; it blocks portal inflow and causes portal hypertension, with varices and splenomegaly but near-normal liver function unless the liver is cirrhotic. Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, or veno-occlusive disease, follows conditioning for hematopoietic cell transplant, especially with busulfan, or drugs such as cyclophosphamide and oxaliplatin, which damage the zone 3 sinusoidal endothelium and obstruct the sinusoids, causing jaundice, painful hepatomegaly, and ascites or weight gain.

Clinical presentation and complications

Ischemic hepatitis is acute, 1–3 days after hypotension, often with no symptoms or with nausea and RUQ pain; JVD depends on the cause of shock, and AST/ALT shows a massive rise, often over 1000 U/L, falling within 7–10 days. Congestive hepatopathy is usually chronic, with RUQ discomfort, hepatomegaly, and peripheral edema; JVD is present with hepatojugular reflux, and there is a mild rise, often with increased bilirubin. Budd-Chiari syndrome is acute or chronic, with a triad of RUQ pain, hepatomegaly, and ascites; JVD is absent, and the rise is variable and very high in acute disease. General symptoms are RUQ pain, hepatomegaly, ascites, jaundice, and nausea. Complications are acute liver failure (coagulopathy with increased INR, hepatic encephalopathy, hypoglycemia), cardiac cirrhosis from long-standing congestion, and portal hypertension (ascites, varices, splenomegaly).

Diagnosis

Any vascular cause is assessed with LFTs and INR. Ischemic hepatitis is supported by a history of hypotension, serial LFTs with a rapid rise then rapid fall, and markedly increased LDH. Congestive hepatopathy is evaluated by echocardiogram and BNP. Budd-Chiari syndrome is evaluated by Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins first, CT or MR venography to confirm, and a hypercoagulability workup (JAK2 V617F). JVD is present in heart failure and absent in Budd-Chiari syndrome. Portal vein thrombosis is shown by Doppler ultrasound, with normal or near-normal LFTs unless the liver is cirrhotic, and a chronic clot forms a portal cavernoma. Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome is diagnosed clinically by a bilirubin of 2 mg/dL or more with 2 of painful hepatomegaly, weight gain over 5%, or ascites, usually within 21 days of transplant, and Doppler shows reduced or reversed portal flow.

Management

Ischemic hepatitis is treated by restoring perfusion and treating the cause of shock (fluids, vasopressors, cardiac support); LFTs normalize within 7–10 days once blood flow is restored. Congestive hepatopathy is treated by treating heart failure (e.g. diuretics). Budd-Chiari syndrome is treated in all patients with anticoagulation and treatment of the underlying cause, then angioplasty or stenting for short venous narrowing, TIPS, and liver transplant for fulminant failure or cirrhosis. Portal vein thrombosis is treated with early anticoagulation, with management of portal hypertension and the cause, and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome with defibrotide, the only approved drug, started early.

Relationships to other conditions

. Low flow injures vulnerable zones in both organs: zone 3 in the liver and the watershed splenic flexure in the colon.

. Both can raise aminotransferases above 1000 U/L, but ischemic hepatitis rises and falls within days with a very high LDH, whereas viral hepatitis rises and falls more slowly.

. Both injure zone 3, so the history separates them.

. Congestion and Budd-Chiari syndrome share portal hypertension with cirrhosis, and SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or more does not separate them.

Hepatocellular Injury: Infectious Causes

Causes of hepatocellular injury VITAMIN + other

  2. IInfectious

Pathophysiology

Viral infection of hepatocytes triggers a cytotoxic T-cell response, which destroys infected cells and causes hepatic inflammation.

  1. Viral infectionOf hepatocytes
  2. Cytotoxic T-cell responseAgainst infected cells
  3. Hepatic inflammationAcute or chronic

What the immune response does

  • AInfected hepatocyteViruses replicate inside hepatocytes
  • BCytotoxic T cellT cells recognize and destroy infected cells
  • CHepatocyte deathDestroyed cells → hepatic inflammation and increased AST and ALT
  • DFibrosisChronic infection → fibrosis → cirrhosis
  • EIntegrationHBV integrates into host DNA → HCC without cirrhosis

Hepatitis viruses A to E

"The vowels hit your bowels": hepatitis A and E are fecal-oral, acute only, and naked.

HDV requires HBV

HDV needs HBsAg from HBV as its envelope, so it only infects people who also have HBV.

Coinfection

  • HBV and HDV acquired at the same time
  • Usually acute and self-limited
  • Both viruses usually cleared

Superinfection

  • HDV acquired by someone with chronic HBV
  • More severe; risk of fulminant hepatitis
  • Usually becomes chronic, with faster progression to cirrhosis

Viral life cycles

+ssRNA viruses HAV, HCV, HEV

  • Attachment and entry into the hepatocyte
  • Uncoating releases +ssRNA into the cytoplasm
  • +ssRNA acts directly as mRNA
  • Translated into a polyprotein, which viral proteases cleave
  • Viral RdRp copies a −RNA template
  • The template makes new +ssRNA genomes
  • Assembly and release

Replicates in the cytoplasm; HCV drugs target NS3/4A, NS5A, and NS5B.

pdsDNA virus HBV

  • Attachment and entry via the NTCP receptor
  • Nucleocapsid carries pdsDNA into the nucleus
  • pdsDNA is repaired into cccDNA
  • Host RNA polymerase II makes mRNAs and pregenomic RNA
  • Viral reverse transcriptase converts pregenomic RNA into new pdsDNA
  • Assembly with an HBsAg envelope and release

cccDNA persists, so HBV is hard to cure; tenofovir and entecavir block reverse transcriptase.

HDV (circular −ssRNA) replicates in the nucleus using host RNA polymerase.

Other viruses

CMV

  • Immunocompromised patients transplant, AIDS
  • Mono-like illness with a negative heterophile test
  • Usually mild hepatitis

HSV

  • Pregnancy (third trimester), neonates, immunocompromised patients
  • Rare; can be fulminant and anicteric

EBV

  • Infectious mononucleosis in adolescents and young adults
  • Mild transaminase rise and hepatosplenomegaly are common

Abscesses and parasites

  • Pyogenic abscessUsually polymicrobial (E. coli, Klebsiella, streptococci, staphylococci, and anaerobes), spreading from the biliary tract or through the portal vein; half of solitary abscesses are in the right lobe
  • Amebic abscessEntamoeba histolytica from contaminated food or water; men aged 18–50 who live in or travel to endemic areas, 10 times more often than women
  • Hydatid cystEchinococcus granulosus eggs from dogs, whose intermediate hosts are sheep and other livestock; cysts grow slowly and form daughter cysts
  • SchistosomiasisS. mansoni and S. japonicum from freshwater snails; eggs carried to the liver cause granulomas and Symmers pipe-stem periportal fibrosis → portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and varices

Review article

Infectious liver injury: the hepatitis viruses and their clinical divergence

Viral infection of hepatocytes triggers a cytotoxic T-cell response, which destroys infected cells and causes hepatic inflammation. Hepatitis A and E are fecal-oral and acute, whereas hepatitis B, C, and D are bloodborne and can become chronic, leading to cirrhosis and HCC. CMV, HSV, and EBV also cause hepatitis. Here, we review their virology, phases, serology, and treatment, and consider how they relate to other liver injuries.

Key points

  • "The vowels hit your bowels": hepatitis A and E are fecal-oral, acute only, and naked.
  • HDV needs HBsAg from HBV as its envelope.
  • In the window period, IgM anti-HBc is the only positive marker, and anti-HBc never comes from vaccination.
  • Anti-HCV stays positive for life, so HCV RNA confirms current infection.
  • Screen for HCC every 6 months in chronic HBV, or HCV with cirrhosis.

Pathophysiology

Viruses replicate inside hepatocytes, and cytotoxic T cells destroy the infected cells, causing hepatic inflammation and increased AST and ALT. Chronic infection leads to fibrosis and then cirrhosis, and HBV integrates into host DNA, so it can cause HCC without cirrhosis.

Virology

HAV is a naked +ssRNA picornavirus spread by the fecal-oral route, with 2–6 weeks of incubation; it is acute only, has no carrier state, and has an inactivated vaccine. HBV is an enveloped, partially double-stranded, circular DNA (pdsDNA) hepadnavirus spread by sex, blood, and perinatally, with 1–6 months of incubation; it becomes chronic in ~90% of infants and under 5% of adults, integrates into host DNA so can cause HCC without cirrhosis, and has a recombinant HBsAg vaccine. HCV is an enveloped +ssRNA flavivirus spread by blood, mainly IV drug use, with 2 weeks–6 months of incubation; it becomes chronic in 75–85%, and high antigenic variation means no vaccine and frequent chronicity. HDV is a circular −ssRNA deltavirus with an HBsAg envelope borrowed from HBV, spread by sex, blood, and perinatally, with incubation similar to HBV; the HBV vaccine protects. HEV is a naked +ssRNA hepevirus spread by the fecal-oral route through contaminated water and undercooked pork, with 2–9 weeks of incubation; it is acute, chronic only if immunocompromised, rarely chronic overall, has no widely available vaccine, and causes fulminant hepatitis in pregnancy with high mortality.

Coinfection and superinfection

HDV only infects people who also have HBV. In coinfection, HBV and HDV are acquired at the same time; disease is usually acute and self-limited, and both viruses are usually cleared. In superinfection, HDV is acquired by someone with chronic HBV; disease is more severe, with a risk of fulminant hepatitis, and usually becomes chronic with faster progression to cirrhosis.

Viral life cycles

+ssRNA viruses (HAV, HCV, HEV) attach, enter the hepatocyte, and uncoat; +ssRNA acts directly as mRNA, is translated into a polyprotein that viral proteases cleave, and viral RdRp copies a −RNA template that makes new genomes, followed by assembly and release. They replicate in the cytoplasm, and HCV drugs target NS3/4A, NS5A, and NS5B. HBV attaches and enters via the NTCP receptor, its nucleocapsid carries pdsDNA into the nucleus, pdsDNA is repaired into cccDNA, host RNA polymerase II makes mRNAs and pregenomic RNA, viral reverse transcriptase converts pregenomic RNA into new pdsDNA, and assembly with an HBsAg envelope is followed by release. cccDNA persists, so HBV is hard to cure, and tenofovir and entecavir block reverse transcriptase. HDV replicates in the nucleus using host RNA polymerase.

Other viruses

CMV affects immunocompromised patients (transplant, AIDS), with a mono-like illness, a negative heterophile test, and usually mild hepatitis. HSV affects pregnancy (third trimester), neonates, and immunocompromised patients; it is rare, and can be fulminant and anicteric. EBV causes infectious mononucleosis in adolescents and young adults, with common mild transaminase rise and hepatosplenomegaly. Beyond viruses, pyogenic liver abscesses are usually polymicrobial, with E. coli, Klebsiella, streptococci, staphylococci, and anaerobes, spreading from the biliary tract or through the portal vein, and half of solitary abscesses lie in the right lobe. Amebic abscesses follow Entamoeba histolytica infection from contaminated food or water, most often in men aged 18–50 who live in or travel to endemic areas. Hydatid cysts come from Echinococcus granulosus eggs shed by dogs, whose intermediate hosts are sheep and other livestock, and grow slowly, forming daughter cysts. Schistosoma mansoni and japonicum, acquired from freshwater, send eggs to the liver, where granulomas lead to Symmers pipe-stem periportal fibrosis, portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and varices.

Clinical presentation and complications

Acute viral hepatitis passes through an asymptomatic incubation phase; a prodromal phase with flu-like illness, RUQ pain, arthralgia, and increased ALT more than AST; an icteric phase with jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, and increased bilirubin; and a convalescent phase resolving over weeks to months. Many infections are anicteric, especially HAV in young children and acute HCV. Outcomes are recovery (HAV, HEV, most adult HBV), fulminant hepatitis (HBV, HDV, HEV in pregnancy), and chronic infection (HBV, HCV, HDV), in which ongoing inflammation causes fibrosis, cirrhosis, HCC, and liver failure; in chronic HBV, DNA integrates into the host genome and causes HCC even without cirrhosis. Extrahepatic manifestations, mostly from immune complexes (HBV) and cryoglobulins (HCV), are arthritis and arthralgia (serum sickness-like in HBV); polyarteritis nodosa (HBV) and mixed cryoglobulinemia vasculitis (HCV); rare myocarditis and pericarditis; glomerulonephritis, including membranous nephropathy (HBV) and MPGN (HCV and HBV); thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, and neutropenia; B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (HCV); and porphyria cutanea tarda and lichen planus (HCV).

Diagnosis

IgM means current or recent infection, and IgG means past infection or immunity. Acute HAV shows IgM anti-HAV, and IgG anti-HAV is also positive after vaccination. Acute HDV shows IgM anti-HDV or HDV RNA with positive HBsAg, and past infection shows IgG anti-HDV; IgM anti-HBc is positive in coinfection and negative in superinfection. Acute HEV shows IgM anti-HEV, or HEV RNA if immunocompromised, and past infection shows IgG anti-HEV; it should be considered in pregnant patients with acute hepatitis. For HBV, acute infection shows positive HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV DNA, with IgM anti-HBc. The window period shows negative HBsAg, HBeAg, HBV DNA, and anti-HBs, anti-HBe that may be positive, and IgM anti-HBc. Recovery shows positive anti-HBs and anti-HBe, with IgG anti-HBc. Immunized patients have only anti-HBs. Chronic, replicative infection (high infectivity) shows positive HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV DNA with IgG anti-HBc, and chronic, non-replicative infection (low infectivity) shows positive HBsAg and anti-HBe, low or undetectable HBV DNA, and IgG anti-HBc. HBsAg for 6 months or more means chronic infection. HCV is screened with anti-HCV antibody; if positive, HCV RNA (PCR) checks for active virus. RNA-negative patients have resolved past infection or a false-positive antibody, and RNA-positive patients have current infection and need fibrosis assessed before treatment using APRI (above 1.0 suggests cirrhosis), FIB-4, or elastography. CMV is evaluated by CMV PCR (blood), with "owl's eye" inclusions on biopsy; HSV by HSV PCR (blood); and EBV by heterophile antibody (Monospot) and EBV serology. A pyogenic abscess is imaged with ultrasound and then contrast CT, with guided aspiration for stains and cultures; an amebic abscess is diagnosed by imaging and serology, and aspiration, if done, yields odorless, brown anchovy paste. Hydatid cysts are staged by ultrasound, with a detached membrane, the water lily sign, or daughter cysts, often with eosinophilia, and schistosomiasis by eggs or antigen in stool and periportal fibrosis on imaging.

Management

HAV is treated supportively, with vaccine or immunoglobulin post-exposure. Acute HBV is treated supportively, with antivirals if severe; chronic HBV is treated with tenofovir or entecavir, or peginterferon-α; and post-exposure and newborns of HBsAg-positive mothers receive vaccine and HBIG. HCV is treated with direct-acting antivirals for 8–12 weeks (e.g. sofosbuvir-based), with cure over 95%. HDV is treated with peginterferon-α and treatment of the HBV. HEV is treated supportively, with ribavirin if chronic. CMV is treated with ganciclovir if immunocompromised, HSV with IV acyclovir started as soon as HSV hepatitis is suspected, and EBV supportively, avoiding contact sports while the spleen is enlarged. HCC screening with ultrasound every 6 months applies in chronic HBV, or HCV with cirrhosis. Pyogenic abscesses are drained and treated with antibiotics; amebic abscesses with metronidazole followed by a luminal agent such as paromomycin, with drainage only in select cases; hydatid cysts with albendazole, adding PAIR or surgery for larger cysts while avoiding spillage, which can cause anaphylaxis; and schistosomiasis with praziquantel.

Relationships to other conditions

. Viral hepatitis rises and falls more slowly, and a very high LDH favors ischemia.

. HEV and HSV both cause severe hepatitis in the third trimester, so viral causes are considered alongside AFLP.

. Autoimmune hepatitis also has a hepatocellular pattern, but viral serologies are negative and ANA, ASMA, and IgG are raised.

. CMV and HSV also cause esophagitis in immunocompromised patients.

Review article

Traumatic liver injury: hemodynamic stability as the decision point

Blunt or penetrating force causes liver lacerations and hematomas, leading to bleeding. Management turns on hemodynamic stability rather than the mechanism alone. Here, we review its causes, complications, and management, and consider how it relates to other causes of RUQ pain.

Key points

  • Hemodynamic stability determines the next test and treatment.
  • Unstable patients have a FAST exam, and stable patients have CT abdomen with IV contrast.
  • Most stable liver injuries heal without surgery.

Pathophysiology

Blunt or penetrating force tears liver tissue, causing RUQ pain. Torn vessels bleed, causing hemoperitoneum and hypovolemic shock, and torn ducts leak, causing biloma and bile peritonitis. Blood that enters the bile ducts causes hemobilia, with RUQ pain, jaundice, and GI bleeding, and blood under the diaphragm causes right shoulder pain.

Etiology

Blunt trauma follows motor vehicle collisions, falls, and assault. Penetrating trauma follows stab wounds and gunshot wounds.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are RUQ pain, right shoulder pain from diaphragm irritation, abdominal distention, and signs of shock. Complications are hemorrhage (hemoperitoneum, hypovolemic shock), bile leak (biloma, bile peritonitis), hemobilia (RUQ pain, jaundice, GI bleeding), and liver abscess.

Diagnosis

Unstable patients have a FAST exam to look for free fluid. Stable patients have CT abdomen with IV contrast to grade the injury. Injuries are graded on the AAST scale from I to VI, and grades I and II make up over half.

Management

Hemodynamically stable patients have nonoperative management with close monitoring, with angioembolization if actively bleeding. Unstable patients with a positive FAST have emergency laparotomy. Most stable liver injuries heal without surgery.

Relationships to other conditions

. Hemobilia can resemble biliary disease, with RUQ pain and jaundice, but GI bleeding after liver trauma points to it.

. Hypovolemic shock from hemorrhage can itself cause ischemic liver injury.

Review article

Autoimmune liver disease: bile duct injury in PBC and PSC, and autoimmune hepatitis

Immune-mediated bile duct damage leads to cholestasis, and retained bile salts cause hepatocellular injury. PBC destroys small intrahepatic ducts, whereas PSC, which is not strictly autoimmune, scars medium and large ducts. Autoimmune hepatitis and IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis complete the group. Here, we review their mechanisms, cholestatic consequences, and treatment, and consider how they relate to IBD and cholangiocarcinoma.

Key points

  • PBC: middle-aged women, AMA-positive, small intrahepatic ducts.
  • PSC: young to middle-aged men, p-ANCA, beaded ducts on MRCP, and most patients have IBD.
  • A cholestatic pattern is first evaluated with RUQ ultrasound, then serology.
  • PSC needs surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder, and colorectal cancer.

Pathophysiology

T cells destroy small intrahepatic bile ducts in PBC, whereas onion-skin fibrosis causes strictures of medium and large ducts in PSC. In both, bile builds up, increasing bile salts in blood, with pruritus, and conjugated bilirubin, with jaundice. Retained bile salts then damage hepatocytes, and ongoing injury leads to fibrosis and cirrhosis.

Etiology and mechanisms

In PBC, AMA is positive in over 90%; T cells destroy small intrahepatic bile ducts, with granulomas around the ducts ("florid duct lesion"), causing loss of bile ducts (ductopenia) and cholestasis. It affects middle-aged women and is associated with other autoimmune diseases: scleroderma (CREST), Hashimoto thyroiditis, rheumatoid arthritis, and Sjögren syndrome. Cancer risk is HCC once cirrhotic. In PSC, p-ANCA is positive in many patients; inflammation and fibrosis of medium and large, intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts, with "onion-skin" fibrosis, cause strictures alternating with dilations ("beaded" ducts on MRCP) and cholestasis. It affects young to middle-aged men and is associated with other p-ANCA-associated diseases: ulcerative colitis, glomerulonephritis, and vasculitis. Cancer risks are HCC, cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder, and colorectal cancer. Autoimmune hepatitis type 1 has ANA and ASMA, in young women with high IgG; type 2 has anti-LKM1, mostly in children. IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis mimics PSC and is steroid-responsive.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are fatigue, pruritus (often the first symptom), jaundice, RUQ discomfort, and xanthomas. Duct destruction or stricture causes cholestasis, with increased bile salts in blood (pruritus), increased conjugated bilirubin (jaundice, dark urine), and increased cholesterol (xanthomas). Decreased bile reaching the gut causes fat malabsorption, with steatorrhea, pale stools, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies (A, D, E, K), and osteoporosis. Toxic bile salts retained in the liver cause hepatocellular injury, fibrosis, biliary cirrhosis, HCC, portal hypertension, and liver failure. In PSC only, chronic bile duct inflammation causes cholangiocarcinoma and recurrent bacterial cholangitis, as bile stagnates behind strictures.

Diagnosis

The cholestatic LFT pattern is markedly increased ALP, increased GGT, increased conjugated bilirubin later, and mildly increased AST/ALT. RUQ ultrasound first rules out extrahepatic obstruction such as gallstones or a mass. Serology follows: AMA, p-ANCA, ANA, ASMA, anti-LKM1, and IgG4. A positive AMA means PBC, with biopsy only if AMA-negative or unclear. p-ANCA or IBD prompts MRCP, in which "beaded" bile ducts mean PSC.

Management

UDCA decreases liver injury and is first line in PBC. Cholestyramine, a bile acid sequestrant, relieves pruritus. Deficiencies are corrected with fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), and calcium and vitamin D for bone health. A dominant stricture in PSC is opened by ERCP with balloon dilation, and end-stage disease is treated by liver transplant. Autoimmune hepatitis is treated with corticosteroids with or without azathioprine, and IgG4-related disease with corticosteroids. PSC needs surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder, and colorectal cancer. In PBC that does not respond to UDCA, obeticholic acid, a farnesoid X receptor agonist, is added.

Relationships to other conditions

. Most PSC patients have IBD, usually ulcerative colitis, so PSC prompts colonoscopy.

. A new dominant stricture with rising CA 19-9 in PSC suggests cholangiocarcinoma. This risk is specific to PSC, not PBC.

. Bile salt deficiency causes fat malabsorption here as it does in other cholestatic disease.

. Both give a cholestatic LFT pattern, but ultrasound finds dilated ducts with stones and non-dilated ducts in PBC.

. IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis can occur with autoimmune pancreatitis.

Buildup of iron, copper, misfolded protein, or fat in hepatocytes causes cellular stress, leading to hepatocellular injury, fibrosis, and cirrhosis.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Misfolded A1AT protein Autosomal codominant
MASLD Fat (triglycerides) Acquired

  2. Buildup in hepatocytesCauses cellular stress
  3. Injury and fibrosisCan progress to cirrhosis

  • BCopperATP7B mutation → decreased copper excretion into bile → copper builds up in the liver
  • CMisfolded proteinA1AT polymerizes → trapped in the hepatocyte ER → hepatocellular injury

  • EFibrosisRepeated cellular stress → fibrosis → cirrhosis

Diagnosis

  • 1HemochromatosisIncreased transferrin saturation (over 45%) First test; increased ferritin; HFE genetic testing (C282Y); liver MRI or biopsy (Prussian blue) if unclear
  • 2Wilson diseaseDecreased serum ceruloplasmin; increased 24-hour urine copper; slit-lamp exam for Kayser-Fleischer rings; liver biopsy (hepatic copper) or ATP7B testing if unclear
  • 3A1AT deficiencyDecreased serum A1AT level; phenotyping or genotyping (PiZZ); liver biopsy: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules; pulmonary function tests and chest CT for emphysema
  • 4MASLDMildly increased ALT more than AST (AST:ALT over 2:1 suggests alcohol); ultrasound: bright (echogenic) liver; fibrosis: FIB-4, then elastography; exclude alcohol, viral hepatitis, and other causes

Treatment

Review article

Metabolic liver disease: iron, copper, misfolded protein, and fat

Buildup of iron, copper, misfolded protein, or fat in hepatocytes causes cellular stress, leading to hepatocellular injury, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Hereditary hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, A1AT deficiency, and MASLD share this path to HCC but differ widely beyond the liver. Here, we review their inheritance, mechanisms, multisystem features, and treatment.

Key points

  • All four can progress through hepatitis and fibrosis to cirrhosis and HCC.
  • Hemochromatosis: decreased hepcidin and increased iron absorption.
  • Wilson disease: ATP7B mutation, low ceruloplasmin, and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
  • A1AT deficiency: protein builds up in the liver and is missing from the lungs.
  • MASLD: cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death.

Pathophysiology

An inherited or acquired defect causes buildup in hepatocytes. In hemochromatosis, decreased hepcidin increases ferroportin activity, and iron causes free radical damage. In Wilson disease, an ATP7B mutation decreases copper excretion into bile, so copper builds up in the liver. In A1AT deficiency, the misfolded protein polymerizes and is trapped in the hepatocyte ER, causing hepatocellular injury. In MASLD, triglycerides accumulate, causing steatosis. Repeated cellular stress leads to fibrosis and cirrhosis.

Hereditary hemochromatosis

Inheritance is autosomal recessive, except ferroportin disease, which is autosomal dominant. Type 1 (HFE, C282Y homozygosity) is most common; type 2A (HJV, hemojuvelin) and type 2B (HAMP, hepcidin) are juvenile, severe, and early in onset; type 3 (TFR2, transferrin receptor 2) is rare; and type 4 (SLC40A1, FPN, ferroportin) resists hepcidin or fails to export iron. HFE, HJV, HAMP, and TFR2 mutations decrease hepcidin, and FPN mutation makes ferroportin resist hepcidin. Increased ferroportin activity increases duodenal iron absorption; iron deposits in the liver, heart, pancreas, and skin, causing free radical damage by the Fenton reaction. Hepcidin normally blocks ferroportin, the only cellular iron exporter.

Wilson disease

Inheritance is autosomal recessive. ATP7B mutation on chromosome 13 decreases copper excretion into bile and loading onto ceruloplasmin; copper builds up in the liver, and free copper in the blood reaches the brain, cornea, kidneys, and RBCs.

A1AT deficiency

Inheritance is autosomal codominant. SERPINA1 mutation (PiZZ genotype) makes misfolded A1AT polymerize. In the liver, it is trapped in the hepatocyte ER (PAS-positive globules), causing hepatocellular injury and cirrhosis. In the lungs, decreased A1AT in blood leaves neutrophil elastase unopposed, causing alveolar wall destruction.

MASLD

MASLD is acquired, and is steatosis plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor, without significant alcohol use (formerly NAFLD). Metabolic syndrome is the main risk factor: central obesity, T2DM, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia (increased TG, decreased HDL), and hypertension. Increased fatty acids reaching the liver and increased fat production cause triglycerides to build up in hepatocytes (steatosis), then lipotoxicity, oxidative stress, and MASH (steatohepatitis).

Clinical presentation and complications

All four can progress from hepatotoxicity to hepatomegaly and hepatitis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, and HCC, with risk especially high in hemochromatosis. Wilson disease can present as acute liver failure with Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia. Beyond the liver, hemochromatosis causes restrictive cardiomyopathy (which can become dilated) and arrhythmias, diabetes mellitus from pancreatic iron, hypogonadism from pituitary iron, hyperpigmentation ("bronze diabetes"), arthropathy of the 2nd and 3rd MCP joints, and infections (Vibrio vulnificus, Yersinia). Wilson disease causes Kayser-Fleischer rings, sunflower cataract, basal ganglia (putamen) disease with tremor, parkinsonism, and psychiatric symptoms, Fanconi syndrome, and Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia. A1AT deficiency causes panniculitis (rare), panacinar emphysema (lower lobes, worse with smoking), and neonatal cholestasis. MASLD causes cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of death, T2DM, CKD, and extrahepatic cancers (e.g. colorectal).

Diagnosis

Hemochromatosis is evaluated first by increased transferrin saturation (over 45%), then increased ferritin, HFE genetic testing (C282Y), and liver MRI or biopsy (Prussian blue) if unclear. Wilson disease is evaluated by decreased serum ceruloplasmin, increased 24-hour urine copper, slit-lamp exam for Kayser-Fleischer rings, and liver biopsy (hepatic copper) or ATP7B testing if unclear. A1AT deficiency is evaluated by decreased serum A1AT level, phenotyping or genotyping (PiZZ), liver biopsy showing PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules, and pulmonary function tests and chest CT for emphysema. MASLD shows mildly increased ALT more than AST (AST:ALT over 2:1 suggests alcohol) and a bright (echogenic) liver on ultrasound; fibrosis is assessed by FIB-4, then elastography, after excluding alcohol, viral hepatitis, and other causes.

Management

Hemochromatosis is treated by therapeutic phlebotomy first, with iron chelation (deferoxamine, deferasirox) if phlebotomy is not possible, and by avoiding iron, vitamin C, alcohol, and raw shellfish. Wilson disease is treated by copper chelation with D-penicillamine or trientine, zinc for maintenance, which blocks intestinal copper absorption, and a low-copper diet that avoids shellfish, liver, nuts, and chocolate. A1AT deficiency is treated by stopping smoking and IV A1AT augmentation therapy for emphysema. MASLD is treated by 7–10% weight loss through diet and exercise first, treating metabolic risk factors (diabetes, lipids, blood pressure), GLP-1 receptor agonists or resmetirom for MASH with fibrosis, and bariatric surgery for severe obesity. Liver transplant treats end-stage disease, and cures the defect in Wilson disease and A1AT deficiency.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both MASLD and alcohol cause steatosis, but ALT exceeds AST in MASLD and AST:ALT is over 2:1 in alcohol.

. Wilson disease is a cause of acute liver failure, and all four feed into cirrhosis.

. A1AT deficiency can cause neonatal cholestasis, and cholestasis itself is the hallmark of PBC and PSC.

Movement disorders. Wilson disease causes parkinsonism and tremor in young patients.

Causes of hepatocellular injury VITAMIN + other

Drugs, toxins, and complications of medical care injure hepatocytes through direct toxicity or immune reactions.

How the agent injures the liver

  • ADirect toxicityIncreased NAPQI → glutathione is used up → zone 3 necrosis
  • BImmune reactionAltered liver proteins after repeat exposure → halothane hepatitis
  • CFatty liverIncreased NADH:NAD+ ratio → increased fatty acid synthesis → steatosis

Three pathways lead to the same result: ADH (cytosol; main pathway), CYP2E1 (induced by chronic drinking), and catalase (peroxisomes; minor).

  2. AcetateVia aldehyde dehydrogenase

  • Amiodarone
  • Methotrexate

  2. 24–72 hoursRUQ pain; rising AST/ALT
  3. 72–96 hoursPeak AST/ALT; liver failure

Always check a paracetamol level after an overdose, even if the patient looks well.

  1. Fatty liverUsually no symptoms; hepatomegaly
  2. Alcoholic hepatitisFever, jaundice, and tender hepatomegaly

  • 3Alcoholic liver diseaseAST:ALT over 2:1 (AST usually under 300 U/L); increased GGT; macrocytosis; alcohol history

Review article

Iatrogenic and toxic liver injury: postoperative, paracetamol, and alcohol

Drugs, toxins, and complications of medical care injure hepatocytes through direct toxicity or immune reactions. Postoperative causes, paracetamol overdose, alcoholic liver disease, and other hepatotoxic drugs each follow a distinct path. Here, we review their mechanisms, staged presentations, and treatment, and consider how they relate to metabolic and vascular liver disease.

Key points

  • The toxic paracetamol dose is over 150 mg/kg, and risk is higher with chronic alcohol use and malnutrition.
  • Always check a paracetamol level after an overdose, even if the patient looks well.
  • NAC replenishes glutathione and works best within 8 hours.
  • Alcoholic liver disease has AST:ALT over 2:1, with AST usually under 300 U/L.

Pathophysiology

Drugs, toxins, and medical care injure hepatocytes directly or through immune reactions. In paracetamol overdose, increased NAPQI uses up glutathione, causing zone 3 necrosis. In halothane hepatitis, altered liver proteins provoke an immune reaction after repeat exposure. In alcohol use, an increased NADH:NAD+ ratio increases fatty acid synthesis, causing steatosis, and acetaldehyde adducts act as new antigens, causing immune activation and alcoholic hepatitis.

Postoperative complications

Intraoperative hypotension causes ischemic hepatitis. Inhaled anesthetics cause halothane hepatitis, which is immune-mediated and follows repeat exposure. Bile duct injury (e.g. cholecystectomy) causes bile leak and bile duct stricture. Blood transfusions and hematoma resorption cause an increased bilirubin load and jaundice. Sepsis and total parenteral nutrition cause cholestasis.

Paracetamol overdose

At a normal dose, ~90% undergoes glucuronidation and sulfation and is safely excreted, and ~5–10% is converted by CYP2E1 to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which glutathione neutralizes, so there is no liver injury. In overdose, glucuronidation and sulfation are saturated, more drug goes through CYP2E1, glutathione is used up, and NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins, causing zone 3 (centrilobular) necrosis. Toxicity is staged: at 0–24 hours, nausea, vomiting, or no symptoms; at 24–72 hours, RUQ pain and rising AST/ALT; at 72–96 hours, peak AST/ALT and liver failure; and at 4 days–2 weeks, recovery or death.

Alcoholic liver disease

Three pathways lead to the same result: ADH (cytosol, main pathway), CYP2E1 (induced by chronic drinking), and catalase (peroxisomes, minor). They produce acetaldehyde with an increased NADH:NAD+ ratio, followed by acetate via aldehyde dehydrogenase. The increased NADH:NAD+ ratio increases fatty acid synthesis and decreases fatty acid breakdown, causing fatty liver (steatosis), which is reversible with abstinence. Acetaldehyde binds proteins, and these acetaldehyde adducts act as new antigens, causing immune activation and free radical damage, leading to alcoholic hepatitis (neutrophils, Mallory-Denk bodies), fibrosis, and cirrhosis. The spectrum runs from fatty liver (usually no symptoms; hepatomegaly) through alcoholic hepatitis (fever, jaundice, tender hepatomegaly) to cirrhosis.

Other hepatotoxic drugs

These include isoniazid, amiodarone, methotrexate, valproate, amoxicillin-clavulanate (cholestatic), and statins (rare). Aspirin given to children during a viral illness, most often influenza or varicella, causes Reye syndrome, an acute encephalopathy with fatty liver failure that begins with vomiting and confusion.

Diagnosis

Paracetamol overdose is evaluated with a 4-hour paracetamol level on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, with LFTs, INR, creatinine, and glucose. Alcoholic liver disease shows AST:ALT over 2:1, with AST usually under 300 U/L, increased GGT, and macrocytosis, with an alcohol history. Drug-induced liver injury rests on the timing of the drug, exclusion of other causes, and improvement after stopping it.

Management

Paracetamol overdose is treated with the antidote NAC, which replenishes glutathione and is best within 8 hours, activated charcoal if within 1–2 hours of ingestion, and transplant evaluation if acute liver failure develops. Alcoholic liver disease is treated by abstinence, the most important measure, nutrition and thiamine, and prednisolone for severe alcoholic hepatitis if the Maddrey score is 32 or more. Postoperative and drug-induced injury is treated by stopping the offending drug, supportive care, and treating the underlying complication.

Relationships to other conditions

. Paracetamol and hypoperfusion both injure zone 3, and intraoperative hypotension links this page to vascular injury.

. Steatosis is shared, and the AST:ALT ratio and alcohol history separate them.

. Paracetamol is a leading cause of acute liver failure, and alcohol of cirrhosis.

. Ethanol and valproate cause pancreatitis as well as liver injury.
