Review article

Liver tumors: distinguishing benign lesions, primary cancers, and metastases

Benign or malignant tumors replace and compress normal liver tissue, and metastases are the most common liver malignancy. Hemangioma, hepatic adenoma, and focal nodular hyperplasia are benign, whereas HCC, cholangiocarcinoma, and angiosarcoma are primary malignancies. Here, we review their features, complications, imaging, and treatment, and consider how they relate to cirrhosis and PSC.

Key points

  • Metastases are the most common liver malignancy, and HCC the most common primary liver cancer.
  • Do not biopsy a hemangioma, because of bleeding risk.
  • In cirrhosis, arterial-phase enhancement with washout diagnoses HCC without biopsy.
  • Hepatic adenoma can rupture, so resect if large (over 5 cm) or bleeding.

Pathophysiology

Tumors replace normal liver, which can cause liver failure, and press on bile ducts, causing obstructive jaundice. Hepatic adenoma and HCC can rupture, causing hemoperitoneum, and HCC can cause polycythemia, hypoglycemia, and hypercalcemia as paraneoplastic effects.

Etiology

Hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor and should not be biopsied, because of bleeding risk. Hepatic adenoma occurs in young women on oral contraceptives and anabolic steroid users, and can rupture and bleed. Focal nodular hyperplasia has a central stellate scar and no malignant potential. Metastases are the most common liver malignancy, from the colon, breast, lung, and pancreas. HCC is the most common primary liver cancer, associated with cirrhosis, HBV, HCV, and aflatoxin. Cholangiocarcinoma is bile duct cancer, associated with PSC and liver flukes. Angiosarcoma is rare, associated with vinyl chloride, arsenic, and Thorotrast. A fibrolamellar variant of HCC affects young patients without cirrhosis.

Clinical presentation and complications

Tumors are often found incidentally, or cause RUQ pain or mass, weight loss, and worsening of known cirrhosis (HCC). Complications are rupture and hemoperitoneum (hepatic adenoma, HCC), paraneoplastic syndromes (HCC: polycythemia, hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia), obstructive jaundice (cholangiocarcinoma), and liver failure.

Diagnosis

Any liver mass is evaluated with multiphase contrast CT or MRI. HCC shows arterial-phase enhancement with washout, with no biopsy needed in cirrhosis, and increased AFP. For metastases, the primary tumor is sought (e.g. colonoscopy, CEA). Unclear imaging is biopsied, but not for hemangioma. Hemangiomas show peripheral, nodular arterial enhancement that fills in toward the center on later phases, and focal nodular hyperplasia, mostly in women aged 20–50, has a central scar. Patients with cirrhosis or chronic HBV are surveyed for HCC with ultrasound, with or without AFP, every 6 months.

Management

Hemangioma and FNH usually need no treatment. Hepatic adenoma is treated by stopping oral contraceptives or steroids, with resection if large (over 5 cm) or bleeding. HCC is treated by resection, transplant (Milan criteria), or ablation if early, and TACE or systemic therapy if advanced. Metastases and cholangiocarcinoma depend on the primary tumor and stage, with resection if possible. Adenomas are resected in all men, and in women if over 5 cm or bleeding, because of the risks of rupture and malignant transformation.

Relationships to other conditions

. Cirrhosis is the main setting for HCC, and HCC screening every 6 months with ultrasound, with or without AFP, is part of its care.

. HBV can cause HCC even without cirrhosis.

. PSC is a major risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.

. HCC is among the malignancies that can cause hepatic vein thrombosis.

Review article

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy: fetal LCHAD deficiency and maternal liver failure

Fetal LCHAD deficiency leads to fatty acid buildup in the maternal liver, causing microvesicular steatosis and acute liver failure in the third trimester. Hypoglycemia and coagulopathy distinguish it from HELLP syndrome. Prompt delivery is the only cure. Here, we review its mechanism, recognition, and management.

Key points

  • AFLP is a third-trimester, fetal-driven cause of maternal liver failure.
  • Hypoglycemia and coagulopathy are common in AFLP and uncommon in HELLP.
  • Prompt delivery is the only cure.
  • The newborn is tested for LCHAD deficiency.

Pathophysiology

In fetal LCHAD deficiency, fetal fatty acids reach the maternal liver and overwhelm its mitochondria, leaving tiny fat droplets in hepatocytes as microvesicular steatosis. Failing hepatocytes cause hypoglycemia, decreased clotting factor synthesis causes increased INR and DIC, and increased ammonia causes encephalopathy, as acute liver failure develops.

Etiology and mechanisms

Fetal LCHAD deficiency, with the mother as a carrier, allows fetal fatty acids to reach the mother. Maternal liver mitochondria are overwhelmed, causing microvesicular steatosis and acute liver failure. Risk factors are the third trimester (usually 30–38 weeks), first pregnancy, twin pregnancy, male fetus, and pre-eclampsia.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, malaise, jaundice, polyuria, and polydipsia. Complications are acute liver failure (hypoglycemia, coagulopathy with DIC, encephalopathy), acute kidney injury, and fetal distress and death.

Diagnosis

Key findings are increased bilirubin, increased AST/ALT (usually under 1000 U/L), decreased glucose, increased INR, decreased fibrinogen, increased ammonia, uric acid, and creatinine, and leukocytosis. Diagnosis is clinical (Swansea criteria), and biopsy is rarely needed.

Management

Prompt delivery is the only cure. Support comprises IV glucose, blood products (FFP, cryoprecipitate), and ICU care. Follow-up includes testing the newborn for LCHAD deficiency and counseling about recurrence.

Relationships to other conditions

HELLP syndrome. Hypoglycemia is common in AFLP and rare in HELLP; coagulopathy is common in AFLP and uncommon in HELLP; hemolysis is uncommon in AFLP and present in HELLP; platelets are normal or mildly low in AFLP and low in HELLP; and hypertension is sometimes present in AFLP and usually present in HELLP. Both are treated with delivery.

. HEV and HSV can also cause fulminant hepatitis in the third trimester, and HSV requires empiric IV acyclovir.

. AFLP is a recognized cause, and shares its big 4 complications.

Acute Liver Failure and Cirrhosis

Pathophysiology

Feature Acute liver failure Cirrhosis
Onset Sudden loss of function Chronic scarring
Mechanism Severe acute injury in a previously healthy liver Repeated injury causes fibrosis and regenerating nodules
Result Encephalopathy and INR 1.5 or more within 26 weeks Distorted architecture raises portal pressure and reduces liver function
  1. Severe or repeated injuryAcute or chronic
  2. Hepatocyte loss or fibrosisWith regenerating nodules in cirrhosis
  3. Lost function and portal hypertensionDepending on the pattern

What the failing liver does

  • AHepatocyte lossSevere acute injury → acute liver failure
  • BFibrosis and nodulesRepeated injury → distorted architecture
  • CPortal hypertensionIncreased sinusoidal pressure → varices, ascites, and splenomegaly
  • DLost synthesisDecreased albumin and clotting factors → ascites, edema, and coagulopathy
  • ELost clearanceDecreased ammonia clearance → hepatic encephalopathy

Review article

Acute liver failure and cirrhosis: sudden and chronic loss of hepatic function

Acute liver failure is a sudden loss of function in a previously healthy liver, whereas cirrhosis is chronic scarring in which repeated injury causes fibrosis and regenerating nodules. Their consequences reflect lost liver function and, in cirrhosis, portal hypertension. Child-Pugh scoring grades cirrhosis severity. Here, we review their causes, complications, workup, and treatment, and consider how every cause of liver injury converges on them.

Key points

  • Acute liver failure is encephalopathy and INR 1.5 or more within 26 weeks in a previously healthy liver.
  • Its big 4 are encephalopathy, coagulopathy, hypoglycemia, and infection.
  • Cirrhosis has two arms: portal hypertension and loss of liver function.
  • Child-Pugh rows spell ABCDE: albumin, bilirubin, coagulation, distention (ascites), and encephalopathy.

Pathophysiology

Severe acute injury causes hepatocyte loss in acute liver failure, whereas repeated injury causes fibrosis and regenerating nodules that distort the architecture in cirrhosis. Increased sinusoidal pressure causes portal hypertension, with varices, ascites, and splenomegaly. Decreased albumin and clotting factor synthesis cause ascites, edema, and coagulopathy, and decreased ammonia clearance causes hepatic encephalopathy.

Mechanisms and etiology

Acute liver failure is severe acute injury in a previously healthy liver, with encephalopathy and INR 1.5 or more within 26 weeks; main causes are paracetamol, viral hepatitis, ischemic injury, Wilson disease, and AFLP. In cirrhosis, repeated injury causes fibrosis and regenerating nodules, and distorted architecture raises portal pressure and reduces liver function; main causes are alcohol, MASLD, HBV, HCV, PBC, PSC, and hemochromatosis.

Acute liver failure: the big 4

Encephalopathy causes altered mental status, asterixis, and increased ICP from cerebral edema. Coagulopathy causes increased PT/INR, intracranial hemorrhage, GI bleeding, and mucocutaneous bleeding. Hypoglycemia follows decreased gluconeogenesis and glycogen stores. Infection includes pneumonia, UTI, and sepsis.

Cirrhosis: portal hypertension

Blood diverts into portosystemic collaterals, causing esophageal varices with life-threatening bleeding, caput medusae, and rectal varices. Increased sinusoidal hydrostatic pressure causes transudative ascites (SAAG 1.1 g/dL or more) and SBP (ascitic neutrophils 250/µL or more). Splanchnic vasodilation from nitric oxide decreases effective arterial volume, with RAAS activation and renal vasoconstriction, causing hepatorenal syndrome (functional kidney failure) and sodium and water retention, worsening ascites. Portosystemic shunting lets ammonia bypass the liver, causing astrocyte swelling, cerebral edema, and hepatic encephalopathy. Splenomegaly causes thrombocytopenia as platelets pool in the spleen.

Cirrhosis: loss of liver function

Decreased ammonia clearance causes hepatic encephalopathy. Decreased clotting factor synthesis causes coagulopathy (increased INR) and bleeding. Decreased bilirubin and bile salt excretion causes jaundice and pruritus. Decreased glucose production causes hypoglycemia. Decreased immune function raises infection risk (SBP, pneumonia, sepsis). Decreased vitamin A, D, E, K processing causes fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies (e.g. osteoporosis, bleeding). Damaged hepatocytes release stored B12, increasing serum B12, which is mostly inactive and rises with severity. Decreased estrogen breakdown increases estrogen, causing spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, and testicular atrophy. Decreased albumin synthesis decreases oncotic pressure, causing ascites and edema.

Child-Pugh score

Points of 1, 2, and 3 are given for albumin (over 3.5, 2.8–3.5, under 2.8 g/dL), bilirubin (under 2, 2–3, over 3 mg/dL), INR (under 1.7, 1.7–2.3, over 2.3), ascites (none, mild, moderate to severe), and encephalopathy (none, grade 1–2, grade 3–4). Class A is 5–6 points (1-year survival about 100%), class B is 7–9 points (about 80%), and class C is 10–15 points (about 45%).

Diagnosis

Acute liver failure is evaluated with LFTs (AST/ALT, bilirubin), complications are checked with INR, glucose, ammonia, and cultures, and the cause is sought with paracetamol, viral and autoimmune serology, and Doppler. Cirrhosis is evaluated with bloods (FBC with low platelets, LFTs, INR, albumin) and ultrasound with elastography showing a nodular, stiff liver, with biopsy as the gold standard if unclear. Complications are screened with EGD and diagnostic paracentesis, and HCC screening is every 6 months with ultrasound, with or without AFP. The MELD score, from bilirubin, creatinine, and INR, predicts short-term mortality and ranks patients for transplant. Hepatopulmonary syndrome is hypoxemia from intrapulmonary vasodilation, with dyspnea and platypnea, confirmed by contrast echocardiography and treated by transplant.

Management

Acute liver failure is managed with ICU care, treating the cause (e.g. NAC), managing the big 4, and early transplant referral. Varices are treated with a non-selective beta-blocker or band ligation. Variceal bleeding is treated with octreotide, IV ABX, and endoscopic banding, with TIPS if refractory. Ascites is treated with sodium restriction, spironolactone with furosemide, and large-volume paracentesis with albumin. SBP is treated with a third-generation cephalosporin plus albumin, with long-term prophylaxis afterwards. Hepatic encephalopathy is treated with lactulose, then rifaximin. Hepatorenal syndrome is treated with albumin plus a vasoconstrictor (e.g. terlipressin) and transplant. End-stage disease is treated by liver transplant.

Relationships to other conditions

. Paracetamol leads to acute liver failure, whereas alcohol leads to cirrhosis.

. Wilson disease can present as acute liver failure, and hemochromatosis and MASLD lead to cirrhosis.

. Budd-Chiari syndrome and congestion also cause portal hypertension, so portal hypertension alone does not mean cirrhosis.

. Cirrhosis is the main setting for HCC.

Review article

Cholelithiasis and biliary colic: gallstone formation and its first symptoms

Excess cholesterol or bilirubin in bile, or bile stasis, leads to crystal formation and gallstones. Most stones are asymptomatic, and biliary colic follows when the gallbladder contracts against an impacted stone. Stone location along the biliary tree determines every later condition. Here, we review stone types, risk factors, and management, and consider how stones lead to cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, and gallstone pancreatitis.

Key points

  • Cholesterol stones are ~75% of gallstones.
  • Their triad is supersaturation, accelerated nucleation, and gallbladder hypomotility.
  • Biliary colic has normal LFTs and no fever; pain over 6 hours or fever suggests cholecystitis.
  • Asymptomatic gallstones need no treatment.

Pathophysiology

Increased cholesterol, or decreased bile salts or phospholipids, supersaturates bile and forms crystals, excess nucleation factors help them grow, and hypomotility keeps bile in the gallbladder long enough for them to become stones. A stone that briefly blocks the cystic duct causes biliary colic, and a persistent block causes cholecystitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

Cholesterol stones are most common (~75%), arise from cholesterol supersaturation, nucleation, and gallbladder hypomotility, and form in the gallbladder. Black pigment stones are less common, arise from chronic hemolysis with increased unconjugated bilirubin (e.g. sickle cell, spherocytosis), cirrhosis, or ileal disease such as Crohn disease, and form in the gallbladder as calcium bilirubinate. Brown pigment stones are less common, though more common in East Asia, arise from bile duct infection with bacteria or parasites (Clonorchis) or from strictures, and form in the bile ducts. Only ~10% of gallstones show on x-ray, depending on their calcium content. The cholesterol triad comprises supersaturation (increased cholesterol secretion into bile, and decreased bile salts or phospholipids to dissolve it), accelerated nucleation (excess nucleation factors such as mucin, and no nucleation inhibitors to stop crystals forming), and gallbladder hypomotility (stasis, giving crystals time to grow into stones). Risk factors are the 6 Fs: female (estrogen raises cholesterol secretion), fat (obesity), fertile (pregnancy, multiparity), forty (age 40 or older), fair (white or Indigenous American ancestry), and family history. Others are rapid weight loss, bariatric surgery, oral contraceptives, estrogen therapy, fibrates, octreotide, fasting, TPN (hypomotility), Crohn disease, and ileal resection (bile salt loss).

Clinical presentation and complications

Cholelithiasis is mostly asymptomatic and often found by chance on imaging. In biliary colic, a heavy, fatty meal triggers CCK release, the gallbladder contracts against an impacted stone, and epigastric or RUQ pain radiates to the back or right scapula, resolving within 6 hours as the stone dislodges. Stones cause disease by location: in the gallbladder, cholelithiasis; in the cystic duct, biliary colic with a brief block or cholecystitis with a persistent block; in the common bile duct, choledocholithiasis, which can lead to cholangitis; and at the ampulla, gallstone pancreatitis. About 1–2% of people with gallstones develop symptoms each year. Complications are acute cholecystitis from a persistent cystic duct block; chronic cholecystitis from repeated colic, which can calcify the wall as porcelain gallbladder; choledocholithiasis, which can lead to cholangitis; gallstone pancreatitis; gallstone ileus, when a large stone passes through a fistula; and gallbladder carcinoma, whose risk rises with stone size and is highest over 3 cm.

Diagnosis

Gallstones are evaluated by RUQ ultrasound, which is first line and shows mobile, shadowing stones. LFTs and FBC assess complications and are normal in biliary colic. Plain x-ray misses most stones, since only ~10% contain enough calcium to show.

Management

Asymptomatic gallstones need no treatment. Biliary colic is treated with pain relief (e.g. NSAIDs), then elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Patients not fit for surgery can have ursodeoxycholic acid, for small cholesterol stones only. Ursodeoxycholic acid dissolves fewer than half of stones.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both come from a cystic duct stone. A brief block gives colic with normal LFTs and no fever; a persistent block gives cholecystitis, with pain over 6 hours and fever.

. Ileal disease causes gallstones by losing bile salts.

. Epigastric pain overlaps, but colic follows a fatty meal and ultrasound shows stones.

  2. Distention and bacterial colonizationIncreased back pressure

  • BDistentionIncreased back pressure → the gallbladder distends

  • 2Mirizzi syndromeStone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck → presses on the common hepatic duct from outside → cholecystitis plus obstructive jaundice; cholestatic LFTs, unlike simple cholecystitis

Symptoms

  • RUQ tenderness
  • Murphy sign
  • Fever
  • Nausea and vomiting

LFTs are usually normal; jaundice suggests a CBD stone or Mirizzi syndrome.

Complications

  • Sepsis
  • Gallbladder empyemapus-filled gallbladder
  • Gangrenous cholecystitisleads to perforation, abscess, and peritonitis

  • Cholecystoenteric fistulaleads to gallstone ileus

  1. Chronic inflammation, large stone

  5. Small bowel obstructionCAVO: colicky pain, abdominal distention, vomiting, and obstipation

  • CauseRepeated biliary colic, with stones in over 90% → ongoing inflammation and fibrosis of the wall
  • SymptomsDull RUQ or epigastric pain after meals, for weeks to months; fever is rare
  • Rokitansky-Aschoff sinusesMucosa herniated into the thickened wall; in ~90% of specimens
  • Porcelain gallbladderWall calcified by chronic inflammation, often found by chance on x-ray or CT; cancer risk is lower than once thought

  • +Unclear ultrasoundHIDA scan: gallbladder does not fill

  • Too unwell for surgery, or acalculousPercutaneous cholecystostomy (drain), with ABX
  • Gangrene, perforation, or emphysematousEmergency cholecystectomy
  • Gallstone ileusEnterolithotomy (remove the stone from the bowel); fistula repair later if needed
  • Mirizzi syndromeCholecystectomy (often open), with ERCP stenting if needed
  • Chronic cholecystitisElective laparoscopic cholecystectomy; low-fat diet if not fit for surgery
  • Porcelain gallbladderCholecystectomy if symptomatic or with selective mucosal calcification; otherwise discuss observation

Review article

Cholecystitis: persistent cystic duct obstruction and gallbladder inflammation

Persistent cystic duct obstruction leads to gallbladder distention and bacterial colonization, causing inflammation of the gallbladder. Calculous disease accounts for ~90–95%, with Mirizzi syndrome and acalculous cholecystitis as important variants. LFTs are usually normal, so jaundice suggests another process. Here, we review its forms, complications, and management, and consider how it relates to biliary colic and choledocholithiasis.

Key points

  • RUQ pain over 6 hours with fever separates cholecystitis from biliary colic.
  • RUQ ultrasound is first line, and HIDA scan is used if ultrasound is unclear.
  • Jaundice suggests a CBD stone or Mirizzi syndrome.
  • Acalculous disease occurs in critically ill patients, with a high risk of gangrene and perforation.

Pathophysiology

A stone obstructs the cystic duct, causing RUQ pain over 6 hours, and increased back pressure distends the gallbladder. Bacterial colonization with E. coli, Klebsiella, and Enterococcus causes fever and sepsis, and the inflamed wall causes RUQ tenderness and Murphy sign. Wall necrosis leads to gangrene, with perforation, abscess, and peritonitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

In calculous cholecystitis (~90–95%), a stone obstructs the cystic duct, causing increased back pressure and gallbladder distention, then bacterial colonization (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus) and gallbladder wall inflammation. In Mirizzi syndrome, a stone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck presses on the common hepatic duct from outside, causing cholecystitis plus obstructive jaundice, with cholestatic LFTs unlike simple cholecystitis. Acalculous cholecystitis occurs in critically ill patients (ICU, burns, sepsis, TPN), with gallbladder stasis and ischemia without a stone, causing inflammation with a high risk of gangrene and perforation. Acalculous disease accounts for ~10% of acute cholecystitis.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are RUQ pain over 6 hours, RUQ tenderness, Murphy sign, fever, and nausea and vomiting. LFTs are usually normal, and jaundice suggests a CBD stone or Mirizzi syndrome. Complications are sepsis, gallbladder empyema (pus-filled gallbladder), gangrenous cholecystitis (leading to perforation, abscess, and peritonitis), emphysematous cholecystitis (gas-forming bacteria, in diabetics), and cholecystoenteric fistula, leading to gallstone ileus. A chronically inflamed gallbladder with a large stone forms a fistula, the stone passes into the bowel, and it lodges at the terminal ileum or ileocecal valve, causing small bowel obstruction (CAVO: colicky pain, abdominal distention, vomiting, obstipation). Emphysematous cholecystitis follows wall ischemia with gas-forming bacteria, especially Clostridium perfringens, mostly in men and diabetics, and carries a high mortality. Chronic cholecystitis follows repeated biliary colic, with stones in over 90%, and causes ongoing inflammation and fibrosis of the wall; it gives dull RUQ or epigastric pain after meals for weeks to months, and fever is rare. Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses, mucosa herniated into the thickened wall, are found in ~90% of specimens. Porcelain gallbladder is a wall calcified by chronic inflammation, often found by chance on x-ray or CT, and its cancer risk is lower than once thought.

Diagnosis

Acute cholecystitis is evaluated by RUQ ultrasound, first line, showing a thick wall, pericholecystic fluid, and sonographic Murphy sign. An unclear ultrasound is followed by HIDA scan, in which the gallbladder does not fill. FBC and LFTs assess inflammation, showing leukocytosis with usually normal LFTs. Mirizzi syndrome is evaluated by MRCP or ERCP, and gallstone ileus by CT, showing Rigler triad. Emphysematous cholecystitis shows gas in the gallbladder wall or lumen on CT. Chronic cholecystitis shows a thick wall and stones on ultrasound, and a HIDA scan with CCK shows an ejection fraction under 35%.

Management

Acute cholecystitis is treated with NPO, IV fluids, pain relief, and IV ABX, then early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours. Patients too unwell for surgery, or with acalculous disease, have percutaneous cholecystostomy (drain) with ABX. Gangrene or perforation requires emergency cholecystectomy. Gallstone ileus is treated by enterolithotomy (removing the stone from the bowel), with fistula repair later if needed. Mirizzi syndrome is treated by cholecystectomy (often open), with ERCP stenting if needed. Emphysematous cholecystitis also needs emergency cholecystectomy. Chronic cholecystitis is treated with elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, or a low-fat diet if the patient is not fit for surgery. Porcelain gallbladder is removed if it causes symptoms or shows selective mucosal calcification; otherwise, observation is discussed with the patient.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both come from a cystic duct stone, but colic is brief, with normal LFTs and no fever.

. Jaundice and a cholestatic pattern move the stone from the cystic duct to the CBD; Mirizzi syndrome mimics this from outside the duct.

. Fever and RUQ pain are shared, but jaundice completes Charcot triad in cholangitis.

. Chronic inflammation with a large stone forms the fistula behind gallstone ileus.

Choledocholithiasis and Gallstone Pancreatitis

Biliary tree diseases Steps 1–4 follow a stone down the tree

  3. 3Choledocho­lithiasis

Pathophysiology

A stone in the common bile duct (CBD) blocks bile flow from the liver, causing cholestasis.

  1. Stone in the CBDBlocks bile flow
  2. CholestasisBile backs up
  3. Jaundice and pale stoolsWith a cholestatic LFT pattern

What the stone does

  • ACBD obstructionA stone stops bile draining into the duodenum
  • BBack pressureIncreased conjugated bilirubin and bile salts → jaundice, pruritus, and dark urine
  • CLess bile in the gutDecreased bile reaching the gut → pale stools
  • DAmpulla obstructionBlocked bile and pancreatic ducts → gallstone pancreatitis
  • EInfectionBacteria behind the blockage → ascending cholangitis

Etiology

  • 1Stone in the common bile ductCBD obstruction → bile cannot drain into the duodenum → increased conjugated bilirubin and bile salts (jaundice, pruritus, dark urine) and decreased bile reaching the gut (pale stools)
  • 2Stone at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater)Ampulla obstruction → blocks both bile and pancreatic ducts → pancreatic enzymes activate inside the pancreas → gallstone pancreatitis (most common cause)

Where the stone forms

  • Secondary stones Up to 90%Form in the gallbladder and migrate into the CBD; usually cholesterol stones
  • Primary stonesForm in the ducts with bile stasis and infection (brown pigment stones); more common in Asia; cause recurrent cholangitis

Complications

  • infection behind the blockage
  • Secondary biliary cirrhosislong-standing obstruction

Diagnosis

  • Increased ALP, GGT
  • Increased conjugated bilirubin
  • AST/ALT can spike early, then fall
  1. RUQ ultrasoundFirst: dilated CBD (over 6 mm, or over 8 mm after cholecystectomy); the stone itself is seen in only 15–40%
  • Low likelihoodNo predictors: cholecystectomy, with intraoperative cholangiography if needed
  • Intermediate likelihoodAbnormal LFTs, dilated CBD, or age over 55: MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound
  • High likelihoodStone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin over 4 mg/dL with a dilated CBD: ERCP diagnoses and removes the stone

  • 1CholedocholithiasisERCP with sphincterotomy and stone removal, then cholecystectomy during the same admission; or both in one operation, by laparoscopic CBD exploration

Choledocholithiasis and gallstone pancreatitis: obstruction of the common channel

A stone in the CBD blocks bile flow from the liver, causing cholestasis, and a stone at the ampulla blocks both bile and pancreatic ducts, causing gallstone pancreatitis. Workup depends on the likelihood of a stone, and treatment aims to clear the duct and remove the gallbladder. Here, we review these mechanisms and their management, and consider how they relate to cholangitis and pancreatitis.

Key points

  • Lipase separates the two: normal in choledocholithiasis and increased 3 or more times in gallstone pancreatitis.
  • High likelihood goes to ERCP; intermediate likelihood goes to MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound.
  • Cholecystectomy is performed during the same admission.

Pathophysiology

A stone in the CBD stops bile draining into the duodenum. Back pressure increases conjugated bilirubin and bile salts, causing jaundice, pruritus, and dark urine, and decreased bile reaching the gut causes pale stools. A stone at the ampulla blocks both bile and pancreatic ducts, causing gallstone pancreatitis, and bacteria behind the blockage cause ascending cholangitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

A stone in the CBD means bile cannot drain into the duodenum, increasing conjugated bilirubin and bile salts, with jaundice, pruritus, and dark urine, and decreasing bile reaching the gut, with pale stools. A stone at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater) blocks both bile and pancreatic ducts, so pancreatic enzymes activate inside the pancreas. Gallstones are the most common cause of pancreatitis. Up to 90% of stones are secondary, forming in the gallbladder and migrating into the CBD, usually as cholesterol stones. Primary stones form in the ducts with bile stasis and infection, as brown pigment stones; they are more common in Asia and cause recurrent cholangitis.

Clinical presentation and complications

Choledocholithiasis causes RUQ pain, jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools, with a cholestatic pattern and normal lipase. Gallstone pancreatitis causes severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting, and may also cause jaundice, with a cholestatic pattern and lipase increased 3 or more times normal. Complications are ascending cholangitis (infection behind the blockage), gallstone pancreatitis, and secondary biliary cirrhosis from long-standing obstruction.

Diagnosis

The cholestatic LFT pattern is increased ALP and GGT, increased conjugated bilirubin, and AST/ALT that can spike early, then fall. RUQ ultrasound comes first, showing a dilated CBD (over 6 mm), although the stone itself is often not seen. Intermediate likelihood (e.g. abnormal LFTs or dilated CBD only) is evaluated by MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound. High likelihood (stone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin over 4 mg/dL with a dilated CBD) proceeds to ERCP, which diagnoses and removes the stone. A dilated CBD is over 6 mm, or over 8 mm after cholecystectomy, and ultrasound shows the stone itself in only 15–40%. Age over 55 is an intermediate predictor, and patients with no predictors proceed to cholecystectomy, with intraoperative cholangiography if needed.

Management

Choledocholithiasis is treated with ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone removal, then cholecystectomy during the same admission. Gallstone pancreatitis is treated with IV fluids, pain relief, and early feeding, with ERCP only if there is cholangitis or ongoing obstruction, and cholecystectomy during the same admission if mild. Alternatively, laparoscopic CBD exploration clears the duct during the cholecystectomy itself.

Relationships to other conditions

. Fever turns an obstructed duct into cholangitis, which needs urgent drainage.

. Cystic duct stones leave LFTs normal, whereas CBD stones produce a cholestatic pattern.

. Stones usually cause painful jaundice, whereas tumors cause painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder.

. Gallstones are the leading cause; the pancreatitis page covers its systemic and local complications.

Ascending Cholangitis

Biliary tree diseases Steps 1–4 follow a stone down the tree

  4. 4Cholangitis

Pathophysiology

Bile duct obstruction lets bacteria ascend from the duodenum, and infected bile under pressure enters the blood, causing sepsis.

  1. Bile duct obstructionUsually a CBD stone
  2. Bacteria ascendFrom the duodenum
  3. Infected bile under pressureEnters the blood

What the obstruction does

  • AObstruction and stasisA blocked duct holds bile still
  • BAscending bacteriaE. coli, Klebsiella, and Enterococcus reach the stagnant bile
  • CRaised pressureInfected bile under pressure → fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice
  • DBacteremiaBacteria and toxins enter the blood → cytokine storm → sepsis

Etiology

Causes of obstruction

  • Most common
  • Benign or malignant stricture
  • Blocked biliary stent, after ERCP

What follows

  • 1Bile duct obstruction and stasisBacteria ascend from the duodenum (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus)
  • 2Infected bile under pressureBacteria and toxins enter the blood

Symptoms and complications

  1. Charcot triadFever, RUQ pain, and jaundice; specific, but all three in only ~25%
  2. Cytokine stormSepsis
  3. Reynolds pentad+ hypotension and confusion

Reynolds pentad means septic shock and needs urgent biliary drainage.

Diagnosis

  • InflammationFBC (leukocytosis), CRP, and blood cultures
  • CholestasisLFTs: cholestatic pattern with increased bilirubin
  • Obstruction and causeUltrasound or CT (dilated bile ducts); MRCP if unclear

The Tokyo Guidelines combine these three findings to diagnose and grade cholangitis.

Treatment

  • ResuscitateIV fluids; vasopressors if in shock
  • Treat infectionBroad-spectrum IV ABX (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam)
  • Drain the bileERCP with stone removal or stent Definitive; percutaneous drainage if ERCP fails
  • TimingSevere (shock or organ failure): urgent drainage; mild: 80–90% respond to ABX, with drainage before discharge
  • Prevent recurrenceCholecystectomy once recovered, if gallstones were the cause

Ascending cholangitis: infected obstruction and the need for drainage

Bile duct obstruction lets bacteria ascend from the duodenum, and infected bile under pressure enters the blood, causing sepsis. A CBD stone is the most common cause. Charcot triad progresses to Reynolds pentad as septic shock develops. Here, we review its causes, recognition, and management, and consider how it relates to other biliary disease.

Key points

  • Charcot triad is fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice.
  • Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and confusion, and means septic shock.
  • ERCP with stone removal or stent is definitive.
  • The Tokyo Guidelines combine inflammation, cholestasis, and obstruction.

Pathophysiology

A blocked duct holds bile still, and E. coli, Klebsiella, and Enterococcus ascend from the duodenum into it. Infected bile under pressure causes fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice, and bacteria and toxins that enter the blood cause a cytokine storm and sepsis.

Etiology and mechanisms

Causes are a CBD stone (most common), benign or malignant stricture, a blocked biliary stent after ERCP, and PSC. Bile duct obstruction and stasis allow bacteria to ascend from the duodenum (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus). Infected bile under pressure allows bacteria and toxins to enter the blood.

Clinical presentation and complications

Charcot triad is fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice. A cytokine storm causes sepsis, leading to Reynolds pentad, which adds hypotension and confusion. Reynolds pentad means septic shock and needs urgent biliary drainage. Charcot triad is specific, but only ~25% of patients have all three features.

Diagnosis

Inflammation is evaluated with FBC (leukocytosis), CRP, and blood cultures; cholestasis with LFTs, showing a cholestatic pattern with increased bilirubin; and obstruction and its cause with ultrasound or CT (dilated bile ducts), with MRCP if unclear. The Tokyo Guidelines combine these three findings to diagnose and grade cholangitis.

Management

Resuscitation uses IV fluids, with vasopressors if in shock. Infection is treated with broad-spectrum IV ABX (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam). Bile is drained by ERCP with stone removal or stent, which is definitive, with percutaneous drainage if ERCP fails. Recurrence is prevented by cholecystectomy once recovered, if gallstones were the cause. Severe disease, with shock or organ failure, needs urgent drainage, while 80–90% of mild cases respond to ABX and are drained before discharge.

Relationships to other conditions

. An uninfected CBD stone causes jaundice and pain without fever; fever marks the step to cholangitis.

. RUQ pain and fever without jaundice suggest cholecystitis rather than cholangitis.

. Strictures in PSC cause recurrent bacterial cholangitis as bile stagnates behind them.

. Fistulas also let gut bacteria enter the bile ducts.

Pathophysiology

Chronic inflammation and pressure from a large stone erode into a neighboring organ, creating a fistula.

  1. Chronic inflammationWith a large stone
  2. ErosionInto a neighboring organ
  3. FistulaUsually to the duodenum

What the erosion does

  • AChronic inflammationInflammation weakens the gallbladder wall
  • BPressure from a large stoneThe stone presses on the weakened wall
  • CFistulaA tract opens into a neighboring organ
  • DStone passageThe stone enters the bowel → gallstone ileus
  • EGut bacteriaBacteria enter the bile ducts → ascending cholangitis

Etiology

  • 1Cholecystoduodenal Most commonGallbladder and duodenum (~68%); main route for gallstone ileus; Bouveret syndrome if the stone blocks the pylorus or duodenum
  • 2CholecystocolicGallbladder and colon (~17%); bile acid diarrhea; stones may pass in the stool
  • 3CholecystogastricGallbladder and stomach (~5%); can cause gastric outlet obstruction
  • 4CholecystocholedochalGallbladder and common bile duct; advanced
  • 5CholedochoduodenalCommon bile duct and duodenum; penetrating duodenal ulcer or CBD stones

Causes

  • Gallstones: most cases, especially large stones
  • Malignancy
  • Trauma or surgery

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms

  • Often none
  • Recurrent cholangitis
  • Diarrhea (cholecystocolic)

Complications

  • Gallstone ileussmall bowel obstruction (CAVO) at the terminal ileum; stones over 2 cm; mostly older women
  • Bouveret syndromegastric outlet obstruction: vomiting and epigastric fullness
  • Ascending cholangitisgut bacteria enter the bile ducts
  • GI bleeding

Diagnosis

  • Suspected fistulaCT abdomen: pneumobilia
  • Gallstone ileusCT: Rigler triad (sensitivity ~93%); x-ray may also show it
  • Fistula openingERCP or upper endoscopy

Treatment

  • Symptomatic fistulaCholecystectomy with fistula repair
  • Gallstone ileusEnterolithotomy first, usually open; fistula repair later if needed
  • Bouveret syndromeEndoscopic stone removal; surgery if this fails

Biliary fistulas: erosion from the biliary tree into neighboring organs

Chronic inflammation and pressure from a large stone erode into a neighboring organ, creating a fistula. Cholecystoduodenal fistulas are most common. Many patients have no symptoms, but stones can pass through and obstruct the bowel. Here, we review fistula types, complications, and treatment, and consider how they relate to cholecystitis and cholangitis.

Key points

  • Cholecystoduodenal fistula is the most common type and the main route for gallstone ileus.
  • Pneumobilia on CT suggests a fistula; Rigler triad suggests gallstone ileus.
  • Gallstone ileus is treated by enterolithotomy first.

Pathophysiology

Chronic inflammation weakens the gallbladder wall, a large stone presses on it, and a tract opens into a neighboring organ. A stone that enters the bowel can cause gallstone ileus, and gut bacteria that enter the bile ducts cause ascending cholangitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

Cholecystoduodenal fistula connects the gallbladder and duodenum and is the main route for gallstone ileus, with Bouveret syndrome if the stone blocks the pylorus or duodenum. Cholecystocolic fistula connects the gallbladder and colon, causing bile acid diarrhea, and stones may pass in the stool. Cholecystogastric fistula connects the gallbladder and stomach and can cause gastric outlet obstruction. Cholecystocholedochal fistula connects the gallbladder and common bile duct, as in advanced Mirizzi syndrome. Choledochoduodenal fistula connects the common bile duct and duodenum, from a penetrating duodenal ulcer or CBD stones. Causes are gallstones (most cases, especially large stones), peptic ulcer disease, malignancy, trauma or surgery, and Crohn disease. Of biliary-enteric fistulas, ~68% are cholecystoduodenal, ~17% cholecystocolic, and ~5% cholecystogastric.

Clinical presentation and complications

Fistulas often cause no symptoms, or recurrent cholangitis, and diarrhea in cholecystocolic disease. Complications are gallstone ileus (small bowel obstruction, CAVO), Bouveret syndrome (gastric outlet obstruction with vomiting and epigastric fullness), ascending cholangitis as gut bacteria enter the bile ducts, and GI bleeding. Gallstone ileus usually impacts at the terminal ileum, mostly with stones over 2 cm, and mainly affects older women.

Diagnosis

A suspected fistula is evaluated by CT abdomen, showing pneumobilia. Gallstone ileus is evaluated by CT, showing Rigler triad. The fistula opening is evaluated by ERCP or upper endoscopy. CT detects Rigler triad with a sensitivity of ~93%, and an x-ray may also show it.

Management

A symptomatic fistula is treated by cholecystectomy with fistula repair. Gallstone ileus is treated by enterolithotomy first, with fistula repair later if needed. Bouveret syndrome is treated by endoscopic stone removal, with surgery if this fails. Enterolithotomy is usually open.

Relationships to other conditions

. Fistulas are a late consequence of chronic inflammation with a large stone.

. A penetrating duodenal ulcer can form a choledochoduodenal fistula, and both can cause gastric outlet obstruction.

. Crohn disease forms fistulas by a different route, through transmural inflammation.

. Bile acid diarrhea from a cholecystocolic fistula is a rare cause to remember in older patients with gallstones.

Biliary tree diseases Steps 1–4 follow a stone down the tree

  6. 6Malignancies

Pathophysiology

Tumors in or around the bile ducts gradually obstruct bile flow, causing painless obstructive jaundice.

  1. Tumor in or around the ductsGrows slowly
  2. Gradual obstructionOf bile flow
  3. Painless obstructive jaundiceWith weight loss

What the tumor does

  • ATumor growthTumor below the cystic duct → slow, steady blockage
  • BBile duct obstructionBile cannot reach the gut → pale stools
  • CBack pressureBile builds up → painless jaundice, pruritus, and dark urine
  • DCourvoisier gallbladderHealthy, stretchy wall → enlarged, palpable, nontender gallbladder

Etiology

  • 1Pancreatic head adenocarcinomaMost common periampullary cancer ; smoking, chronic pancreatitis, and diabetes
  • 2Ampullary adenocarcinomaBlocks bile early, so found earlier and has a better prognosis; may cause intermittent jaundice; FAP and Lynch syndrome
  • 3Duodenal adenocarcinomaRare; may also cause GI bleeding or obstruction; FAP, Lynch syndrome, and celiac disease
  • 4Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumorsFrom islet cells; may secrete hormones (insulinoma, gastrinoma, vipoma, glucagonoma); MEN1
  • 5Bile duct adenocarcinoma (cholangiocarcinoma)Perihilar (Klatskin) ~50%, distal ~40%, intrahepatic ~10%; , liver flukes (Clonorchis), choledochal cysts, hepatitis B or C, and cirrhosis
  • 6Gallbladder carcinomaOften found late, or by chance after cholecystectomy (over half); older women; gallstones (especially over 3 cm), porcelain gallbladder (lower risk than once thought), polyps over 1 cm, and PSC

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms

  • Painless jaundice
  • Pruritus
  • Dark urine, pale stools
  • Weight loss
  • Palpable, nontender gallbladder

Courvoisier law

  • Malignant obstructionTumor below the cystic duct (pancreatic head, ampulla, distal CBD) → slow, steady blockage; gallbladder wall is healthy and stretchy → enlarged, palpable, nontender gallbladder with painless jaundice
  • Gallstone obstructionStone in the CBD → repeated inflammation has already scarred the gallbladder → shrunken gallbladder that cannot distend, usually with pain

Courvoisier law: painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder is unlikely to be caused by gallstones, so suspect malignancy.

Complications

  • Ascending cholangitis
  • Liver metastases
  • Gastric outlet obstruction

Diagnosis

  • CholestasisLFTs
  • Tumor markersCA 19-9 and CEA: not for screening
  • ImagingUltrasound, then CT or MRCP: double duct sign
  • Tissue diagnosisERCP brushings or endoscopic ultrasound biopsy

Treatment

  • 1–3Periampullary tumorsPancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) if resectable
  • 5CholangiocarcinomaResection (bile duct, often with part of the liver); transplant in selected cases
  • 6Gallbladder carcinomaCholecystectomy alone if confined to the mucosa; otherwise with liver resection and lymph node removal
  • +Unresectable diseaseBiliary stent to relieve jaundice; chemotherapy

Biliary tract and periampullary malignancies: painless obstruction of bile flow

Tumors in or around the bile ducts gradually obstruct bile flow, causing painless obstructive jaundice. Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma is the most common periampullary cancer, and cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma arise within the biliary tree. Courvoisier law separates malignant from gallstone obstruction. Here, we review their features, workup, and treatment, and consider how they relate to gallstone disease and PSC.

Key points

  • Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder suggests malignancy.
  • The double duct sign supports a periampullary tumor.
  • CA 19-9 and CEA are not for screening.
  • Resectable periampullary tumors are treated by pancreaticoduodenectomy.

Pathophysiology

A tumor below the cystic duct causes a slow, steady blockage of bile flow. Bile cannot reach the gut, causing pale stools, and builds up behind the block, causing painless jaundice, pruritus, and dark urine. Because the gallbladder wall is healthy and stretchy, it enlarges into a palpable, nontender gallbladder.

Etiology

Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma is the most common periampullary cancer, with risk factors of smoking, chronic pancreatitis, and diabetes. Ampullary adenocarcinoma blocks bile early, so it is found earlier and has a better prognosis, may cause intermittent jaundice, and is linked to FAP. Duodenal adenocarcinoma is rare, may also cause GI bleeding or obstruction, and is linked to FAP, Lynch syndrome, and celiac disease. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from islet cells and may secrete hormones (insulinoma, gastrinoma, vipoma, glucagonoma), with MEN1 as a risk factor. Bile duct adenocarcinoma (cholangiocarcinoma) is intrahepatic, perihilar, or distal, with perihilar (Klatskin) most common, and risk factors of PSC, liver flukes (Clonorchis), and choledochal cysts. Gallbladder carcinoma is often found late, or by chance after cholecystectomy, in older women, with risk factors of gallstones (especially large), porcelain gallbladder, polyps over 1 cm, and PSC. Lynch syndrome also raises the risk of ampullary cancer. Of cholangiocarcinomas, ~50% are perihilar, ~40% distal, and ~10% intrahepatic, and hepatitis B or C and cirrhosis also raise the risk. More than half of gallbladder carcinomas are found by chance at cholecystectomy; the risk is highest with stones over 3 cm, and the risk from porcelain gallbladder is lower than once thought.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms are painless jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools, weight loss, and a palpable, nontender gallbladder. In malignant obstruction, a tumor below the cystic duct (pancreatic head, ampulla, distal CBD) causes slow, steady blockage of a healthy, stretchy gallbladder, producing an enlarged, palpable, nontender gallbladder with painless jaundice. In gallstone obstruction, a stone in the CBD meets a gallbladder already scarred by repeated inflammation, which cannot distend, usually with pain. Courvoisier law states that painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder is unlikely to be caused by gallstones, so malignancy is suspected. Complications are ascending cholangitis, liver metastases, and gastric outlet obstruction.

Diagnosis

Cholestasis is evaluated by LFTs. Tumor markers are CA 19-9 and CEA, which are not for screening. Imaging is ultrasound, then CT or MRCP, which may show the double duct sign. Tissue diagnosis is by ERCP brushings or endoscopic ultrasound biopsy.

Management

Periampullary tumors are treated by pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) if resectable. Cholangiocarcinoma is treated by resection (bile duct, often with part of the liver), with transplant in selected cases. Gallbladder carcinoma is treated by cholecystectomy with liver resection and lymph node removal. Unresectable disease is treated with a biliary stent to relieve jaundice, and chemotherapy. Gallbladder carcinoma confined to the mucosa needs only cholecystectomy.

Relationships to other conditions

. Pain and a shrunken gallbladder favor stones; painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder favors malignancy.

. PSC raises the risk of cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma.

. Chronic pancreatitis is a risk factor for pancreatic head adenocarcinoma.

. Gastrinomas and vipomas link pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors to chronic secretory diarrhea.

. Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma overlaps with primary liver malignancy.

Acute Pancreatitis

Pathophysiology

Premature activation of trypsin inside the pancreas leads to autodigestion, causing local and systemic inflammation.

  1. Premature trypsin activationInside the pancreas
  2. AutodigestionOf pancreatic tissue
  3. Local and systemic inflammationCan cause SIRS

What trypsin does

  • ATrypsin activationTrypsin is activated inside the pancreas
  • BAutodigestionEnzymes digest the pancreas → epigastric pain
  • CCytokine releaseIncreased IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α → SIRS
  • DLeaky capillariesIncreased capillary permeability → third spacing → hypovolemia and shock
  • EFat saponificationLipase digests fat → fatty acids bind calcium → hypocalcemia

Etiology

I GET SMASHED

Letter Cause Notes
I Idiopathic No cause found in about 10–20%
G Most common Stone blocks the ampulla
E Ethanol 2nd most common Direct acinar toxicity, protein plugs in ducts
T Trauma Blunt abdominal trauma, e.g. bicycle handlebar injury
S Steroids —
M Mumps Also other infections, e.g. coxsackievirus, CMV
A Autoimmune IgG4-related autoimmune pancreatitis, SLE, polyarteritis nodosa
S Scorpion sting Tityus trinitatis (Trinidad)
H Hypercalcemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hypothermia Triglycerides usually over 1000 mg/dL
E ERCP Most common complication of ERCP
D Drugs Azathioprine, valproate, thiazides, furosemide, sulfonamides, didanosine

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms

  • Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Fever, tachycardia
  • Epigastric tenderness, guarding

Acute process

  1. Trypsin activated inside the pancreas
  2. Pancreatic autodigestionEpigastric pain; increased IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α
  3. SIRS and local pancreatic complications

Systemic complications (SIRS)

  • Leaky capillariesIncreased capillary permeability → third spacing → hypovolemia, fluid in the lungs, and fluid in the abdomen → shock, AKI, ARDS, exudative ascites, and abdominal compartment syndrome
  • ClottingIncreased tissue factor → increased clotting throughout small vessels → platelets and clotting factors used up, and red cells sheared (schistocytes) → DIC
  • MetabolicLipase digests surrounding fat → fatty acids bind calcium (fat saponification) → hypocalcemia; hyperglycemia from islet damage

Local pancreatic complications

  • Interstitial edematous pancreatitisPancreatic edema → fluid collects around the pancreas → pseudocyst (after 4 weeks; no epithelium) → infection, rupture, and compression: small bowel or gastric outlet obstruction
  • Necrotizing pancreatitisTissue necrosis → acute necrotic collection and enzymes erode blood vessels → walled-off necrosis (after 4 weeks) and retroperitoneal bleeding (Cullen and Grey Turner signs)

Repeated attacks can lead to chronic pancreatitis.

Chronic pancreatitis

  • CausesAlcohol in adults, though under 10% of heavy drinkers develop it; smoking; in children, cystic fibrosis and genes such as PRSS1, SPINK1, and CFTR
  • MechanismProtein plugs in the ducts → calcification and stones → fibrosis replaces the gland
  • PainChronic epigastric pain, often better leaning forward, with pain-free periods
  • Exocrine failureSteatorrhea and weight loss once over 90% of the gland is damaged
  • Endocrine failurePancreatogenic (type 3c) diabetes
  • CancerRaised risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma

Diagnosis

Any 2 of 3 criteria

  • PainAcute, severe epigastric pain, often radiating to the back
  • EnzymesLipase (or amylase) at least 3 times the upper limit of normal; lipase is more specific
  • ImagingTypical findings on contrast CT abdomen (or MRI, ultrasound)

Find the cause and judge severity

  • CauseRUQ ultrasound for gallstones in every patient; LFTs (ALT over 150 suggests gallstones); triglycerides, calcium, alcohol history, and medications
  • ComplicationsContrast CT if the diagnosis is unclear, or after 48–72 hours if the patient is not improving; CT too early can miss necrosis
  • SeverityFBC, creatinine, BUN, oxygen saturation, and scores such as BISAP

Severity (revised Atlanta classification)

  • MildNo organ failure and no local complications
  • Moderately severeOrgan failure lasting under 48 hours, or local complications
  • SevereOrgan failure lasting over 48 hours

Chronic pancreatitis

  • ImagingCT or MRCP: calcifications, the hallmark, with duct dilation, strictures, or stones
  • Exocrine functionFecal elastase (normal over 500 µg/g), or 72-hour fecal fat over 7 g a day, the most definitive test

Treatment

  • Supportive careIV fluids (goal-directed, e.g. Hartmann solution), pain relief, and early oral feeding; enteral feeding if severe
  • Treat the causeGallstones: cholecystectomy during the same admission
    Alcohol: stop drinking
    Hypertriglyceridemia: insulin infusion
    Drugs: stop the offending drug
  • Infected necrosisABX (e.g. carbapenem); delayed drainage or necrosectomy, ideally after 4 weeks; no prophylactic ABX
  • PseudocystObserve; drain only if symptomatic or complicated

Chronic pancreatitis

  • Every patientStop alcohol and smoking
  • PainParacetamol, NSAIDs, or pregabalin first, opioids only if these fail; celiac plexus block; ERCP or shock wave lithotripsy for obstructing stones or strictures
  • SteatorrheaPancreatic enzyme replacement with meals; it does not relieve pain

  2. Goosenberg E, Lappin SL. Chronic Pancreatitis. 2025. In: StatPearls. StatPearls Publishing. NBK482325
  3. Al Zureikat Q, Goosenberg E, Sood T. Pancreatic Pseudocyst. 2026. In: StatPearls. StatPearls Publishing. NBK557594

Acute pancreatitis: autodigestion and its local and systemic consequences

Premature activation of trypsin inside the pancreas leads to autodigestion, causing local and systemic inflammation. Gallstones and ethanol are the leading causes in the I GET SMASHED mnemonic. Diagnosis requires 2 of 3 criteria, and severity is graded by organ failure and local complications. Here, we review its causes, complications, and management, and consider how it relates to biliary disease and malabsorption.

Key points

  • Gallstones are the most common cause, and ethanol the second.
  • Diagnosis requires any 2 of pain, enzymes, and imaging.
  • RUQ ultrasound is obtained in every patient.
  • CT too early can miss necrosis.
  • Prophylactic ABX are not given.

Pathophysiology

Trypsin is activated inside the pancreas, and the enzymes digest the gland, causing epigastric pain. Increased IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α cause SIRS. Increased capillary permeability causes third spacing, with hypovolemia and shock, and lipase digests surrounding fat, releasing fatty acids that bind calcium and cause hypocalcemia.

Etiology and mechanisms

I GET SMASHED covers idiopathic disease, with no cause found in about 10–20%; gallstones, the most common cause, in which a stone blocks the ampulla; ethanol, the second most common, through direct acinar toxicity and protein plugs in ducts; trauma, such as blunt abdominal trauma from a bicycle handlebar injury; steroids; mumps and other infections, such as coxsackievirus and CMV; autoimmune causes, including IgG4-related autoimmune pancreatitis, SLE, and polyarteritis nodosa; scorpion sting (Tityus trinitatis, Trinidad); hypercalcemia, hypertriglyceridemia (usually over 1000 mg/dL), and hypothermia; ERCP, of which it is the most common complication; and drugs, including azathioprine, valproate, thiazides, furosemide, sulfonamides, and didanosine.

Clinical presentation and complications

Patients have severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea and vomiting, fever, tachycardia, and epigastric tenderness and guarding. Trypsin activated inside the pancreas causes autodigestion, with epigastric pain and increased IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α, leading to SIRS and local complications. Systemically, increased capillary permeability causes third spacing, with hypovolemia and fluid in the lungs and abdomen, leading to shock, AKI, ARDS, exudative ascites, and abdominal compartment syndrome. Increased tissue factor causes clotting throughout small vessels, consuming platelets and clotting factors and shearing red cells (schistocytes), leading to DIC. Lipase digests surrounding fat, and fatty acids bind calcium (fat saponification), causing hypocalcemia; islet damage causes hyperglycemia. Locally, interstitial edematous pancreatitis causes pancreatic edema and fluid around the pancreas, forming a pseudocyst after 4 weeks, with no epithelium, which can cause infection, rupture, and compression with small bowel or gastric outlet obstruction. Necrotizing pancreatitis causes tissue necrosis and an acute necrotic collection, becoming walled-off necrosis after 4 weeks; enzymes erode blood vessels, causing retroperitoneal bleeding (Cullen and Grey Turner signs). Repeated attacks can lead to chronic pancreatitis. Chronic pancreatitis is most often caused by alcohol in adults, though under 10% of heavy drinkers develop it, and by smoking; in children, cystic fibrosis and genes such as PRSS1, SPINK1, and CFTR are responsible. Protein plugs in the ducts calcify and form stones, and fibrosis replaces the gland. It causes chronic epigastric pain, often better leaning forward, with pain-free periods; steatorrhea and weight loss once over 90% of the gland is damaged; pancreatogenic (type 3c) diabetes; and a raised risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

Diagnosis

Any 2 of 3 criteria are required: acute, severe epigastric pain, often radiating to the back; lipase (or amylase) at least 3 times the upper limit of normal, with lipase more specific; and typical findings on contrast CT abdomen, MRI, or ultrasound. The cause is sought with RUQ ultrasound for gallstones in every patient, LFTs (ALT over 150 suggests gallstones), triglycerides, calcium, alcohol history, and medications. Contrast CT is obtained if the diagnosis is unclear, or after 48–72 hours if the patient is not improving, as CT too early can miss necrosis. Severity is assessed with FBC, creatinine, BUN, oxygen saturation, and scores such as BISAP. By the revised Atlanta classification, mild disease has no organ failure and no local complications, moderately severe disease has organ failure lasting under 48 hours or local complications, and severe disease has organ failure lasting over 48 hours. Chronic pancreatitis is shown by calcifications, its hallmark, on CT or MRCP, with duct dilation, strictures, or stones, and exocrine function is assessed with fecal elastase (normal over 500 µg/g) or a 72-hour fecal fat over 7 g a day, the most definitive test.

Management

Supportive care comprises goal-directed IV fluids (e.g. Hartmann solution), pain relief, and early oral feeding, with enteral feeding if severe. The cause is treated: cholecystectomy during the same admission for gallstones, stopping drinking for alcohol, insulin infusion for hypertriglyceridemia, and stopping the offending drug. Infected necrosis is treated with ABX (e.g. carbapenem) and delayed drainage or necrosectomy, ideally after 4 weeks, with no prophylactic ABX. Pseudocysts are observed, and drained only if symptomatic or complicated. In chronic pancreatitis, every patient stops alcohol and smoking. Pain is treated with paracetamol, NSAIDs, or pregabalin first and opioids only if these fail, with celiac plexus block, and ERCP or shock wave lithotripsy for obstructing stones or strictures. Steatorrhea is treated with pancreatic enzyme replacement with meals, which does not relieve pain.

Relationships to other conditions

. A stone at the ampulla blocks both bile and pancreatic ducts. A cholestatic LFT pattern and ALT over 150 favor a gallstone cause.

. Repeated attacks lead to chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic insufficiency.

. Epigastric pain overlaps; radiation to the back and increased lipase favor pancreatitis, and pain that changes with meals favors PUD.

. Autoimmune pancreatitis can occur with IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis.

. Painless jaundice favors a pancreatic head tumor over pancreatitis.

Appendicitis

Pathophysiology

Obstruction of the appendix lumen leads to increased pressure, infection, and ischemia, causing inflammation and eventually perforation.

  1. Obstruction of the lumenFecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia, or neoplasm
  2. Increased pressure and infectionWith distention
  3. Ischemia and inflammationCan lead to perforation

What the obstruction does

  • AObstructionA fecalith or lymphoid tissue blocks the lumen
  • BDistention and infectionIncreased intraluminal pressure → periumbilical visceral pain
  • CIschemiaPressure compresses the wall → infarction, and inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum → sharp RLQ pain
  • DPerforationDead wall ruptures → abscess and peritonitis

Etiology

  • 1FecalithMost common in adults
  • 2Lymphoid hyperplasiaChildren; after viral infection
  • 3Neoplasme.g. carcinoid; older adults

What follows

  1. Increased intraluminal pressure
  2. Distention and infection
  3. Ischemia and infarction
  4. Perforation and abscess

Symptoms and complications

Migrating pain

  1. Periumbilical painVisceral pain (T8–T10)
  2. Inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneumOver 12–24 hours
  3. Sharp, localized RLQ pain

Associated with:

  • Anorexia
  • Nausea and vomiting after the pain
  • Low-grade fever

Examination signs

SignHow it is elicitedSuggests
McBurney pointTenderness one-third of the way from the right ASIS to the umbilicusTypical appendix position
Rovsing signPressing on the LLQ causes pain in the RLQPeritoneal irritation in the RLQ
Psoas signPain on extending the right hip (patient lying on the left side)Retrocecal appendix irritating the iliopsoas
Obturator signPain on internally rotating the flexed right hipPelvic appendix irritating the obturator internus
Rebound tenderness, guardingPain when pressure is released; tense abdominal wallPeritonitis

Complications

  • Perforationafter 48–72 hours; young children and older adults
  • Abscess or phlegmon

  • AdultsCT AP with contrast: appendix over 6 mm, fat stranding

Review article

Appendicitis: luminal obstruction, migrating pain, and perforation

Obstruction of the appendix lumen leads to increased pressure, infection, and ischemia, causing inflammation and eventually perforation. Pain classically migrates from the periumbilical region to the RLQ as inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum. Here, we review its causes, examination signs, age-specific imaging, and treatment, and consider how it relates to diverticulitis and other causes of abdominal pain.

Key points

  • Fecalith is the most common cause in adults, and lymphoid hyperplasia in children.
  • Pain migrates from visceral (T8–T10) to parietal over 12–24 hours.
  • Imaging depends on the patient: CT AP in adults, and ultrasound first in children and pregnancy.
  • Diagnosis is often clinical.

Pathophysiology

A fecalith or lymphoid tissue blocks the lumen, and increased intraluminal pressure causes distention and infection, with periumbilical visceral pain. Pressure then compresses the wall, causing ischemia and infarction, inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, causing sharp RLQ pain, and the dead wall ruptures, causing abscess and peritonitis.

Etiology and mechanisms

Obstruction arises from a fecalith, most common in adults; lymphoid hyperplasia, in children and after viral infection; or a neoplasm, such as carcinoid, in older adults. Increased intraluminal pressure causes distention and infection, then ischemia and infarction, then perforation and abscess.

Clinical presentation and complications

Periumbilical visceral pain (T10) moves to sharp, localized RLQ pain as inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum over 12–24 hours, with anorexia, nausea and vomiting after the pain, and low-grade fever. McBurney point is tenderness one-third of the way from the right ASIS to the umbilicus and suggests typical appendix position. Rovsing sign is pain in the RLQ on pressing the LLQ, suggesting peritoneal irritation in the RLQ. Psoas sign is pain on extending the right hip with the patient lying on the left side, suggesting a retrocecal appendix irritating the iliopsoas. Obturator sign is pain on internally rotating the flexed right hip, suggesting a pelvic appendix irritating the obturator internus. Rebound tenderness and guarding, with pain when pressure is released and a tense abdominal wall, suggest peritonitis. Complications are perforation after 48–72 hours, particularly in young children and older adults; abscess or phlegmon; and generalized peritonitis and sepsis.

Diagnosis

Bloods show leukocytosis with left shift and CRP, β-hCG is obtained in anyone who could be pregnant to rule out ectopic pregnancy, and urinalysis is performed. Adults have CT AP with contrast, showing an appendix over 6 mm and fat stranding. Children and pregnant patients have ultrasound first to avoid radiation, with MRI if unclear in pregnancy. Diagnosis is often clinical (e.g. Alvarado score).

Management

Uncomplicated appendicitis is treated by laparoscopic appendectomy with perioperative ABX, or ABX alone in selected cases. Perforation with generalized peritonitis requires emergency appendectomy with IV ABX. Perforation with a contained abscess is treated with IV ABX and percutaneous drainage, with appendectomy later if needed.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both are blind pouches obstructed by a fecalith, with abscess and perforation as complications. Appendicitis causes RLQ pain, and diverticulitis LLQ pain.

. RLQ pain is shared; a longer history with diarrhea and weight loss favors Crohn disease.

. Carcinoid is a cause of appendiceal obstruction in older adults, and can cause secretory diarrhea.

Ectopic pregnancy. This is the mimic to exclude, so β-hCG is obtained in anyone who could be pregnant.

GI Bleeding and Obstruction

Approach

The ligament of Treitz, at the duodenojejunal flexure, divides upper from lower GI bleeding, and obstruction announces itself with CAVO: colicky pain, abdominal distention, vomiting, and obstipation.

  • Bleeding above the ligament of TreitzUpper GI bleeding: hematemesis, coffee-ground vomit, and melena; 75% of acute GI bleeds
  • Bleeding below itLower GI bleeding: hematochezia, from the small bowel beyond the third part of the duodenum, the colon, rectum, and anus
  • ObstructionCAVO; the level of the blockage sets the pattern and the cause

Note: Hematochezia usually means a lower source, but a brisk upper bleed can cause it too, so the patient's hemodynamics matter as much as the color of the blood.

Upper versus lower bleeding

  • Upper
  • 1Esophageal varicesPortal pressure over 12 mm Hg; 11% of upper bleeds
  • 2Esophagitis24% of upper bleeds
  • 3Mallory-Weiss tearMucosal tear at the junction with the stomach after retching; 5–15%
  • 4Peptic ulcer disease Most commonH. pylori and NSAIDs; 32–36% of upper bleeds
  • 5Gastritis and duodenitis18–22% and 13%
  • 6Aortoenteric fistulaAortic aneurysm or graft eroding into the bowel
  • Lower
  • 7Small bowel5–10% of bleeds: angiodysplasia (the most common cause over 50), tumors, Crohn disease, NSAID ulcers, and Meckel diverticulum
  • 8AngiodysplasiaRight colon in older adults; aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome), ESRD, and von Willebrand disease
  • 9Colorectal cancer and polypsOccult bleeding with iron deficiency anemia on the right; obstruction on the left
  • 10Ischemic colitisPain, then bloody diarrhea, at the watershed areas
  • 11Diverticulosis Most commonPainless, large bleeds; about 64% of rectal bleeding over 50
  • 12ColitisIBD, infection, and radiation
  • 13Hemorrhoids and anal fissureBright red blood; the commonest causes in young and middle-aged adults

Telling them apart

FeatureUpperLower
BoundaryAbove the ligament of TreitzBelow it
Share of acute bleeds75%Most of the rest; 5–10% from the small bowel
Typical bloodHematemesis, coffee-ground vomit, and melenaHematochezia, bright red or maroon
BUN:creatinineOver 30, as blood is digested and absorbedUsually normal
Commonest causePeptic ulcer diseaseDiverticulosis in older adults; hemorrhoids and fissures in younger adults
Risk scoreGlasgow-Blatchford: 0–1 can go home; 6 or more needs intervention in over 50%Oakland: 8 or less is low risk
First testEGD within 24 hours, or 12 hours if varicealColonoscopy, best at 24–72 hours after preparation
If the first test fails or bleeding is briskCTACTA

Upper GI bleeding

Signs and symptoms

  • Hematemesis
  • Coffee-ground vomit
  • Melena: black, sticky, tarry stool
  • Hematochezia if brisk
  • Syncope
  • Shock
  • Iron deficiency anemia (low MCV) if chronic

Finding the cause

If there isPoints to
Epigastric pain, NSAIDs, or H. pylori
Cirrhosis, alcohol use, splenomegaly, or ascites; also portal hypertensive gastropathy
Retching or vomiting, then hematemesis; alcohol use or hiatal herniaMallory-Weiss tear
Odynophagia, heartburn, or pills taken lying down
Aspirin with clopidogrel, or anticoagulants, especially at 75 or olderAny lesion bleeds more; risk up to 17% a year on combined treatment
Prior aortic graft or aneurysm, with back painAortoenteric fistula
Weight loss and early satiety
No cause on first lookDieulafoy lesion, GAVE, hemobilia, or hemosuccus pancreaticus

Management

  1. Resuscitate2 large-bore IV lines and fluids; intubate if the airway is at risk; transfuse if Hb is under 7 g/dL
  2. Risk scoreGlasgow-Blatchford
  3. Drugs before endoscopyIV PPI; if varices are suspected, octreotide or terlipressin with ABX in cirrhosis
  4. EGDWithin 24 hours, or 12 hours if variceal, with endoscopic hemostasis
  5. After hemostasisHigh-dose PPI for 72 hours for high-risk ulcers; CTA if EGD finds no source

Lower GI bleeding

Signs and symptoms

  • Hematochezia
  • Maroon stool or clots
  • Blood on the paper or dripping (anorectal)
  • Pain on defecation (fissure)
  • Change in bowel habit or weight loss (cancer)
  • Tenesmus (proctitis)
  • Iron deficiency anemia (occult bleeding)

Finding the cause

If there isPoints to
A large, painless bleed in an older adult
An older adult with aortic stenosis, ESRD, or von Willebrand diseaseAngiodysplasia, mostly right colon
Iron deficiency anemia, weight loss, or change in bowel habitColorectal cancer: anemia on the right, obstruction on the left
Pain, then bloody diarrhea, in someone with vascular disease or shock
Bloody diarrhea with fever, travel, or a food source
Bloody diarrhea with tenesmus in a young adult
Bright red blood on the paper, painlessHemorrhoids
Pain on defecation, constipation, or strainingAnal fissure, the most common cause in infants and toddlers
A child with painless bleedingMeckel diverticulum
A child aged 6–36 months with red currant jelly stool and colicky painIntussusception
No source on EGD or colonoscopySmall bowel bleeding, most often angiodysplasia over 50: capsule endoscopy
Massive hematochezia with shockAlso consider a brisk upper source

Management

  1. ResuscitateRestore volume; check blood count and clotting
  2. Risk scoreOakland
  3. ColonoscopyGold standard in stable patients, best at 24–72 hours after preparation; hemostasis or polypectomy
  4. CTAFor ongoing or severe bleeding

Obstruction

CAVO

  • Colicky painCrampy, with peristalsis against the blockage; constant and severe if the bowel strangulates
  • Abdominal distentionGas and fluid above the blockage
  • VomitingEarly in proximal obstruction, gastric at first and bilious as the blockage lies further down; late in colonic obstruction
  • ObstipationNo stool or flatus; partial obstruction may still let some through

What the blockage does

  • AProximal distentionIncreased pressure → distention and vomiting; early, high-pitched bowel sounds
  • BFluid lossVomiting and third-spacing → dehydration, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis
  • CDistal collapseBowel beyond the blockage empties → obstipation; no gas in the rectum on x-ray
  • DStrangulationVenous outflow fails, then arterial inflow → ischemia, necrosis, perforation, and sepsis

Small versus large bowel

FeatureSmall bowelLarge bowel
Most common causePostoperative adhesions, up to 74%; then herniasColorectal cancer; then volvulus and diverticulitis
VomitingEarly, especially when proximalLate, once an incompetent ileocecal valve lets contents back
DistentionCommon; marked in complete obstructionMarked, and progressive with a competent ileocecal valve
DangerStrangulationCecal perforation with a competent ileocecal valve (closed loop)
ImagingCT, the gold standard, shows the transition point, ischemia, and perforationX-ray: dilated colon without rectal gas; CT

Causes of obstruction

If there isPoints to
Prior abdominal surgeryAdhesions, the leading cause of small bowel obstruction
A tender lump in the groin or abdominal wallIncarcerated or strangulated hernia, 2–10%
Older adult with weight loss, anemia, or alternating diarrhea and constipationColorectal cancer, usually descending or sigmoid colon
Bedbound older adult with chronic constipation; coffee bean sign on x-raySigmoid volvulus, average age 70
Distended right colon in middle ageCecal volvulus, typically in the fifth decade
Pneumobilia and a gallstone in the bowel
Crohn disease, diverticulitis, ischemia, or radiationInflammatory or fibrotic stricture
Child aged 6–36 months with red currant jelly stoolIntussusception
Newborn with bilious vomitingMalrotation with volvulus
After surgery, on opioids, or with low potassium; sparse or absent bowel soundsIleus, a functional obstruction without a transition point
Massive colonic distention without a blockage in a sick inpatientAcute colonic pseudo-obstruction; cecal perforation in 15%

Management

  1. ResuscitateIsotonic IV fluids; correct hypokalemia and alkalosis
  2. DecompressNGT, which also relieves vomiting and lowers aspiration risk
  3. Look for strangulationConstant pain, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, acidosis, or peritonitis
  4. Operate or waitSurgery for strangulation, ischemia, perforation, or complete obstruction; partial obstruction often settles without it
  • Sigmoid volvulusEndoscopic decompression, then elective sigmoid resection, because it recurs
  • Cecal volvulusRight hemicolectomy or ileocolic resection
  • IleusTreat the cause: stop opioids and correct electrolytes

Note: In ileus, bowel sounds are sparse or absent, whereas mechanical obstruction gives loud, high-pitched sounds early.
