Review article

GI bleeding and obstruction: locating the source from the blood, the patient, and the pattern of symptoms

Gastrointestinal bleeding is divided by the ligament of Treitz into upper and lower bleeding, which differ in how the blood appears, which causes dominate, how the bleeding is scored, and which test comes first. Obstruction presents with colicky pain, abdominal distention, vomiting, and obstipation, and its level and cause shape both the presentation and the danger. Here, we take a bird's eye view of the causes, signs, and initial management of upper and lower GI bleeding and of small and large bowel obstruction, and consider how they relate to the condition pages that describe each cause.

Key points

  • Upper GI bleeding, above the ligament of Treitz, makes up 75% of acute GI bleeds and presents with hematemesis, coffee-ground vomit, and melena; a BUN:creatinine ratio over 30 points upward.
  • Peptic ulcer disease is the most common upper source, followed by esophagitis, gastritis, duodenitis, varices, and Mallory-Weiss tears.
  • Diverticulosis is the most common lower source in older adults, hemorrhoids and fissures in younger adults, and anal fissure in infants and toddlers; a brisk upper bleed can also cause hematochezia.
  • Upper bleeding is scored with the Glasgow-Blatchford score and investigated by EGD within 24 hours, or 12 hours if variceal; lower bleeding is scored with the Oakland score and investigated by colonoscopy, with CTA for brisk bleeding.
  • Obstruction presents with CAVO; adhesions are the leading cause of small bowel obstruction and colorectal cancer of large bowel obstruction, and strangulation or a closed loop with a competent ileocecal valve is the main danger.

Approach

The ligament of Treitz, at the duodenojejunal flexure, divides upper from lower GI bleeding. Bleeding above it causes hematemesis, coffee-ground vomit, and melena and accounts for 75% of acute GI bleeds, whereas bleeding below it, from the small bowel beyond the third part of the duodenum, the colon, the rectum, or the anus, causes hematochezia. Hematochezia usually means a lower source, but a brisk upper bleed can cause it too, so hemodynamics matter as much as the color of the blood. Obstruction announces itself with CAVO, colicky pain, abdominal distention, vomiting, and obstipation, and the level of the blockage sets both the pattern and the likely cause.

Upper versus lower bleeding

Among upper sources, peptic ulcer disease is the most common, at 32–36%, driven by H. pylori and NSAIDs, followed by esophagitis at 24%, gastritis at 18–22%, duodenitis at 13%, esophageal varices at 11%, which form when portal pressure exceeds 12 mm Hg, and Mallory-Weiss tears at 5–15%. An aortoenteric fistula, in which an aortic aneurysm or graft erodes into the bowel, is rare but dangerous. Among lower sources, the small bowel accounts for 5–10% of bleeds, from angiodysplasia, the most common cause over 50, tumors, Crohn disease, NSAID ulcers, and Meckel diverticulum. In the colon, angiodysplasia affects the right colon of older adults and is linked to aortic stenosis in Heyde syndrome, to ESRD, and to von Willebrand disease; colorectal cancer and polyps bleed occultly, causing iron deficiency anemia on the right and obstruction on the left; ischemic colitis causes pain and then bloody diarrhea at the watershed areas; diverticulosis causes painless, large bleeds and accounts for about 64% of rectal bleeding over 50; and colitis from IBD, infection, or radiation causes bloody diarrhea. Hemorrhoids and anal fissures cause bright red blood and are the commonest causes in young and middle-aged adults.

The two differ in other ways too. Upper bleeding raises the BUN:creatinine ratio above 30, because blood is digested and absorbed, whereas lower bleeding usually leaves it normal. Upper bleeding is scored with the Glasgow-Blatchford score, on which 0–1 can go home and 6 or more predicts intervention in over half, and is investigated first by EGD within 24 hours, or 12 hours if variceal. Lower bleeding is scored with the Oakland score, on which 8 or less is low risk, and is investigated by colonoscopy, best at 24–72 hours after bowel preparation. When the first test fails or bleeding is brisk, CTA localizes the source in either.

Upper GI bleeding

Patients present with hematemesis, coffee-ground vomit, melena (black, sticky, tarry stool), hematochezia if bleeding is brisk, syncope, or shock, and chronic bleeding causes iron deficiency anemia with a low MCV. The history points to the cause: epigastric pain, NSAIDs, or H. pylori to peptic ulcer disease; cirrhosis, alcohol use, splenomegaly, or ascites to varices or portal hypertensive gastropathy; retching or vomiting followed by hematemesis, with alcohol use or a hiatal hernia, to a Mallory-Weiss tear; odynophagia, heartburn, or pills taken lying down to esophagitis; a prior aortic graft or aneurysm with back pain to an aortoenteric fistula; and weight loss and early satiety to a gastric tumor. Aspirin with clopidogrel or anticoagulants makes any lesion bleed more, with a risk of up to 17% a year on combined treatment at 75 or older. When no cause is seen, a Dieulafoy lesion, GAVE, hemobilia, or hemosuccus pancreaticus is considered.

Management begins with resuscitation through 2 large-bore IV lines, intubation if the airway is at risk, and transfusion when hemoglobin falls below 7 g/dL. The Glasgow-Blatchford score then guides care. An IV PPI is given before endoscopy, and when varices are suspected, octreotide or terlipressin with ABX in cirrhosis. EGD within 24 hours, or 12 hours if variceal, achieves hemostasis, after which high-risk ulcers receive high-dose PPI for 72 hours, and CTA is used if EGD finds no source.

Lower GI bleeding

Patients present with hematochezia, maroon stool or clots, or blood on the paper or dripping from an anorectal source; pain on defecation suggests a fissure, a change in bowel habit or weight loss suggests cancer, tenesmus suggests proctitis, and occult bleeding causes iron deficiency anemia. A large, painless bleed in an older adult suggests diverticulosis; an older adult with aortic stenosis, ESRD, or von Willebrand disease suggests angiodysplasia, mostly in the right colon; iron deficiency anemia, weight loss, or a change in bowel habit suggests colorectal cancer; pain and then bloody diarrhea in someone with vascular disease or shock suggests ischemic colitis; bloody diarrhea with fever, travel, or a food source suggests infectious colitis; and bloody diarrhea with tenesmus in a young adult suggests IBD. Painless bright red blood on the paper suggests hemorrhoids, and pain on defecation with constipation or straining suggests an anal fissure, the most common cause in infants and toddlers. In children, painless bleeding suggests Meckel diverticulum, and red currant jelly stool with colicky pain at 6–36 months suggests intussusception. When EGD and colonoscopy find nothing, the source is usually in the small bowel, most often angiodysplasia over 50, and capsule endoscopy follows; massive hematochezia with shock should also raise the possibility of a brisk upper source.

Management again begins with restoring volume and checking the blood count and clotting. The Oakland score guides admission, colonoscopy in stable patients, best performed at 24–72 hours after preparation, diagnoses and treats the source by hemostasis or polypectomy, and CTA is used for ongoing or severe bleeding.

Obstruction

Obstruction causes colicky, crampy pain as peristalsis works against the blockage, which becomes constant and severe if the bowel strangulates; abdominal distention from gas and fluid above the blockage; vomiting, which comes early in proximal obstruction, gastric at first and bilious as the blockage lies further down, and late in colonic obstruction; and obstipation, though partial obstruction may still let some stool and flatus through. Above the blockage, rising pressure causes distention and vomiting, with loud, high-pitched bowel sounds early. Vomiting and third-spacing of fluid cause dehydration, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Beyond the blockage, the bowel empties, causing obstipation and an absence of rectal gas on x-ray. If the bowel strangulates, venous outflow fails and then arterial inflow, leading to ischemia, necrosis, perforation, and sepsis.

Small bowel obstruction is most often caused by postoperative adhesions, in up to 74%, and then hernias; vomiting comes early, especially when the blockage is proximal; distention is common and marked when obstruction is complete; strangulation is the main danger; and CT is the gold standard, showing the transition point, ischemia, and perforation. Large bowel obstruction is most often caused by colorectal cancer, followed by volvulus and diverticulitis; vomiting comes late, once an incompetent ileocecal valve lets contents back into the small bowel; distention is marked and progressive when the valve is competent, creating a closed loop at risk of cecal perforation; and x-rays show a dilated colon without rectal gas, followed by CT.

Causes of obstruction

Prior abdominal surgery points to adhesions, the leading cause of small bowel obstruction, and a tender lump in the groin or abdominal wall to an incarcerated or strangulated hernia, which accounts for 2–10%. An older adult with weight loss, anemia, or alternating diarrhea and constipation suggests colorectal cancer, usually of the descending or sigmoid colon. A bedbound older adult with chronic constipation and a coffee bean sign on x-ray suggests sigmoid volvulus, at an average age of 70, whereas a distended right colon in middle age suggests cecal volvulus, typically in the fifth decade. Pneumobilia with a gallstone in the bowel suggests gallstone ileus; Crohn disease, diverticulitis, ischemia, or radiation can cause inflammatory or fibrotic strictures; red currant jelly stool at 6–36 months suggests intussusception; and bilious vomiting in a newborn suggests malrotation with volvulus. Ileus, a functional obstruction without a transition point, follows surgery, opioids, or low potassium and gives sparse or absent bowel sounds, and acute colonic pseudo-obstruction causes massive colonic distention without a blockage in sick inpatients, with cecal perforation in 15%.

Management begins with isotonic IV fluids, correction of hypokalemia and alkalosis, and decompression by nasogastric tube, which also relieves vomiting and lowers the risk of aspiration. Strangulation is sought through constant pain, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, acidosis, or peritonitis. Surgery is needed for strangulation, ischemia, perforation, or complete obstruction, whereas partial obstruction often settles without it. Sigmoid volvulus is decompressed endoscopically and then resected electively, because it recurs; cecal volvulus is treated by right hemicolectomy or ileocolic resection; and ileus is treated by addressing its cause, stopping opioids and correcting electrolytes. In ileus, bowel sounds are sparse or absent, whereas mechanical obstruction gives loud, high-pitched sounds early.

Relationships to other conditions

and . Both cause upper GI bleeding with hematemesis and melena and are both investigated by urgent EGD, but their drugs differ: ulcers are treated with high-dose PPI, whereas suspected varices add octreotide or terlipressin and ABX in cirrhosis. Cirrhosis, alcohol use, and splenomegaly favor varices, and NSAIDs and epigastric pain favor ulcers.

and . Both cause lower GI bleeding in older adults, but diverticular bleeding is painless and large, whereas ischemic colitis brings pain first and then bloody diarrhea at the watershed areas, often after shock or in vascular disease.

. Colicky pain with distention, vomiting, and obstipation points to obstruction, whereas constant, severe pain with peritonitis signals strangulation or perforation, the same features that turn the approach to abdominal pain toward surgery.

The location of pain narrows the organs involved, its character and triggers narrow the process, signs beyond the abdomen and specific examination findings point to particular conditions, and tests then confirm the leading diagnosis.

Review article

Localizing abdominal pain: from where it hurts to the test that confirms it

Abdominal pain is localized by its site, its character and triggers, the signs it brings beyond the abdomen, and specific examination findings, and is confirmed by targeted bloods, stool tests, imaging, and endoscopy. Dangerous causes outside the gut must be excluded early. Here, we review how each step narrows the differential and which test answers each question.

Key points

  • Visceral pain is dull and poorly localized; somatoparietal pain from the parietal peritoneum is sharp and localized.
  • Pain out of proportion to the examination suggests acute mesenteric ischemia.
  • Myocardial infarction, ruptured AAA, aortic dissection, ectopic pregnancy, and torsion must be excluded early.
  • An upright CXR is the first test for suspected perforation, and RUQ ultrasound for RUQ pain.

Approach

The location of pain narrows the organs involved, its character and triggers narrow the process, signs beyond the abdomen and specific examination findings point to particular conditions, and tests confirm the leading diagnosis. Visceral pain arises from stretch of hollow organs, with receptors in the serosa, mesentery, muscle, and mucosa, and is dull and poorly localized. Somatoparietal pain arises from inflamed or stretched parietal peritoneum and is sharp and localized, as when appendicitis reaches the RLQ. Referred pain occurs when visceral and somatic nerves share a spinal level, as in left shoulder pain with splenic rupture.

Location

Right upper quadrant pain suggests biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, cholangitis, acute hepatitis and liver abscess, and Budd-Chiari syndrome and portal vein thrombosis. Epigastric pain suggests peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, GERD, and acute and chronic pancreatitis; exclude myocardial infarction. Left upper quadrant pain suggests splenic infarct, abscess, or rupture (Kehr sign: left shoulder pain); pancreatitis. Periumbilical pain suggests early appendicitis, before it localizes; embolism to the proximal SMA (mesenteric ischemia). Right lower quadrant pain suggests appendicitis at McBurney point, terminal ileal Crohn disease, and right-sided diverticulitis; ectopic pregnancy and ovarian torsion. Suprapubic and pelvic pain suggests ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, ovarian or testicular torsion, urinary tract infection or obstruction, and incarcerated hernia. Left lower quadrant pain suggests diverticulitis, ischemic colitis, and ulcerative colitis. Diffuse pain suggests acute mesenteric ischemia, bowel obstruction, perforation with peritonitis, and ruptured AAA; pneumonia or PE can cause diffuse upper pain.

Character of pain

Colicky RUQ or epigastric pain after a fatty meal, gone within 6 hours; normal LFTs, no fever points to biliary colic. RUQ pain over 6 hours, fever, and Murphy sign points to acute cholecystitis. Fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice (Charcot triad), with hypotension and confusion in Reynolds pentad points to ascending cholangitis. Burning epigastric pain, worse with eating points to gastric ulcer. Burning epigastric pain, better with eating, worse fasting and at night points to duodenal ulcer. Heartburn and regurgitation points to GERD. Severe epigastric or LUQ pain radiating to the back, with vomiting points to acute pancreatitis. Chronic epigastric pain, better leaning forward, with steatorrhea points to chronic pancreatitis. Periumbilical pain moving to the RLQ over 12–24 hours, anorexia, then vomiting points to appendicitis. Sudden, severe pain out of proportion to the examination; the patient writhes points to acute mesenteric ischemia. Pain 15–30 minutes after meals, lasting up to 4 hours, with fear of eating and weight loss points to chronic mesenteric ischemia. LLQ pain, fever, and leukocytosis points to diverticulitis. LLQ pain and hematochezia after shock or vasopressors points to ischemic colitis. RLQ pain, chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and perianal disease points to crohn disease. Bloody diarrhea with tenesmus points to ulcerative colitis. Recurrent pain related to defecation, with changes in stool frequency or appearance points to IBS. Pain, vomiting, obstipation, and distention points to bowel obstruction, including gallstone ileus. Sudden pain, then a rigid abdomen; the patient lies still points to perforation with peritonitis, such as a perforated ulcer. Painless rectal bleeding points to diverticular bleeding; under age 2, Meckel diverticulum.

Causes outside the gut

Epigastric pain with cardiac risk factors, dyspnea, sweating, or exertional symptoms suggests myocardial infarction, evaluated with ECG and troponin. Abdominal, back, or flank pain with hypotension and a pulsatile mass suggests ruptured AAA, evaluated with bedside ultrasound if unstable; CT if stable. Sharp, tearing pain with pulse deficits suggests aortic dissection, evaluated with CT angiogram of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Pain and vaginal bleeding 6–8 weeks after the last period suggests ectopic pregnancy, evaluated with β-hCG, then transvaginal ultrasound. Severe pelvic pain and vomiting with an adnexal mass suggests ovarian torsion, evaluated with pelvic ultrasound. Severe testicular and lower abdominal pain in a young male suggests testicular torsion, evaluated with testicular examination; scrotal ultrasound. LUQ pain after trauma, referred to the left shoulder suggests splenic rupture (Kehr sign), evaluated with imaging, with resuscitation.

Signs beyond the abdomen

Jaundice points to biliary obstruction, hepatitis, or hemolysis; see Reading Liver Function Tests. Painless jaundice with a palpable, nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier law) points to periampullary or biliary malignancy. Dark urine, pale stools, and pruritus points to cholestasis, such as a bile duct stone. Pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum, uveitis, arthralgia, or oral aphthous ulcers points to IBD; pyoderma gangrenosum accompanies ulcerative colitis in 5–12% and Crohn disease in 1–2%. Dermatitis herpetiformis points to celiac disease. Angular cheilitis or a smooth, pale tongue; a beefy, red tongue points to iron deficiency; B12 or folate deficiency, as in malabsorption or autoimmune gastritis. Virchow node, Sister Mary Joseph nodule, or Krukenberg tumor points to metastatic gastric cancer. Acanthosis nigricans or Trousseau syndrome points to gastric cancer, as a paraneoplastic sign. Cullen sign (periumbilical bruising) or Grey Turner sign (flank bruising) points to intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal bleeding, as in necrotizing pancreatitis. Asterixis, fetor hepaticus, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, ascites, or caput medusae points to cirrhosis and liver failure. Kayser-Fleischer rings points to wilson disease. Bronze skin with diabetes points to hemochromatosis. Xanthelasma points to chronic cholestasis, such as PBC. Flushing, wheezing, and tricuspid valve disease points to carcinoid syndrome. Migratory large-joint arthralgia with weight loss and diarrhea points to whipple disease. Pneumaturia and fecaluria points to enterovesical fistula, from diverticulitis or Crohn disease.

Examination

Distention and visible peristalsis suggests bowel obstruction. Dilated veins draining away from the umbilicus suggests portal hypertension. Pulsatile mass suggests AAA. High-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds suggests ileus or early small bowel obstruction. Absent bowel sounds suggests late obstruction, intestinal ischemia, ileus, or peritonitis. Shifting dullness suggests ascites. Murphy sign: inspiration stops as the gallbladder meets the hand suggests acute cholecystitis. Tenderness at McBurney point, a third of the way from the ASIS to the umbilicus suggests appendicitis. Rovsing sign: LLQ pressure causes RLQ pain suggests appendicitis. Psoas sign: pain on passive extension of the right hip suggests retrocecal appendicitis. Obturator sign: pain on internally rotating the flexed right hip; sensitivity only 8% suggests pelvic appendicitis or abscess. Rebound tenderness, involuntary guarding, or rigidity suggests peritonitis. Succussion splash suggests delayed gastric emptying, as in gastric outlet obstruction. Rectal examination suggests GI bleeding; adds little in appendicitis. Pelvic or testicular examination suggests pelvic disease or torsion in lower abdominal pain.

Investigations

For any significant abdominal pain, obtain FBC, electrolytes, creatinine, glucose, calcium, LFTs, and lipase; β-hCG if pregnancy is possible; urinalysis. For peritonitis, sepsis, or suspected perforation, obtain upright CXR first, for free air; blood cultures; then CT AP with contrast. For RUQ pain, obtain LFTs and lipase; RUQ ultrasound first; HIDA if cholecystitis is unclear; MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound for a bile duct stone. For epigastric pain, obtain ECG and troponin if cardiac risk; lipase; EGD for suspected ulcer; urea breath test or stool antigen for H. pylori. For suspected appendicitis, diverticulitis, or obstruction, obtain CT AP with contrast in adults; ultrasound first in children and pregnancy. For suspected mesenteric ischemia, obtain CT angiogram; lactate rises only late (Intestinal Ischemia). For chronic diarrhea or suspected IBD, obtain fecal calprotectin and CRP; stool culture, O&P, and C. difficile; colonoscopy with biopsy (IBD). For suspected malabsorption, obtain tTG-IgA with total IgA, then duodenal biopsy; fecal elastase; hydrogen breath test (Malabsorption). For painless rectal bleeding in a young child, obtain meckel scan (Diverticular Diseases). EGD is used for persistent upper abdominal pain or pain with alarm features; persistent vomiting; dysphagia or odynophagia; refractory GERD and Barrett surveillance; upper GI bleeding; chronic diarrhea or malabsorption; iron deficiency anemia with a suspected upper source. Colonoscopy is used for rectal bleeding, changed bowel habit, weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, positive FOBT, and chronic diarrhea (with biopsies); screening from age 45–50. Not needed for uncomplicated abdominal pain or diarrhea under 4 weeks; avoided in peritonitis and acute diverticulitis. ERCP is used for mainly therapeutic: removing bile duct stones, stenting strictures, and draining cholangitis.

Relationships to other conditions

. Jaundice and RUQ pain lead to the LFT pattern, which separates hepatocellular, cholestatic, and hemolytic causes.

. Its migrating pain shows the shift from visceral to somatoparietal pain.

. Pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen distinguishes it from peritonitis, where the abdomen is rigid.

Reading Liver Function Tests

Approach

Most of the panel measures injury or cholestasis rather than function: AST and ALT reflect hepatocyte injury, ALP and GGT reflect bile flow, and bilirubin, albumin, and INR reflect what the liver can still do. The pattern matters more than any single value, and trends matter more than a single result.

  1. PatternHepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed
  2. DegreeHow many times the ULN
  3. Synthetic functionBilirubin, albumin, INR
  4. Clinical pictureSymptoms and signs
  5. Targeted testsSerology, imaging

Normal LFTs do not exclude liver disease: MASLD, fibrosis, and compensated cirrhosis can all have normal enzymes.

What each test measures

TestComes fromRises or falls inNormal range
ALTHepatocyte cytosol; the most liver-specificHepatocellular injury4–36 IU/L

BilirubinHeme breakdown; conjugated by UGT1A1 in hepatocytesHemolysis, conjugation defects, liver injury, or obstruction2–17 µmol/L; direct 0–6
AlbuminMade only by the liver; half-life 14–21 daysFalls slowly in chronic liver disease35–50 g/L
PT/INRClotting factors made by the liver; II, VII, IX, and X need vitamin KRises quickly when synthesis failsPT 10.9–12.5 s

How high

Degree of AST or ALT riseTypical causes
Mild: under 5 × ULNMASLD; alcohol, often with AST:ALT of 2:1 or more; chronic hepatitis B or C; drugs such as statins, NSAIDs, and antiepileptics; early hemochromatosis; muscle and thyroid disease

Bilirubin: where the block is

  • 1Too much hemeUnconjugated: hemolysis, a large hematoma, or ineffective erythropoiesis (megaloblastic or sideroblastic anemia); rarely over 4 mg/dL
  • 2Uptake and conjugationUnconjugated: Gilbert syndrome (UGT1A1 at 30–50%; jaundice with fasting, illness, menstruation, or exertion; no treatment), Crigler-Najjar syndrome, and drugs that block UGT1A1
  • 3Hepatocyte injury and excretion into bileConjugated, often mixed: hepatitis, cirrhosis, drugs, and ; Dubin-Johnson syndrome (MRP2; black liver) and Rotor syndrome (no pigment)
  • 4Bile duct obstructionConjugated, with high ALP and GGT: , strictures, , and → pale stools, dark urine, and pruritus

In urine and stool

  1. Conjugated bilirubin in bileReaches the distal ileum and colon
  2. UrobilinogenGut bacteria deconjugate and reduce it; it is colorless
  3. Urobilin and stercobilinOxidized, they turn stool orange-brown
  4. Urine10–20% is reabsorbed, and some urobilin reaches the urine, giving it its yellow color
  • UrineOnly conjugated bilirubin is water soluble, so only it darkens urine; unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin, so bilirubin in urine means a conjugated rise
  • StoolStool color depends on bilirubin reaching the gut, so when bile flow stops, stools turn pale

Review article

Reading liver function tests: patterns of injury, cholestasis, and failing function

The liver panel mostly measures injury and cholestasis rather than function: AST and ALT reflect hepatocyte injury, ALP and GGT reflect bile flow, and bilirubin, albumin, and INR reflect synthetic reserve. The pattern, the degree of rise, and the trend, read with the clinical picture, point to the cause. Here, we review each test, the main patterns, the bilirubin pathway, and how combinations of results and signs narrow the differential.

Key points

  • ALT is the most liver-specific enzyme; AST also comes from muscle, heart, and red cells.
  • A high ALP with a normal GGT suggests bone rather than liver.
  • Massive rises over 10000 IU/L suggest paracetamol toxicity or profound ischemia.
  • Falling AST and ALT with rising bilirubin and INR mean a failing liver, not recovery.

Approach

Most of the panel measures injury or cholestasis rather than function: AST and ALT reflect hepatocyte injury, ALP and GGT reflect bile flow, and bilirubin, albumin, and INR reflect what the liver can still do. The pattern matters more than any single value, and trends more than a single result. Normal LFTs do not exclude liver disease, since MASLD, fibrosis, and compensated cirrhosis can all have normal enzymes.

The tests

ALT comes from hepatocyte cytosol; the most liver-specific, changes in hepatocellular injury, and has a normal range of 4–36 IU/L. AST comes from liver, muscle, heart, kidney, brain, and red cells; cytosol and mitochondria, changes in hepatocellular injury, alcohol, muscle injury, and hemolysis, and has a normal range of 5–30 IU/L. ALP comes from canalicular membrane and bile duct epithelium; also bone, placenta, and intestine, changes in cholestasis; bone disease, pregnancy, and growth, and has a normal range of 30–120 IU/L. GGT comes from bile ducts; induced by alcohol and drugs, changes in confirms that a high ALP comes from the liver, and has a normal range of 6–50 IU/L. Bilirubin comes from heme breakdown; conjugated by UGT1A1 in hepatocytes, changes in hemolysis, conjugation defects, liver injury, or obstruction, and has a normal range of 2–17 µmol/L; direct 0–6. Albumin comes from made only by the liver; half-life 14–21 days, changes in falls slowly in chronic liver disease, and has a normal range of 35–50 g/L. PT/INR comes from clotting factors made by the liver; II, VII, IX, and X need vitamin K, changes in rises quickly when synthesis fails, and has a normal range of PT 10.9–12.5 s.

Patterns

In the hepatocellular pattern, AST and ALT rise much more than ALP; causes include ALT higher: viral hepatitis, MASLD, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, ischemic hepatitis and acute Budd-Chiari syndrome, autoimmune hepatitis, drugs and toxins, and celiac disease. AST higher: alcohol, cirrhosis, and nonhepatic causes (hemolysis, myopathy, thyroid disease, exercise). In the cholestatic pattern, ALP and GGT rise, often with bilirubin, more than AST and ALT; causes include bile duct obstruction, PBC and PSC, drugs, infiltration (sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, lymphoma), metastases, and cystic fibrosis. In the mixed pattern, both rise; causes include overlapping processes, or a pattern changing over time. In the isolated bilirubin pattern, bilirubin alone; fractionate it; causes include unconjugated: hemolysis or Gilbert syndrome. Conjugated: Dubin-Johnson or Rotor syndrome. In the isolated ALP pattern, ALP alone; check GGT; causes include normal GGT: bone, pregnancy, or growth. High GGT: a hepatobiliary source. In the synthetic failure pattern, low albumin, high INR, and rising bilirubin; causes include acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis; AST and ALT may already be falling. Falling AST and ALT with rising bilirubin and INR mean a failing liver, not recovery.

Degree of rise

A mild rise, under 5 × ULN suggests MASLD; alcohol, often with AST:ALT of 2:1 or more; chronic hepatitis B or C; drugs such as statins, NSAIDs, and antiepileptics; early hemochromatosis; muscle and thyroid disease. A moderate rise, 5–15 × ULN suggests acute viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and drug-induced injury; alcoholic hepatitis rarely exceeds 300–500 IU/L. A severe rise, over 15 × ULN suggests acute hepatitis A, B, or E; severe drug injury; toxins such as Amanita phalloides; ischemic hepatitis. A massive rise, over 10000 IU/L suggests paracetamol toxicity, profound ischemia after cardiac arrest or shock, and, rarely, HSV hepatitis in pregnancy or immunocompromise.

Bilirubin

Bilirubin moves from red cells to the liver, where UGT1A1 conjugates it, then into bile and the gut, where bacteria form urobilinogen and stercobilin. Excess heme from hemolysis, a large hematoma, or ineffective erythropoiesis raises unconjugated bilirubin, rarely above 4 mg/dL. Defective uptake and conjugation also raise unconjugated bilirubin, as in Gilbert syndrome, with UGT1A1 at 30–50% and jaundice after fasting, illness, menstruation, or exertion that needs no treatment, in Crigler-Najjar syndrome, and with drugs that block UGT1A1. Hepatocyte injury and defective excretion raise conjugated, often mixed, bilirubin, as in hepatitis, cirrhosis, drugs, and PBC, and in Dubin-Johnson syndrome (MRP2, with a black liver) and Rotor syndrome (without pigment). Bile duct obstruction by stones, strictures, PSC, or tumors raises conjugated bilirubin with ALP and GGT, causing pale stools, dark urine, and pruritus. Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and darkens urine, whereas unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and does not, so bilirubin in urine means a conjugated rise.

In the distal ileum and colon, bacteria deconjugate and reduce conjugated bilirubin to colorless urobilinogen, which is oxidized to urobilin and stercobilin and turns stool orange-brown; 10–20% is reabsorbed, and some urobilin reaches the urine, giving it its yellow color. Urine and stool color therefore point to where bilirubin handling fails. Jaundice with normal urine and stool, acholuric jaundice, means an unconjugated rise from hemolysis, Gilbert syndrome, or Crigler-Najjar syndrome. Dark, tea- or cola-colored urine with normal or slightly pale stool means a conjugated rise from hepatocyte injury, as in hepatitis, cirrhosis, drugs, and the Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndromes, whereas dark urine with pale, clay-colored or light gray acholic stool and pruritus means bile duct obstruction or cholestasis from stones, strictures, PSC, or tumors, with high ALP and GGT. Pale, greasy, foul-smelling stool that floats is steatorrhea, from too few bile salts in obstruction or from pancreatic insufficiency. On urine dipstick, bilirubin means a conjugated rise, often before jaundice is visible; more urobilinogen means more bilirubin made, as in hemolysis, more reabsorbed from the colon, or less cleared by a diseased liver; and absent urobilinogen means complete obstruction, since no bilirubin reaches the gut to form it. Red or brown urine that is negative for bilirubin suggests hemoglobin from intravascular hemolysis. Black, tarry stool is melena from upper GI bleeding rather than a liver test pattern, and pale stool with dark urine beyond 2 weeks of age in an infant suggests biliary atresia.

Synthetic function

Albumin: half-life 14–21 days, so it falls in chronic, not acute, liver disease; also low in malnutrition, inflammation, nephrotic syndrome, burns, sepsis, and protein-losing enteropathy. PT/INR: clotting factors have short half-lives, so it rises quickly; also prolonged by vitamin K deficiency, warfarin, DIC, and antiphospholipid antibodies. With a vitamin K test, INR that corrects with parenteral vitamin K points to deficiency, as in malabsorption; failure to correct means severe hepatocellular dysfunction. Bilirubin, albumin, and INR feed the Child-Pugh and MELD scores.

Combining results with the picture

Cholestatic pattern with fever, RUQ pain, and jaundice suggests ascending cholangitis, and calls for blood cultures, ultrasound, then ERCP. Cholestatic pattern with RUQ pain and a dilated CBD suggests choledocholithiasis, and calls for MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound; ERCP if likelihood is high. Cholestatic pattern with painless jaundice, weight loss, and a palpable gallbladder suggests periampullary or biliary malignancy, and calls for CT or MRCP; CA 19-9. Cholestatic pattern with itch and fatigue in a middle-aged woman suggests PBC, and calls for AMA, positive in over 90%. Cholestatic pattern with ulcerative colitis suggests PSC, and calls for MRCP: beaded ducts; p-ANCA. AST:ALT of 2:1 or more with raised GGT and heavy drinking suggests alcohol-related liver disease, and calls for maddrey score if alcoholic hepatitis. Very high ALT after paracetamol ingestion suggests paracetamol toxicity, and calls for paracetamol level; NAC. ALT over 1000 after shock, cardiac arrest, or heart failure suggests ischemic hepatitis, and calls for treat the low-flow state. ALT-predominant rise with viral risk factors suggests viral hepatitis, and calls for HAV IgM, HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, and HCV antibody. ALT-predominant rise in a young woman with high IgG suggests autoimmune hepatitis, and calls for ANA and ASMA (type 1); anti-LKM1 (type 2). Mild rise with obesity, diabetes, or dyslipidemia suggests MASLD, and calls for ultrasound; fibrosis score such as FIB-4. Hepatocellular rise with diabetes, bronze skin, or arthropathy suggests hemochromatosis, and calls for transferrin saturation over 45%, then ferritin and HFE testing. Hepatocellular rise in a young patient with tremor, psychiatric change, or Kayser-Fleischer rings suggests wilson disease, and calls for ceruloplasmin. Hepatocellular rise with early lower-lobe emphysema suggests α1-antitrypsin deficiency, and calls for α1-antitrypsin level. Raised transaminases and hypoglycemia in the third trimester suggests acute fatty liver of pregnancy, and calls for swansea criteria. Isolated unconjugated bilirubin after fasting or illness, with normal enzymes and FBC suggests gilbert syndrome, and calls for no treatment needed. Unconjugated bilirubin with anemia suggests hemolysis, and calls for FBC and blood film. High INR and encephalopathy within 26 weeks, with no prior liver disease suggests acute liver failure, and calls for find the cause; transplant referral. Low albumin, high INR, ascites, and varices suggests cirrhosis, and calls for child-Pugh and MELD scores.

Relationships to other conditions

. RUQ pain and jaundice lead here, and the LFT pattern decides between imaging the ducts and testing for hepatitis.

. Bilirubin, albumin, and INR measure the failing liver and feed the Child-Pugh and MELD scores.

. A cholestatic pattern with a dilated duct is its signature.
